In the human body: oxygen 65%, carbon 18.5%, hydrogen 9.5%, nitrogen 3.3%. Macromolecules are made of many repeating monomer units and have high molecular weight; micromolecules are individual units with low molecular weight. A mammalian cell is about: water 70%, protein 18%, carbohydrate 4%, lipids 3%, RNA 1.1%, DNA 0.25%, other organic substances 2% and inorganic ions 1%.

The four fundamental molecules: carbohydrates (C, H, O) provide fuel, store reserve food, and cellulose and chitin are structural; proteins (units: amino acids) are the most abundant organic compounds in protoplasm — enzymes, haemoglobin carrying O₂, myoglobin storing O₂, hormones and antibodies; lipids are hydrophobic, store food and build organelles and plasma membranes; nucleic acids (unit: nucleotide) — DNA is hereditary material and RNAs synthesise proteins under its instructions.

Key Points

  • Biochemistry studies biological molecules; molecular biology studies macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids.
  • Hydrogen bonds are weak and dotted; covalent bonds share electrons; ionic bonds transfer electrons.
  • Hydrophilic substances dissolve in water; hydrophobic substances cluster away from water.
  • H, C, O, N, S and P make about 99% of living mass.
  • The four fundamental molecules are carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

mcqs.q: What is biochemistry the study of?
options: Biological molecules, their processing and their significance for living organisms
Only the physical structure of rocks and minerals
Only the behaviour of whole animal populations
Only the classification of plants by their flowers
mcqs.why: The notes define biochemistry as the study of biological molecules, their processing and significance for living organisms, important for agriculture, pharmaceuticals, genetics and biotechnology.

mcqs.q: What does molecular biology deal with?
options: The movement of water through soil and rocks only
The structure and function of macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids, explaining gene expression, DNA replication, transcription and translation
The naming of newly discovered animal species only
The measurement of blood pressure in hospital patients
mcqs.why: Molecular biology deals with the structure and function of macromolecules such as proteins and nucleic acids, and explains gene expression, DNA replication, transcription and translation.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes a hydrogen bond?
options: A strong bond in which two atoms share pairs of electrons equally
A bond formed when one atom donates electrons completely to another atom
A weak attraction between hydrogen and a negatively charged atom such as oxygen, chlorine or fluorine, with no sharing of electrons, shown as a dotted line
A bond that only occurs between two carbon atoms in a chain
mcqs.why: A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction between hydrogen and a negatively charged atom such as oxygen, chlorine or fluorine, with no sharing of electrons; alone weak, in large numbers in water, proteins and DNA it creates strong attraction.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of a covalent bond situation described in the notes?
options: Sodium donating an electron to chloride to form ions
Hydrogen being attracted to fluorine without any electron sharing
Oil molecules clustering together away from water
Oxygen sharing electrons with two hydrogens in a water molecule
mcqs.why: In a covalent bond two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons; the notes give oxygen sharing with two hydrogens in water, and also carbon-carbon, peptide and glycosidic bonds.

mcqs.q: How is an ionic bond formed, according to the notes?
options: One atom donates electrons to another, creating positive and negative ions that attract each other, as with sodium and chloride
Two atoms share a pair of electrons between their nuclei
A hydrogen atom is attracted to a negatively charged atom by a dotted-line bond
Nonpolar molecules cluster together to avoid contact with water
mcqs.why: An ionic bond forms when one atom donates electrons to another, creating positive and negative ions that attract; it is less common in biological molecules but occurs between some amino acids in proteins and in enzyme-substrate interaction.

mcqs.q: Which substances are given as examples of hydrophilic substances?
options: Oils and fats, which cluster together away from water
Salts, sugars and some amino acids, which dissolve in water
Waxes, which are completely insoluble in water
The fatty acid tails of phospholipids in a membrane
mcqs.why: Hydrophilic means water-loving: polar or charged substances such as salts, sugars and some amino acids dissolve in water and form hydrogen or ionic interactions with it.

mcqs.q: In the plasma membrane, how are phospholipids arranged in relation to water?
options: Their hydrophobic heads face the water while their hydrophilic tails face away
Both heads and tails face the water on the outside of the membrane
Their hydrophilic heads face the water while their hydrophobic tails face away from the water
Both heads and tails turn inward so neither part touches water
mcqs.why: The notes state that in the plasma membrane phospholipid heads are hydrophilic and face water, while the tails are hydrophobic and face away from water.

mcqs.q: Which six elements make up about 99% of living mass?
options: Hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, calcium, iron and sodium
Carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, potassium, chlorine and zinc
Oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, magnesium, copper and iodine
Hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur and phosphorus
mcqs.why: Living organisms are composed of 25 elements, only 16 essential for life, and the six most common — hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur and phosphorus — are about 99% of living mass.

mcqs.q: What percentage of the human body is oxygen, as given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give the human body composition as oxygen 65%, carbon 18.5%, hydrogen 9.5% and nitrogen 3.3%, so oxygen alone accounts for 65%.

mcqs.q: In a mammalian cell, what percentage is protein?
mcqs.why: A mammalian cell is about water 70%, protein 18%, carbohydrate 4%, lipids 3%, RNA 1.1%, DNA 0.25%, other organic substances 2% and inorganic ions 1%, so protein is 18%.

lessons.title: Condensation, Hydrolysis and Properties of Water
lessons.notes_html:
Polymers are made and broken by two opposite reactions, condensation and hydrolysis. Water is the most abundant component of protoplasm — bodies contain about 70–90% water — and without it life cannot exist.

3.4 Condensation and Hydrolysis

  • Condensation (dehydration synthesis) — small molecules join to form a large molecule or polymer; water is released and energy is used. An OH is removed from one monomer and an H⁺ from the other. Example: disaccharides and polysaccharides from monosaccharides (glucose, galactose, fructose).
  • Hydrolysis (hydration) — breakdown of a polymer into monomers; water is used, one monomer gets H⁺ and the other OH⁻, with the help of enzymes, and energy is released when a bond is broken.

Condensation joins monomers and removes water; hydrolysis uses water to split polymers.

3.5 Properties of Water

  • High polarity — sharing of electrons is fairly equal in a nonpolar bond (O₂, N₂) but not in a polar covalent bond. Water is polar: hydrogens carry a slight positive charge, oxygen a slight negative charge (angle 104.5°). It is a universal solvent for polar substances, ionic compounds, electrolytes and molecules with charged groups, such as sugar.
  • Hydrogen bonding — attraction between hydrogen covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom (oxygen, nitrogen, fluorine) and another polar group. Each water molecule can form four hydrogen bonds. Water is liquid at suitable temperature, boils at 100°C and freezes at 0°C.
  • High specific heat — heat needed to raise 1 gram of water by 1°C (15°C to 16°C) is one calorie or 4.18 joules per gram per degree. Most energy is used breaking hydrogen bonds, so temperature changes slowly; body and environmental temperature stay stable — water is a thermostabilizer. Bone and seed contain only 20% water, brain 85%, blood 88% and jellyfish 99%.
  • High heat of vaporisation — heat to convert 1 ml of liquid to vapour without changing temperature; for water 574 kcal/kg, due to hydrogen bonds. Important in sweating, panting and transpiration, and in moderating environmental temperature.
  • Cohesion and adhesion — cohesion is attraction between similar molecules, adhesion between dissimilar molecules. Water molecules stick together and flow together, and stick to walls such as the xylem wall, due to hydrogen bonding and polarity.
  • Hydrophobic exclusion — contact area between water and hydrophobic substances is reduced; oil drops on water join into a single drop. This maintains the integrity of the lipid bilayer of plasma membranes.
  • Ionization — a molecule gains or loses electrons to form ions. Water releases equal H⁺ and OH⁻ ions, which take part in metabolism and maintain pH. H⁺ exists as hydronium (H₃O⁺), a hydrogen ion bound to a water molecule; hydronium controls pH, enzyme activity and energy production.
  • Lower density of ice — density decreases below 4°C, so ice is lighter than water and floats; water is the only substance whose solid is less dense than its liquid, because it has maximum hydrogen bonds. Ice insulates water below and increases survival in winter.

Key Points

  • Condensation joins monomers, releases water and uses energy; hydrolysis splits polymers, uses water and releases energy.
  • Water is polar, forms four hydrogen bonds per molecule, boils at 100°C and freezes at 0°C.
  • High specific heat and heat of vaporisation keep temperatures stable and cool the body.
  • Ice is less dense than water, floats, and insulates water below it.

mcqs.q: What happens in a condensation (dehydration synthesis) reaction?
options: A polymer is split into monomers, water is used and energy is released
Small molecules join to form a large molecule or polymer, water is released and energy is used
Water is added across a bond so that a disaccharide becomes two monosaccharides
Monomers are broken down by enzymes into carbon dioxide and water
mcqs.why: In condensation an OH is removed from one monomer and an H from the other, small molecules join into a polymer, water is released and energy is used — the opposite of hydrolysis.

mcqs.q: What happens during hydrolysis of a polymer?
options: Water is released as monomers join together and energy is used up
Two monosaccharides join to form a disaccharide plus water
Water is used to split the polymer into monomers, one monomer receiving H and the other OH, with the help of enzymes, and energy is released when a bond is broken
A polymer is built up without any involvement of water molecules
mcqs.why: Hydrolysis is the breakdown of a polymer into monomers: water is used, one monomer gets H and the other OH, enzymes help, and energy is released when a bond is broken.

mcqs.q: What is the bond angle in a water molecule and how are its charges distributed?
options: 180 degrees, with oxygen positive and both hydrogens negative
90 degrees, with all three atoms carrying equal charges
120 degrees, with no charge difference between the atoms
104.5 degrees, with the hydrogens carrying a slight positive charge and oxygen a slight negative charge
mcqs.why: Water is polar: the angle is 104.5 degrees, hydrogens carry a slight positive charge and oxygen a slight negative charge, making water a universal solvent for polar and ionic substances.

mcqs.q: How many hydrogen bonds can each water molecule form?
options: Four hydrogen bonds
One hydrogen bond
Two hydrogen bonds
Six hydrogen bonds
mcqs.why: The notes state each water molecule can form four hydrogen bonds; this hydrogen bonding underlies water's high specific heat, cohesion and the lower density of ice.

mcqs.q: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of 5 grams of water by 1 degree Celsius?
options: 1 calorie, which is 4.18 joules
5 calories, which is 20.9 joules
50 calories, which is 209 joules
0.5 calories, which is 2.09 joules
mcqs.why: Working: the specific heat of water is 1 calorie (4.18 joules) per gram per degree. For 5 g raised by 1 degree: 5 x 1 = 5 calories, and 5 x 4.18 = 20.9 joules. Most of this energy is used breaking hydrogen bonds, so temperature changes slowly.

mcqs.q: What is the heat of vaporisation of water and why does it matter?
options: 100 kcal/kg; it explains why ice floats on liquid water
4.18 kcal/kg; it is the heat needed to raise water by one degree
574 kcal/kg; it is important in sweating, panting and transpiration and in moderating environmental temperature
1000 kcal/kg; it is important only for the freezing of lakes
mcqs.why: The heat needed to convert 1 ml of liquid to vapour without changing temperature is 574 kcal/kg for water, due to hydrogen bonds; it matters in sweating, panting, transpiration and moderating environmental temperature.

mcqs.q: Water sticking to the wall of a xylem vessel is an example of which property?
options: Cohesion, the attraction between similar molecules
Hydrophobic exclusion, the clustering of oil drops in water
Ionization, the release of equal hydrogen and hydroxide ions
Adhesion, the attraction between dissimilar molecules
mcqs.why: Cohesion is attraction between similar molecules and adhesion is attraction between dissimilar molecules; water sticking to walls such as the xylem wall, due to hydrogen bonding and polarity, is adhesion.

mcqs.q: What is the importance of hydrophobic exclusion for the cell?
options: It reduces the contact area between water and hydrophobic substances and so maintains the integrity of the lipid bilayer of plasma membranes
It dissolves oils completely so they can pass through membranes freely
It converts hydrophobic substances into hydrophilic ones inside the cell
It breaks down the lipid bilayer so substances can enter the cell
mcqs.why: In hydrophobic exclusion the contact area between water and hydrophobic substances is reduced — oil drops on water join into a single drop — and this maintains the integrity of the lipid bilayer of plasma membranes.

mcqs.q: Why does ice float on water, and what is the benefit?
options: Ice is denser than water so it sinks and warms the water below it
Below 4 degrees Celsius water's density decreases, so ice is lighter than water, floats, and insulates the water below, increasing survival in winter
Ice contains trapped air bubbles that make it heavy enough to sink slowly
Water is the only substance whose solid is denser than its liquid form
mcqs.why: Density decreases below 4 degrees Celsius because ice has maximum hydrogen bonds; water is the only substance whose solid is less dense than its liquid, so ice floats and insulates the water below.

mcqs.q: What percentage of water is present in the human brain, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes compare water contents: bone and seed contain only 20% water, brain 85%, blood 88% and jellyfish 99%, so the brain contains 85% water.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates and Monosaccharides
lessons.notes_html:
Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1:2:1, general formula Cn(H₂O)n, so they are called hydrated carbon. Their source is green living things — plants, cyanobacteria, algae and many bacteria.

3.6 What Carbohydrates Are

Some molecules have the same ratio but are not carbohydrates, e.g. lactic acid (C₃H₆O₃) and acetic acid (C₂H₄O₂), and some carbohydrates do not fulfil the formula, e.g. rhamnose (C₆H₁₂O₅) and deoxyribose (C₅H₁₀O₄). So: carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. Aldehydes have a carbonyl group (C = O) at the end of a chain, bonded to hydrogen and an R-group (in glucose, ribose); they are easily oxidised and are powerful reducing agents. Ketones have the carbonyl group within the chain, bonded to two R-groups; such sugars are ketose sugars.

MonosaccharideOligosaccharidePolysaccharide
One sugar; simplest, cannot be hydrolysed; highly soluble, sweetest; glucose, ribose, fructose2–10 sugars; less soluble, less sweet; maltose, sucrose, lactoseMore than 10 sugars; complex, insoluble or sparingly soluble, tastes less; starch, glycogen, cellulose

3.7 Monosaccharides

Monosaccharides (mono: one, saccharide: sugar) are the simplest carbohydrates, cannot be hydrolysed further, contain 3 to 7 carbons, and are building blocks of complex carbohydrates. They are very sweet and easily soluble. All carbons except one have a hydroxyl group; the remaining carbon has an aldehyde group (aldo sugar) or ketone group (keto sugar), so they are reducing sugars. An asymmetric carbon bonds with four different atoms or groups — in glucose, galactose and mannose, carbons 2, 3, 4 and 5 are asymmetrical.

  • Trioses (C₃H₆O₃) — glyceraldehyde, dihydroxyacetone. Tetroses (C₄H₈O₄) — erythrose, erythrulose. Pentoses (C₅H₁₀O₅) — ribose, deoxyribose, ribulose. Hexoses (C₆H₁₂O₆) — glucose, mannose, fructose, galactose; glucose is the most common monosaccharide and the starting respiratory substrate. Heptoses (C₇H₁₄O₇) — glucose-heptose, sedoheptulose.

The molecular formula of a hexose is C₆H₁₂O₆; a structural formula shows the arrangement of atoms. Pentoses and hexoses usually form rings in water: a six-member ring is pyranose (glucopyranose), a five-member ring is furanose (ribofuranose). If the OH on carbon 1 is below the ring plane it is alpha-glucose; if above, beta-glucose. Different forms of the same chemical are isomers.

3.8 Isomers and Stereoisomers of Glucose

Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structure. Structural isomers have atoms and functional groups joined in different ways, e.g. glucose and fructose. Stereoisomers have the same bond structure but different positioning in space, e.g. D-glucose and L-glucose. Alpha and beta glucose have 16 stereoisomers in three groups:

EnantiomersDiastereoisomersEpimers
Non-superimposable mirror images; D and L glucoseH and OH differ at more than one asymmetrical carbon; D-glucose and D-altroseH and OH differ at only one asymmetrical carbon; D-glucose and D-mannose

Laboratory left-handed (L) sugars (tagatose, sucralose) taste like D-glucose and help diabetic and obese patients, but are expensive and overuse causes diarrhoea. They are not digested — the body makes no enzymes or receptors for them — and are not converted into fats.

Key Points

  • Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, general formula Cn(H₂O)n.
  • Monosaccharides have 3–7 carbons, are sweet, soluble reducing sugars and cannot be hydrolysed further.
  • Hexoses are C₆H₁₂O₆; glucose is the most common monosaccharide.
  • Enantiomers are mirror images, diastereoisomers differ at more than one carbon, epimers at only one.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of carbohydrates and the ratio of their elements?
options: Cn(H2O)2n, with carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2:1:1
C2n(H2O)n, with carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1:1:2
Cn(H2O)n, with carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1:2:1
CnHnOn, with carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1:1:1
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 1:2:1 with general formula Cn(H2O)n, which is why they are called hydrated carbon.

mcqs.q: Why are carbohydrates defined as polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones rather than only by the formula Cn(H2O)n?
options: Because the formula Cn(H2O)n has never been observed in any sugar molecule
Because all carbohydrates contain nitrogen in addition to carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
Because aldehydes and ketones are the only molecules found in living cells
Because some molecules fit the ratio but are not carbohydrates, such as lactic acid and acetic acid, while some carbohydrates such as rhamnose and deoxyribose do not fulfil the formula
mcqs.why: Lactic acid (C3H6O3) and acetic acid (C2H4O2) fit the ratio but are not carbohydrates, and rhamnose (C6H12O5) and deoxyribose (C5H10O4) are carbohydrates that break the formula, so carbohydrates are defined as polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones.

mcqs.q: Where is the carbonyl group located in an aldehyde sugar?
options: At the end of the chain, bonded to hydrogen and an R-group, as in glucose and ribose
Within the chain, bonded to two R-groups on either side
Attached to the nitrogen atom of an amino group
At the centre of a six-membered pyranose ring only
mcqs.why: Aldehydes have a carbonyl group (C=O) at the end of a chain, bonded to hydrogen and an R-group, as in glucose and ribose; they are easily oxidised and are powerful reducing agents.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes a ketose sugar from an aldose sugar?
options: In a ketose sugar the carbonyl group is at the end of the chain bonded to hydrogen
In a ketose sugar the carbonyl group lies within the chain, bonded to two R-groups
A ketose sugar contains no carbonyl group at all in its molecule
A ketose sugar always contains exactly seven carbon atoms
mcqs.why: Ketones have the carbonyl group within the chain, bonded to two R-groups, and such sugars are ketose sugars; aldose sugars instead carry an aldehyde group on the remaining carbon.

mcqs.q: Which statement about monosaccharides is correct?
options: They contain 10 or more carbons and are insoluble in water
They can be hydrolysed into two or more simpler sugars
They contain 3 to 7 carbons, are very sweet and easily soluble, are reducing sugars, and cannot be hydrolysed further
They are tasteless and form the storage polymers of cells
mcqs.why: Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates: they cannot be hydrolysed further, contain 3 to 7 carbons, are building blocks of complex carbohydrates, and all carbons except one bear a hydroxyl group so they are reducing sugars.

mcqs.q: Which set correctly lists pentoses and their molecular formula?
options: Glucose, mannose and fructose, with formula C6H12O6
Glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone, with formula C3H6O3
Erythrose and erythrulose, with formula C4H8O4
Ribose, deoxyribose and ribulose, with formula C5H10O5
mcqs.why: Pentoses are C5H10O5 — ribose, deoxyribose and ribulose; trioses are C3H6O3, tetroses C4H8O4 and hexoses C6H12O6.

mcqs.q: Which fact about glucose is stated in the notes?
options: Glucose is the most common monosaccharide and the starting respiratory substrate, with formula C6H12O6
Glucose is a pentose sugar found only in DNA molecules
Glucose is the least common hexose and cannot be used in respiration
Glucose is an oligosaccharide made of two simpler sugar units
mcqs.why: Hexoses are C6H12O6 — glucose, mannose, fructose and galactose — and glucose is the most common monosaccharide and the starting respiratory substrate.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a pyranose and a furanose ring?
options: A pyranose is a five-member ring while a furanose is a six-member ring
A pyranose is a six-member ring, as in glucopyranose, while a furanose is a five-member ring, as in ribofuranose
A pyranose ring contains nitrogen while a furanose ring contains sulphur
A pyranose is a straight chain while a furanose is a branched chain
mcqs.why: Pentoses and hexoses usually form rings in water: a six-member ring is pyranose (glucopyranose) and a five-member ring is furanose (ribofuranose).

mcqs.q: In alpha-glucose, where is the OH group on carbon 1 positioned?
options: Above the plane of the ring
Inside the centre of the ring structure
Below the plane of the ring
Replaced by a hydrogen atom entirely
mcqs.why: If the OH on carbon 1 is below the ring plane the sugar is alpha-glucose; if it is above the plane it is beta-glucose. Different forms of the same chemical are isomers.

mcqs.q: What is an epimer? Give the example from the notes.
options: A non-superimposable mirror image, for example D-glucose and L-glucose
A stereoisomer differing at more than one asymmetrical carbon, for example D-glucose and D-altrose
A structural isomer with atoms joined in a completely different order, for example glucose and fructose
A stereoisomer in which H and OH differ at only one asymmetrical carbon, for example D-glucose and D-mannose
mcqs.why: Alpha and beta glucose have 16 stereoisomers in three groups: enantiomers are mirror images, diastereoisomers differ at more than one asymmetrical carbon, and epimers differ at only one — D-glucose and D-mannose.

lessons.title: Oligosaccharides, Glycosidic Bonds and Polysaccharides
lessons.notes_html:
Monosaccharides join by glycosidic linkage to form oligosaccharides and polysaccharides — the transport, storage and structural forms of carbohydrate.

3.9 Oligosaccharides and Disaccharides

Two to ten monosaccharides joined by glycosidic linkage form oligosaccharides (disaccharides, trisaccharides, tetrasaccharides). The most common are disaccharides — condensation products of two monosaccharides, general formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, less sweet and less soluble than monosaccharides. The bond may break on hydrolysis, yielding two monosaccharides again.

  • Maltose (malt sugar) — two alpha glucose. In fruits and in the digestive tract as a breakdown product of starch by amylase; used in brewing to synthesise alcohol. Produced from barley starch by amylase — this process is malting.
  • Lactose (milk sugar) — galactose-beta-1,4-glucose; energy source for young mammals, 4 to 6 percent in cow milk and 5–8 percent in human milk. Hydrolysis gives glucose + galactose.
  • Sucrose (cane sugar) — most abundant disaccharide in nature; hydrolysed to glucose + fructose. From sugar cane or sugar beet, also in pineapple, sorghum and sweet fruit; the main transport sugar in plants.
  • Cellobiose — present in traces; released during digestion of cellulose by cellulase of microorganisms.

3.10 Glycosidic Bond

A glycosidic bond is the bond between two monosaccharides, formed by condensation. It normally joins carbon 1 to carbon 4 of the neighbouring unit; in sucrose it joins carbon 1 of glucose to carbon 2 of fructose; in branched chains a 1–6 glycosidic bond forms.

3.11 Polysaccharides

Polysaccharides have more than 10 monosaccharides linked by glycosidic linkage, branched or unbranched, tasteless and insoluble or sparingly soluble, and are the most abundant carbohydrates in nature. Homopolysaccharides are made from one kind of monosaccharide (starch, glycogen, cellulose, chitin); heteropolysaccharides from different kinds (agar, hemicellulose, pectin, peptidoglycan). They store food and energy and give structure. Their large size makes them insoluble, so they exert no osmotic or chemical influence in the cell, fold into compact shapes, and convert easily to sugars by hydrolysis when required.

PolysaccharideStructure and role
StarchPlant storage polymer of glucose. Amylose 15–20%: straight chain, 1–4 linkage, soluble in warm water. Amylopectin 80–85%: branched, 1–6 linkage at branches, insoluble
CelluloseMost abundant carbohydrate in nature; structural, main constituent of plant and algal cell walls. Humans lack cellulase and cannot digest it; herbivores can, because gut microorganisms (bacteria, yeast, protozoans) secrete cellulase
GlycogenAnimal starch: highly branched polymer of glucose, stored in liver and muscles, also in fungi; insoluble, converted back to glucose when needed
ChitinNitrogenous structural homopolysaccharide related to cellulose; in fungal cell walls (fungal cellulose) and arthropod exoskeletons. Second most abundant organic molecule on Earth; derivative of N-acetyl glucosamine, a modified beta glucose

Iodine test: potato turns dark blue (starch present); glycogen solution turns red (glycogen present); cellulose solution remains unchanged (no starch or glycogen).

Key Points

  • Disaccharides (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) form by condensation and split by hydrolysis.
  • Maltose = glucose + glucose; lactose = glucose + galactose; sucrose = glucose + fructose.
  • Glycosidic bonds normally join carbon 1 to carbon 4; branches use 1–6 bonds.
  • Starch and glycogen store energy; cellulose and chitin give structure.

mcqs.q: A disaccharide is formed when two hexoses (each C6H12O6) join by condensation. What is the formula of the disaccharide?
options: C6H10O5
mcqs.why: Working: condensation removes one water molecule. Two hexoses give C12 H24 O12; subtract H2O: H 24-2 = 22 and O 12-1 = 11, giving C12H22O11, the general formula of disaccharides given in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is maltose, and how is it produced in malting?
options: Maltose is two alpha glucose units; in malting it is produced from barley starch by the enzyme amylase
Maltose is glucose joined to fructose, produced from sugar cane juice
Maltose is galactose joined to glucose, produced in the mammary glands
Maltose is a single glucose unit released during cellulose digestion
mcqs.why: Maltose (malt sugar) is two alpha glucose, found in fruits and in the digestive tract as a breakdown product of starch by amylase; producing it from barley starch by amylase is malting, and it is used in brewing.

mcqs.q: What is the composition of lactose and its amount in cow's milk?
options: Glucose joined to fructose; 10 to 12 percent in cow milk
Galactose joined to glucose (galactose-beta-1,4-glucose); 4 to 6 percent in cow milk and 5-8 percent in human milk
Two glucose units; 1 to 2 percent in cow milk only
Glucose joined to ribose; it is absent from human milk
mcqs.why: Lactose (milk sugar) is galactose-beta-1,4-glucose, an energy source for young mammals, 4 to 6 percent in cow milk and 5-8 percent in human milk; hydrolysis gives glucose plus galactose.

mcqs.q: Which statement about sucrose is correct?
options: It is made of two galactose units and is found only in milk
It is the main storage sugar of animals, stored in liver and muscles
It is the most abundant disaccharide in nature, hydrolyses to glucose plus fructose, and is the main transport sugar in plants
It is released during digestion of cellulose by microbial cellulase
mcqs.why: Sucrose (cane sugar) comes from sugar cane or sugar beet and also occurs in pineapple, sorghum and sweet fruit; hydrolysis yields glucose + fructose and it is the main transport sugar in plants.

mcqs.q: Where does the glycosidic bond normally join two monosaccharides, and what is the exception in sucrose?
options: It normally joins carbon 2 to carbon 5; in sucrose it joins carbon 3 to carbon 6
It normally joins carbon 1 to carbon 6; in sucrose it joins carbon 4 to carbon 4
It normally joins two phosphate groups; in sucrose it joins two hydroxyl groups
It normally joins carbon 1 to carbon 4 of the neighbouring unit; in sucrose it joins carbon 1 of glucose to carbon 2 of fructose
mcqs.why: A glycosidic bond is formed by condensation between two monosaccharides; it normally joins carbon 1 to carbon 4, in sucrose carbon 1 of glucose to carbon 2 of fructose, and in branched chains a 1-6 bond forms.

mcqs.q: How do amylose and amylopectin differ in starch?
options: Amylose is 15-20 percent, a straight chain with 1-4 linkage, soluble in warm water; amylopectin is 80-85 percent, branched with 1-6 linkage at branches, and insoluble
Amylose is 80-85 percent and branched; amylopectin is 15-20 percent and a straight chain
Both are branched chains that are completely insoluble in warm water
Amylose stores energy in animals while amylopectin forms plant cell walls
mcqs.why: Starch is the plant storage polymer of glucose: amylose 15-20% is a straight 1-4 linked chain soluble in warm water, while amylopectin 80-85% is branched with 1-6 linkages at branches and is insoluble.

mcqs.q: Why can humans not digest cellulose, while herbivores can?
options: Humans lack the enzyme amylase needed to break down all plant material
Humans lack the enzyme cellulase; herbivores can digest it because gut microorganisms such as bacteria, yeast and protozoans secrete cellulase
Cellulose is made of fructose units that human cells cannot absorb
Herbivores produce cellulase in their own salivary glands and stomach lining
mcqs.why: Cellulose is the most abundant carbohydrate in nature and the main constituent of plant and algal cell walls; humans lack cellulase, but herbivores digest it through cellulase secreted by gut microorganisms.

mcqs.q: What is glycogen and where is it stored?
options: A straight-chain polymer of fructose stored in plant seeds and roots
A structural polymer of glucose forming the walls of plant cells
A highly branched polymer of glucose, the animal starch, stored in the liver and muscles and also found in fungi, converted back to glucose when needed
A nitrogenous polymer found in arthropod exoskeletons and fungal walls
mcqs.why: Glycogen is animal starch: a highly branched, insoluble polymer of glucose stored in liver and muscles, also in fungi, and converted back to glucose when needed; in the iodine test a glycogen solution turns red.

mcqs.q: What is chitin and where is it found?
options: A storage polysaccharide of plants made only of alpha glucose units
A disaccharide found in milk that yields glucose and galactose
A heteropolysaccharide of agar and pectin found in seaweed cell walls
A nitrogenous structural homopolysaccharide, a derivative of N-acetyl glucosamine, found in fungal cell walls and arthropod exoskeletons; it is the second most abundant organic molecule on Earth
mcqs.why: Chitin is a nitrogenous structural homopolysaccharide related to cellulose, a derivative of N-acetyl glucosamine (a modified beta glucose), found in fungal cell walls (fungal cellulose) and arthropod exoskeletons.

mcqs.q: Which of the following are all homopolysaccharides?
options: Starch, glycogen, cellulose and chitin, each made from one kind of monosaccharide
Agar, hemicellulose, pectin and peptidoglycan
Maltose, sucrose, lactose and cellobiose
Glucose, fructose, galactose and ribose
mcqs.why: Homopolysaccharides are made from one kind of monosaccharide — starch, glycogen, cellulose and chitin — whereas heteropolysaccharides such as agar, hemicellulose, pectin and peptidoglycan are made from different kinds.

lessons.title: Proteins: Amino Acids, Peptide Bonds and Roles
lessons.notes_html:
Proteins are the most complex and important organic compounds in food, found in all plants and animals. The word comes from the Greek proteios, meaning primary or of prime importance.

3.12 Proteins and Amino Acids

Proteins are essential components of protoplasm, form the structural framework of cells, and are linked with cell division and heredity. Enzymes, hormones, antigens and antibodies are proteins. They are polymers of amino acids containing C, H, O and N; most also contain sulphur and phosphorus, a few iron, copper and iodine. Protein is the most abundant organic compound in cells.

Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. About 170 types are discovered, 25 are involved in protein synthesis, and most proteins are made of 20 types. Each has a central alpha carbon with an NH₂ (amino group) on one side, a COOH (carboxyl group) on the other, hydrogen on the third side, and a different R (radical) group on the fourth. Nine are essential (indispensable) — adults cannot synthesise them, so they are required in diet: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine. The rest are non-essential (dispensable) — the body can synthesise them, e.g. alanine, glycine, serine, tyrosine.

3.13 Peptide Linkage

Amino acids link to form a polypeptide chain by a peptide (amide) linkage, formed by condensation between the amino group (N-terminal) of one amino acid and the carboxyl group (C-terminal) of another, releasing water. One or more polypeptide chains unite to form a protein.

3.14 Significance of the Sequence of Amino Acids

Each protein has a unique, specific arrangement of amino acids, essential for its function; if any amino acid is out of place the protein fails. Example: sickle cell anaemia. Normal red blood cells are disc-shaped; haemoglobin has two alpha chains of 141 amino acids and two beta chains of 146 amino acids. In sickle cell anaemia, amino acid 6 of the beta chain is valine instead of glutamate; haemoglobin carries insufficient oxygen and red blood cells become sickle-shaped.

3.15 Classification and Levels of Structure

Fibrous proteinsGlobular proteins
Chains in fibrils; insoluble in water; non-crystalline, elastic; structural. Keratin (nails, hair), fibrin (blood clot), myosin (muscle), silk fibres, collagen (skin, bones, ligament, tendon)Spherical or ellipsoid by multiple folding; soluble in water, salt solution, acids, bases or alcohol; disorganised by environmental changes. Enzymes, antibodies, many hormones, haemoglobin, myoglobin

Levels: primary — linear sequence of amino acids; secondary — hydrogen bonding of the backbone folds the chain into alpha helix and pleated sheet; tertiary — three-dimensional folding from side-chain interactions; quaternary — more than one polypeptide chain.

3.16 Role of Proteins

  • Structural — keratin in feathers, horns, beaks, hair; collagen in bones and cartilages; histone arranges DNA into chromosomes; elastin in tendons and ligaments.
  • Functional — enzymes catalyse all cellular reactions; transport — haemoglobin transports oxygen and CO₂, myoglobin stores oxygen in red muscles (as named in the book); defence — fibrinogen and prothrombin clot blood; hormones regulate metabolism; storage — ovalbumin (egg white) and casein (milk); contractility — actin and myosin, and tubulin helps chromosome movement in anaphase; nucleoproteins form genes and chromatin.

Biuret test: biuret solution added to food changes from blue to violet if protein is present.

Key Points

  • Each amino acid has NH₂, COOH, H and a different R group on a central alpha carbon; nine are essential in diet.
  • A peptide bond joins amino acids by condensation, releasing water.
  • In sickle cell anaemia valine replaces glutamate at position 6 of the beta chain.
  • Fibrous proteins are insoluble and structural; globular proteins are soluble, folded and functional.

mcqs.q: What is the basic structure of an amino acid?
options: A central alpha carbon bearing an NH2 (amino) group, a COOH (carboxyl) group, a hydrogen, and a different R (radical) group
A central carbon bearing two amino groups, two carboxyl groups and no R group
A ring of six carbons with a phosphate group and a nitrogen base attached
A three-carbon glycerol backbone joined to three long fatty acid chains
mcqs.why: Each amino acid has a central alpha carbon with NH2 on one side, COOH on the other, hydrogen on the third side and a different R group on the fourth; the R group makes each amino acid distinct.

mcqs.q: How many types of amino acids are involved in most proteins, according to the notes?
options: Most proteins are made of 170 types, out of 25 discovered
Most proteins are made of 20 types, out of about 170 discovered and 25 involved in protein synthesis
Most proteins are made of 9 types, all of them essential in the diet
Most proteins are made of 25 types, and none can be synthesised by the body
mcqs.why: About 170 amino acid types are discovered, 25 are involved in protein synthesis, and most proteins are made of 20 types — nine of which are essential in the diet.

mcqs.q: What makes an amino acid 'essential'?
options: The body can synthesise it easily, like alanine, glycine and serine
It is found only in plant proteins and never in animal proteins
Adults cannot synthesise it, so it is required in the diet; there are nine, including lysine, methionine and tryptophan
It contains sulphur and phosphorus in its R group structure
mcqs.why: Nine amino acids are essential (indispensable) — histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine — because adults cannot synthesise them; the rest, such as alanine and glycine, are non-essential.

mcqs.q: How is a peptide (amide) linkage formed?
options: By hydrolysis of two amino acids, using up a molecule of water
By a hydrogen bond forming between the R groups of two amino acids
By an ionic bond between the phosphate groups of two amino acids
By condensation between the amino group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of another, releasing water
mcqs.why: Amino acids link into a polypeptide chain by a peptide linkage formed by condensation between the amino (N-terminal) group of one amino acid and the carboxyl (C-terminal) group of another, releasing water.

mcqs.q: What single change causes sickle cell anaemia?
options: In the beta chain of haemoglobin, amino acid 6 is valine instead of glutamate, so haemoglobin carries insufficient oxygen and red blood cells become sickle-shaped
In the alpha chain, amino acid 141 is removed from the end of the chain
In the beta chain, amino acid 6 is glutamate instead of valine in patients
The whole beta chain is replaced by an alpha chain of 141 amino acids
mcqs.why: Normal haemoglobin has two alpha chains of 141 amino acids and two beta chains of 146; in sickle cell anaemia valine replaces glutamate at position 6 of the beta chain, showing that the exact sequence of amino acids is essential for function.

mcqs.q: How many amino acids are there in total in one haemoglobin molecule, given its chain composition in the notes?
options: 287 amino acids
574 amino acids
146 amino acids
282 amino acids
mcqs.why: Working: haemoglobin has two alpha chains of 141 amino acids and two beta chains of 146. Total = 2 x 141 + 2 x 146 = 282 + 292 = 574 amino acids.

mcqs.q: Which description fits fibrous proteins?
options: Spherical molecules formed by multiple folding, soluble in water, salt solution, acids and bases
Proteins that are easily disorganised by any change in the environment
Chains arranged in fibrils, insoluble in water, non-crystalline and elastic, with a structural role — for example keratin, fibrin, myosin and collagen
Proteins that act only as enzymes, antibodies and hormones in the cell
mcqs.why: Fibrous proteins have chains in fibrils, are insoluble in water, non-crystalline and elastic, and are structural — keratin in nails and hair, fibrin in blood clots, myosin in muscle and collagen in skin, bones, ligaments and tendons.

mcqs.q: Which description fits globular proteins?
options: Long chains in fibrils that never dissolve in any solvent
Flat sheets of protein found only in nails, hair and silk fibres
Proteins whose shape cannot be changed by the environment at all
Spherical or ellipsoid by multiple folding, soluble in water, salt solution, acids, bases or alcohol — for example enzymes, antibodies, many hormones, haemoglobin and myoglobin
mcqs.why: Globular proteins are spherical or ellipsoid by multiple folding, soluble in water, salt solution, acids, bases or alcohol, and disorganised by environmental changes; examples are enzymes, antibodies, many hormones, haemoglobin and myoglobin.

mcqs.q: What is the secondary level of protein structure?
options: Hydrogen bonding of the backbone folds the chain into an alpha helix and pleated sheet
The linear sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain
The three-dimensional folding produced by side-chain interactions
The arrangement of more than one polypeptide chain in a protein
mcqs.why: The levels are: primary — linear sequence of amino acids; secondary — hydrogen bonding of the backbone folding the chain into alpha helix and pleated sheet; tertiary — 3D folding from side-chain interactions; quaternary — more than one polypeptide chain.

mcqs.q: What does the biuret test show?
options: A food turns dark blue if starch is present in the sample
Biuret solution added to food changes from blue to violet if protein is present
A solution turns red if glycogen is dissolved in it
A food turns brick red if a reducing sugar is present
mcqs.why: In the biuret test, biuret solution added to food changes from blue to violet if protein is present; by contrast the iodine test turns potato dark blue for starch and a glycogen solution red.

lessons.title: Lipids: Acylglycerols, Phospholipids, Terpenes, Waxes, Steroids and Prostaglandins
lessons.notes_html:
Lipids are a heterogeneous group of organic compounds, insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as alcohol, ether, chloroform, acetone and benzene, with a greasy or oily consistency — fats, oils, waxes and cholesterol.

3.17 Nature of Lipids

Lipids contain C, H and O, but with a lower percentage of oxygen than carbohydrates, so they are lighter and much less soluble in water. Being hydrophobic they form membranes, act as storage compounds, and give double the energy of carbohydrates due to a high proportion of C–H bonds: 1 gram of carbohydrate gives 4.1 Kcal, protein 4.6 Kcal, and lipid 9 Kcal.

3.18 Classes of Lipids

Classified by solubility and hydrolysis products into acylglycerols, phospholipids, terpenes and waxes.

  • Acylglycerols (neutral fats) — esters of fatty acids and glycerol, the most abundant lipids. An ester forms when an alcohol reacts with a fatty acid, releasing water; here the alcohol is glycerol, a three-carbon compound with an OH on each carbon. A fatty acid is a long straight chain of even-numbered carbons (2–30) with a carboxyl group at the end. With one, two or three fatty acids the molecule is a monoglycerol, diglycerol or triglycerol; triglyceride is most common. About 30 fatty acid types exist, e.g. acetic acid (2 carbons), stearic acid (18 carbons). Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds (palmitic acid, spelled palmatic in the book): solid at room temperature, more energy, mostly from animals. Unsaturated fatty acids have double bonds (oleic acid): liquid, less energy, usually from plants.
  • Phospholipids — major components of all cell membranes, forming bilayers because they are amphiphilic. One molecule has two hydrophobic fatty acid tails and a hydrophilic head (glycerol backbone + phosphate group): fatty acids attach to carbons 1 and 2 of glycerol, phosphoric acid to carbon 3, and sometimes choline, serine or ethanolamine attaches to the phosphate. Heads face outward to water, tails inward away from water. Most common is phosphatidylcholine (lecithin). Too much fat in diet causes obesity and cardiovascular disorders such as high blood pressure and heart attack.
  • Terpenes — large, diverse compounds from plants and some insects, built from the isoprene unit, a five-carbon unsaturated hydrocarbon, C₅H₈ — also the basic unit for steroids, vitamins A, E, K and rubber. Two units: monoterpene (menthol); four: diterpene (vitamin A); six: triterpene (ambrein, from gums and resin); eight: tetraterpene (carotenoid); rubber is a polyterpene.
  • Waxes — long alkyl chains, completely water insoluble, generally solid at room temperature. Beeswax is the most common animal wax; plants have epicuticular waxes. They protect, act as a water barrier and prevent abrasive damage. Cutin on leaves and fruits and suberin in roots are waxes; waxes also store energy in microscopic aquatic plants and animals.

A phospholipid bilayer: hydrophilic heads face water, hydrophobic tails face each other inside.

3.19 Steroids and Prostaglandins

  • Steroids — non-fatty-acid lipids with a core of 17 carbon atoms in 4 interlocked rings (three six-sided, the fourth five-sided); types vary by functional groups on the fourth ring. Cholesterol is structural in cell membranes and brain tissue; sex hormones (estrogen, progesterone, testosterone), vitamin D (calcium metabolism) and bile salts (emulsify fats) are steroids.
  • Prostaglandins — named from the prostate gland, first isolated from seminal fluid in 1935; hormone-like lipids found in almost every tissue, derived from fatty acids, each with 20 carbons including a 5-carbon ring. Aspirin-like drugs inhibit their synthesis (found in 1971). They dilate and contract smooth muscle, aggregate and disaggregate platelets, regulate inflammation and hormones, control cell growth, sensitise pain neurons, and regulate fever and menstrual cramping. Synthetic prostaglandins induce parturition and treat peptic ulcer.

Key Points

  • Lipids are hydrophobic and give 9 Kcal per gram.
  • A triglyceride is glycerol + three fatty acids joined by ester bonds.
  • Phospholipids are amphiphilic and form membrane bilayers; lecithin is most common.
  • Terpenes are built from isoprene (C₅H₈); steroids have 17 carbons in 4 rings; prostaglandins have 20 carbons.

mcqs.q: Which property correctly describes lipids as a group?
options: They dissolve readily in water because they are polar molecules
They are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as alcohol, ether, chloroform, acetone and benzene, with a greasy or oily consistency
They are soluble only in water and in dilute acids and bases
They contain a higher percentage of oxygen than carbohydrates do
mcqs.why: Lipids are a heterogeneous group — fats, oils, waxes and cholesterol — insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents; they contain C, H and O with a lower percentage of oxygen than carbohydrates, so they are lighter and much less soluble.

mcqs.q: How much energy is obtained from 10 grams of lipid, using the value in the notes?
options: 41 Kcal
46 Kcal
90 Kcal
9 Kcal
mcqs.why: Working: 1 gram of lipid gives 9 Kcal, so 10 g x 9 Kcal/g = 90 Kcal. For comparison, 1 gram of carbohydrate gives 4.1 Kcal and protein 4.6 Kcal, so lipids give about double the energy of carbohydrates because of their high proportion of C-H bonds.

mcqs.q: What is a triglyceride (triglycerol)?
options: A glycerol molecule joined to a single fatty acid and two phosphate groups
Three glycerol molecules joined to one long fatty acid chain
A fatty acid chain of 18 carbons with a carboxyl group at its end
A glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds; glycerol is a three-carbon compound with an OH group on each carbon
mcqs.why: Acylglycerols are esters of fatty acids and glycerol, the most abundant lipids; an ester forms when an alcohol reacts with a fatty acid releasing water. With one, two or three fatty acids the molecule is a monoglycerol, diglycerol or triglycerol, and the triglyceride is most common.

mcqs.q: What is a saturated fatty acid?
options: A fatty acid with no double bonds, solid at room temperature, giving more energy, and mostly obtained from animals
A fatty acid with several double bonds, liquid at room temperature, from plants
A fatty acid containing a phosphate group and a nitrogen base
A fatty acid with an odd number of carbons and no carboxyl group
mcqs.why: Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds, are solid at room temperature, give more energy and come mostly from animals; fatty acids generally are long straight chains of even-numbered carbons (2-30) with a carboxyl group at the end.

mcqs.q: What is an unsaturated fatty acid? Give the example from the notes.
options: A fatty acid with no double bonds, solid at room temperature — for example stearic acid with 18 carbons
A fatty acid with double bonds, liquid, giving less energy and usually obtained from plants — for example oleic acid
A fatty acid that has been joined to glycerol to form a wax
A fatty acid found only in the membranes of animal cells
mcqs.why: Unsaturated fatty acids have double bonds, are liquid, give less energy and are usually from plants, e.g. oleic acid; saturated ones such as stearic acid (18 carbons) have no double bonds and are solid.

mcqs.q: How do phospholipids form a bilayer in cell membranes?
options: Each molecule has one tail and three heads, all of which face the water
Heads face inward toward each other and tails face outward to the water
Each molecule has two hydrophobic fatty acid tails and a hydrophilic head; heads face outward to the water and tails face inward away from water, because phospholipids are amphiphilic
The molecules dissolve in the water on both sides of the membrane
mcqs.why: Phospholipids are major components of all cell membranes: fatty acids attach to carbons 1 and 2 of glycerol and phosphoric acid to carbon 3, sometimes with choline, serine or ethanolamine on the phosphate; being amphiphilic they form bilayers with heads out and tails in.

mcqs.q: What is the most common phospholipid named in the notes?
options: Phosphatidylserine, also called cephalin
Phosphatidylethanolamine from root suberin
A triglyceride of glycerol and stearic acid
Phosphatidylcholine, also called lecithin
mcqs.why: The most common phospholipid is phosphatidylcholine (lecithin); in phospholipids choline, serine or ethanolamine may attach to the phosphate group of the hydrophilic head.

mcqs.q: A tetraterpene such as a carotenoid is built from eight isoprene units. How many carbon atoms does it contain?
options: 40 carbon atoms
8 carbon atoms
20 carbon atoms
17 carbon atoms
mcqs.why: Working: each isoprene unit is a five-carbon unsaturated hydrocarbon, C5H8, so eight units give 8 x 5 = 40 carbons. The notes likewise give two units for a monoterpene, four for a diterpene and six for a triterpene; rubber is a polyterpene.

mcqs.q: What is the core structure of a steroid?
options: 20 carbon atoms including a single 5-carbon ring
17 carbon atoms arranged in 4 interlocked rings, three six-sided and the fourth five-sided; types vary by functional groups on the fourth ring
Three fatty acid chains joined to a glycerol backbone
Five-carbon isoprene units joined into one long straight chain
mcqs.why: Steroids are non-fatty-acid lipids with a core of 17 carbon atoms in 4 interlocked rings; cholesterol, sex hormones, vitamin D and bile salts are steroids, whereas prostaglandins have 20 carbons including a 5-carbon ring.

mcqs.q: Which statement about prostaglandins is correct?
options: They are proteins that carry oxygen in red blood cells
They were first isolated from the liver in 1971 as enzymes
They are hormone-like lipids derived from fatty acids, each with 20 carbons including a 5-carbon ring; aspirin-like drugs inhibit their synthesis
They are steroids with 17 carbons that emulsify fats in the intestine
mcqs.why: Prostaglandins were named from the prostate gland and first isolated from seminal fluid in 1935; they dilate and contract smooth muscle, regulate inflammation, fever and menstrual cramping, and aspirin-like drugs inhibit their synthesis (found in 1971).

lessons.title: Nucleic Acids, DNA, RNA, Central Dogma and Conjugated Molecules
lessons.notes_html:
Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides: DNA carries hereditary information and RNA helps in, or controls, protein synthesis. They were first isolated in 1869 by Friedrich Miescher (spelled Fredrick in the book) from pus cells and salmon sperms as nuclein; Jones in 1920 proved there are two types, DNA and RNA. Partial hydrolysis yields nucleotides or nucleosides; complete hydrolysis yields bases, pentose sugars and phosphate ions.

3.20 Nucleotide, Nucleoside and Bases

  • Nucleoside — a nitrogen base linked to a pentose sugar by an N-glycosidic bond. Nucleotide — a nucleoside + phosphoric acid, existing as mono-, di- or triphosphate esters. DNA is made of deoxyribonucleotides, RNA of ribonucleotides.
  • Pyrimidine bases — single six-corner ring: thymine, cytosine, uracil. Purine bases — two rings: adenine, guanine.
  • Pentose sugars — deoxyribose (C₅H₁₀O₄, in DNA) and ribose (C₅H₁₀O₅, in RNA); deoxyribose has one oxygen less at carbon 2. Phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) forms an ester linkage with the OH group of the sugar.

3.21 ATP and 3.22 NAD

ATP is a mononucleotide: adenine + ribose + three phosphate groups. Adenine + ribose forms the nucleoside adenosine; adding one, two or three phosphoric acids by condensation gives AMP, ADP and ATP. ATP is the energy currency of the cell — its hydrolysis releases energy for muscle contraction, active transport, nerve impulses and protein synthesis. When two nucleotides join they form a dinucleotide: NAD has one nucleotide with a nicotinamide base and one with adenine, linked by their phosphates, and is derived from niacin (vitamin B). NAD carries electrons in redox reactions: NAD⁺ accepts two electrons and a proton to become NADH, a reducing agent. FAD is another dinucleotide coenzyme, becoming FADH₂.

3.23 Phosphodiester Linkage

This covalent bond forms the backbone of DNA and RNA, linking the 3rd carbon of one pentose to the 5th carbon of the next through a phosphate group. In formation, nucleoside triphosphates (ATP, GTP) are used; the 3-OH of the growing chain attacks the phosphate of the incoming triphosphate, the bond forms, and the other two phosphates are released as pyrophosphate (PPi), whose hydrolysis to two Pi is highly exergonic and makes the reaction effectively irreversible.

3.24 DNA: Watson and Crick Model

In 1951 Chargaff found adenine equals thymine and cytosine equals guanine (purines : pyrimidines = 1:1). In 1953 Watson, Crick, Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin worked out the double helix; Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962, and Franklin provided X-ray diffraction evidence. DNA nucleotides contain deoxyribose, phosphate and a base (purines adenine, guanine; pyrimidines thymine, cytosine). Two strands twist into an antiparallel double helix like a circular ladder — sugar and phosphate make the sides, bases make the rungs. Adenine pairs with thymine (two hydrogen bonds) and cytosine with guanine (three), so strands are complementary. Diameter is 2 nm, a full turn every 3.4 nm, with 10 base pairs per turn. DNA amount is fixed for a species; germ cells have half the DNA of somatic cells.

DNA double helix: antiparallel sugar-phosphate backbones with A–T and G–C pairs inside.

3.25–3.26 RNA and Its Types

RNA is a single, unbranched chain of ribonucleotides with bases adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil; only Reovirus RNA is double-stranded. Some RNA coils into hair-pin loops by hydrogen bonds (A = U, G = C) within the same molecule. It is made in the nucleus from one DNA template strand, is mostly in the cytoplasm, helps DNA in protein synthesis, and is hereditary material in some animal and all plant viruses. The three types are made by transcription:

TypeRole
mRNA (3–4%)Carries information from DNA to ribosomes; its coding sequence determines the amino acid sequence
tRNA (about 15%)About 80 nucleotides; transfers a specific amino acid to the growing chain; at least 20 types per cell, about 45 kinds in humans
rRNA (about 80%)Catalytic component of the ribosome, a platform for protein synthesis; largest and most abundant RNA, made in the nuclear organizer region

3.27 Central Dogma and 3.28 Conjugated Molecules

Central dogma: genes in DNA are copied into mRNA by transcription, and mRNA is converted into polypeptide chains by translation at ribosomes; proteins link genotype (DNA) to phenotype. DNA replication is DNA to DNA by DNA polymerase. Conjugated molecules combine two classes of molecules: lipoproteins (lipid + protein, in cell, mitochondrial, endoplasmic reticulum and nuclear membranes); nucleoproteins (nucleic acid + protein, e.g. ribosomes and chromosomes); glycolipids (glucose + lipid, in cell membranes, joined by a glycosidic bond); glycoproteins (glucose + protein, functioning as hormones, transport and structural proteins and receptors; blood group antigens contain glycoproteins).

Key Points

  • A nucleotide = base + pentose sugar + phosphate; a nucleoside is base + sugar only.
  • Purines have two rings; pyrimidines have one ring.
  • ATP is a mononucleotide energy currency; NAD is a dinucleotide redox coenzyme.
  • DNA is an antiparallel double helix, 2 nm wide, 10 base pairs per turn, A–T with 2 hydrogen bonds and G–C with 3.
  • Central dogma: DNA to RNA by transcription, RNA to protein by translation.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a nucleoside and a nucleotide?
options: A nucleoside contains three phosphate groups while a nucleotide contains none
A nucleoside is found only in DNA while a nucleotide is found only in RNA
A nucleoside is a nitrogen base linked to a pentose sugar by an N-glycosidic bond; a nucleotide is a nucleoside plus phosphoric acid
A nucleoside is a complete DNA molecule while a nucleotide is a single base
mcqs.why: A nucleoside is base + pentose sugar joined by an N-glycosidic bond; adding phosphoric acid gives a nucleotide, which exists as mono-, di- or triphosphate esters. DNA is made of deoxyribonucleotides and RNA of ribonucleotides.

mcqs.q: How do purine and pyrimidine bases differ in structure, and which bases belong to each?
options: Purines have a single ring — thymine and uracil; pyrimidines have two rings — adenine and guanine
Both groups have two rings, but purines contain sulphur and pyrimidines contain phosphorus
Purines are sugars with five carbons while pyrimidines are phosphate compounds
Purines have two rings — adenine and guanine; pyrimidines have a single six-corner ring — thymine, cytosine and uracil
mcqs.why: Pyrimidine bases have a single six-corner ring (thymine, cytosine, uracil) and purine bases have two rings (adenine, guanine); complete hydrolysis of nucleic acids yields bases, pentose sugars and phosphate ions.

mcqs.q: How does deoxyribose differ from ribose?
options: Deoxyribose (C5H10O4, in DNA) has one oxygen less than ribose (C5H10O5, in RNA), the difference being at carbon 2
Deoxyribose has one extra oxygen at carbon 2 compared with ribose
Deoxyribose contains six carbons while ribose contains five carbons
Deoxyribose is found in RNA while ribose is found only in DNA
mcqs.why: The pentose sugars are deoxyribose (C5H10O4) in DNA and ribose (C5H10O5) in RNA; deoxyribose has one oxygen less at carbon 2, and phosphoric acid (H3PO4) forms an ester linkage with the OH group of the sugar.

mcqs.q: What is the structure and role of ATP?
options: ATP is a dinucleotide of two adenine nucleotides that carries electrons in redox reactions

ATP is a mononucleotide of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups, and is the energy currency of the cell, its hydrolysis powering muscle contraction, active transport, nerve impulses and protein synthesis
ATP is a protein that stores oxygen in red muscles for later use
ATP is a polysaccharide that stores glucose in the liver and muscles
mcqs.why: Adenine + ribose forms the nucleoside adenosine; adding one, two or three phosphoric acids by condensation gives AMP, ADP and ATP. ATP is the energy currency of the cell.

mcqs.q: What is NAD and what does it do in redox reactions?
options: NAD is a mononucleotide of adenine and ribose that stores hereditary information
NAD is a pyrimidine base that pairs with adenine in the DNA double helix

NAD is a dinucleotide with one nicotinamide nucleotide and one adenine nucleotide linked by their phosphates, derived from niacin (vitamin B); NAD+ accepts two electrons and a proton to become NADH, a reducing agent
NAD is a phospholipid that forms the bilayer of the plasma membrane
mcqs.why: When two nucleotides join they form a dinucleotide: NAD carries electrons in redox reactions, NAD+ accepting two electrons and a proton to become NADH; FAD is another dinucleotide coenzyme, becoming FADH2.

mcqs.q: What does a phosphodiester linkage join in DNA and RNA?
options: The nitrogen base of one nucleotide directly to the base of the next nucleotide
Two phosphate groups of adjacent nucleotides without any sugar involvement
Carbon 1 of one sugar to carbon 4 of the next sugar in a carbohydrate chain
The 3rd carbon of one pentose sugar to the 5th carbon of the next pentose through a phosphate group, forming the backbone
mcqs.why: The phosphodiester bond is the covalent backbone of DNA and RNA; in its formation the 3-OH of the growing chain attacks the phosphate of an incoming nucleoside triphosphate and the other two phosphates are released as pyrophosphate (PPi).

mcqs.q: A DNA segment contains 100 base pairs. Using the dimensions in the notes, what is its length?
options: 34 nm, because 100 base pairs make 10 full turns of 3.4 nm each
20 nm, because 100 base pairs make 10 turns of 2 nm each
340 nm, because each base pair adds 3.4 nm of length
3.4 nm, because the whole segment forms a single turn
mcqs.why: Working: DNA has 10 base pairs per turn and a full turn every 3.4 nm. 100 base pairs / 10 = 10 turns, and 10 x 3.4 nm = 34 nm. The 2 nm figure is the diameter of the helix, not the length per turn.

mcqs.q: In a DNA sample, adenine makes up 30% of the bases. What are the percentages of the other bases, by Chargaff's rule as stated in the notes?
options: Thymine 20%, guanine 30% and cytosine 20%
Thymine 30%, guanine 20% and cytosine 20%
Thymine 30%, guanine 30% and cytosine 10%
Thymine 70%, guanine 0% and cytosine 0%
mcqs.why: Working: Chargaff found adenine equals thymine and cytosine equals guanine, with purines : pyrimidines = 1:1. If A = 30%, then T = 30%; the remaining 100 - 60 = 40% is split equally, so G = 20% and C = 20%.

mcqs.q: Which type of RNA is the largest and most abundant, and what is its share and role?
options: mRNA, about 80% of RNA, which transfers specific amino acids to the growing chain
tRNA, about 80% of RNA, which carries information from DNA to the ribosomes
rRNA, about 80% of RNA, the catalytic component of the ribosome and a platform for protein synthesis, made in the nuclear organizer region
rRNA, about 15% of RNA, which is only about 80 nucleotides long
mcqs.why: The three types made by transcription are mRNA (3-4%, carries information from DNA to ribosomes), tRNA (about 15%, about 80 nucleotides, transfers a specific amino acid) and rRNA (about 80%, largest and most abundant, the catalytic ribosome component).

mcqs.q: What does the central dogma describe?
options: DNA is converted directly into protein without any RNA intermediate step
Proteins are copied back into DNA by reverse translation at ribosomes
RNA replicates itself into DNA using the enzyme DNA polymerase only
Genes in DNA are copied into mRNA by transcription, and mRNA is converted into polypeptide chains by translation at ribosomes, linking genotype to phenotype
mcqs.why: Central dogma: DNA to RNA by transcription and RNA to protein by translation at ribosomes; proteins link genotype (DNA) to phenotype, while DNA replication is DNA to DNA by DNA polymerase.

lessons.title: Enzymes: Biological Catalysts and the Active Site
lessons.notes_html:
Thousands of chemical reactions take place in the body of a living organism. The sum of all these reactions is called metabolism. A special group of chemicals responsible for facilitating and speeding up these reactions is called enzymes. They catalyse almost all metabolic reactions in the body, e.g. in the digestive tract.

The term enzyme was derived from a Greek word enzymon, meaning leavened. The first enzyme was discovered by Payen and Persoz from germinating barley seeds in 1833 and named diastase. The term enzyme was introduced by Wilhelm Kuhne in 1877. Enzymes are biological polymers that catalyse chemical reactions. They are thermolabile biocatalysts: mostly protein in nature, specific in function and coded by DNA.

Enzymes work both inside and outside the cell. The substance on which an enzyme acts is called the substrate. When an enzyme combines with the substrate it forms an enzyme-substrate complex. After the reaction, product is formed and the enzyme itself remains unchanged, so it can be used again. A few catalytic RNA molecules called ribozymes can also catalyse a specific substrate, e.g. peptidyl transferase controls polypeptide elongation during translation.

4.1 Active Site of Enzyme (Structure)

Enzymes are generally globular proteins: a linear chain of amino acids which gives rise to a three-dimensional structure. The sequence of amino acids specifies the structure of the active site, which determines the catalytic activity of the enzyme. The active site is a specific, charge-bearing, three-dimensional cavity. Its shape is designed according to the reactant (substrate), so it is specific for a particular substrate, although some related reactants can also bind to it. An enzyme may have one or more active sites.

  • Binding site — Where the substrate attaches by non-covalent bonds (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions).
  • Catalytic site — Where catalysis of the substrate takes place, i.e. conversion of substrate into products. It is a very small portion, comprising a small number of amino acids, usually ranging from 3 to 12.
  • Allosteric site — Another site an enzyme may contain; binding here causes conformational changes that increase or decrease enzyme activity.

The active site of an enzyme: the binding site holds the substrate, the catalytic site changes it, and the allosteric site controls activity.

Chemical Nature of Enzymes

Each enzyme has its own specific structure, which is required for its proper functioning. A complete functional enzyme is called a holoenzyme. It consists of two parts: the apoenzyme, the proteinaceous part of the enzyme (mostly inactive), and the cofactor, the non-proteinaceous part. Some enzymes are composed only of protein, with no cofactor attached, e.g. lipase.

Key Points

  • Enzymes are thermolabile biocatalysts: mostly proteins, specific in function, coded by DNA, and unchanged after the reaction.
  • The active site is a charge-bearing 3D cavity with a binding site and a catalytic site of only 3 to 12 amino acids.
  • Holoenzyme = apoenzyme (protein part) + cofactor (non-protein part).
  • Ribozymes are catalytic RNA molecules, an exception to the protein nature of enzymes.

mcqs.q: What is metabolism?
options: The breakdown of food only in the digestive tract of an animal
The single reaction by which glucose is converted into energy
The process by which enzymes are produced inside the nucleus
The sum of all the chemical reactions that take place in the body of a living organism
mcqs.why: Thousands of chemical reactions take place in the body; the sum of all these reactions is called metabolism, and enzymes catalyse almost all metabolic reactions in the body.

mcqs.q: Who introduced the term 'enzyme' and when?
options: Wilhelm Kuhne in 1877; the word comes from the Greek enzymon, meaning leavened
Payen and Persoz in 1833, from the Latin word for barley
Emil Fischer in 1894, from the Greek word for key
Daniel Koshland in 1958, from the Latin word for glove
mcqs.why: The term enzyme was derived from the Greek word enzymon meaning leavened and was introduced by Wilhelm Kuhne in 1877; Payen and Persoz instead discovered the first enzyme, diastase, in 1833.

mcqs.q: What was the first enzyme discovered, and from what source?
options: Urease, discovered from soya bean seeds by Wilhelm Kuhne
Diastase, discovered by Payen and Persoz from germinating barley seeds in 1833
Peptidyl transferase, discovered in ribosomes during translation
Luciferase, discovered in fireflies by Emil Fischer
mcqs.why: The first enzyme was discovered by Payen and Persoz from germinating barley seeds in 1833 and named diastase; the term enzyme itself came later, in 1877.

mcqs.q: Which set of properties correctly describes enzymes in general?
options: Heat-stable inorganic catalysts that are consumed during each reaction
Non-specific catalysts made only of RNA that work only outside cells
Thermolabile biocatalysts, mostly protein in nature, specific in function, coded by DNA, and unchanged after the reaction so they can be used again
Protein catalysts that are permanently altered by every reaction they speed up
mcqs.why: Enzymes are biological polymers that catalyse reactions, work inside and outside the cell, and after forming product the enzyme itself remains unchanged, so it can be used again.

mcqs.q: What are the substrate and the enzyme-substrate complex?
options: The substrate is the final product released at the end of a reaction
The substrate is the non-protein part of a holoenzyme enzyme
The substrate is a site on the enzyme where an inhibitor attaches
The substrate is the substance on which an enzyme acts; when the enzyme combines with it, they form an enzyme-substrate complex, after which product is formed
mcqs.why: The substance on which an enzyme acts is the substrate; enzyme + substrate form an enzyme-substrate complex, product is then formed and the enzyme remains unchanged and reusable.

mcqs.q: What is a ribozyme? Give the example from the notes.
options: A catalytic RNA molecule that can catalyse a specific substrate, for example peptidyl transferase, which controls polypeptide elongation during translation
A protein enzyme that needs a metal ion cofactor to become active
An inactive enzyme stored below zero degrees Celsius in cells
A non-protein cofactor that binds permanently to an apoenzyme
mcqs.why: A few catalytic RNA molecules called ribozymes can also catalyse a specific substrate — peptidyl transferase controls polypeptide elongation during translation — an exception to enzymes being mostly protein.

mcqs.q: Which description of the active site is correct?
options: A flat, uncharged groove that can accept any substrate of any shape
A specific, charge-bearing, three-dimensional cavity whose shape is designed according to the substrate, determined by the sequence of amino acids
A site made entirely of the cofactor, with no amino acids involved
A temporary site that exists only after the product has been released
mcqs.why: Enzymes are generally globular proteins; the amino acid sequence specifies the structure of the active site, a specific charge-bearing 3D cavity specific for a particular substrate, though some related reactants can also bind. An enzyme may have one or more active sites.

mcqs.q: What is the function of the binding site of an enzyme?
options: It is where the substrate is converted into products during catalysis
It is where an allosteric regulator changes the enzyme's activity
It is where the substrate attaches by non-covalent bonds such as hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions
It is where the cofactor is permanently and tightly bound
mcqs.why: The active site has a binding site, where the substrate attaches by non-covalent bonds (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions), and a catalytic site, where catalysis takes place.

mcqs.q: What is special about the catalytic site of an enzyme?
options: It covers most of the enzyme surface and contains hundreds of amino acids
It is the site where inhibitors permanently destroy the enzyme
It exists only in enzymes that follow the induced fit model
It is where conversion of substrate into products takes place, and it is a very small portion of the enzyme, comprising usually only 3 to 12 amino acids
mcqs.why: The catalytic site is a very small portion of the active site, usually ranging from 3 to 12 amino acids, where the substrate is converted into products.

mcqs.q: What is a holoenzyme, and which enzyme is given as protein-only?
options: A complete functional enzyme made of an apoenzyme (protein part) plus a cofactor (non-protein part); lipase is an example of an enzyme composed only of protein, with no cofactor
An enzyme made only of a cofactor with no protein part at all; hexokinase is the protein-only example
The inactive form of an enzyme before its substrate binds to it
An enzyme that has been denatured by heating to 45-50 degrees Celsius
mcqs.why: A complete functional enzyme is a holoenzyme: apoenzyme (proteinaceous, mostly inactive) + cofactor (non-proteinaceous); some enzymes such as lipase are composed only of protein with no cofactor attached.

lessons.title: Enzyme Cofactors: Inorganic Ions, Coenzymes and Prosthetic Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Enzyme cofactors are non-protein molecules or ions that help an enzyme function properly. Without these cofactors, many enzymes cannot catalyse reactions. Cofactors help enzymes in different ways, like binding the substrate, stabilizing the enzyme structure, and participating in the chemical reactions.

Types of Cofactor

A cofactor can be an inorganic metal ion, or an organic compound like flavin or haeme. The three types are compared below.

TypeHow it attachesExamples and work
Inorganic metal ionsLoosely attached activators, easily separatedFe, Mg, Zn, Ca, Cu, K and Co ions. They help in making the enzyme-substrate complex, by moulding the active site or the shape of the substrate.
CoenzymesOrganic, detachable and loosely attached; released from the active site during the reactionNADH, NADPH, FADH₂ and ATP. Most vitamins are coenzymes or components of coenzymes, which is why vitamins are needed in our daily diet.
Prosthetic groupsTightly bound, hence a permanent part of the enzymeHaeme in haemoglobin and myoglobin, biotin, flavin and ubiquinone.

Examples from the Book

  • Metal ion as activator — ATP + Glucose + Hexokinase + Mg → ADP + Glucose 6-phosphate. The Mg ion activates hexokinase.
  • Coenzyme in action — Ethyl alcohol + Alcohol dehydrogenase + NAD → Acetaldehyde + NADH₂. The coenzyme NAD carries hydrogen during the reaction.
  • Prosthetic group — Haeme stays permanently bound in haemoglobin and myoglobin.

So the apoenzyme alone is mostly inactive. It becomes a working holoenzyme only when the correct cofactor joins it, and the kind of attachment — loose or permanent — separates metal ions and coenzymes from prosthetic groups.

Key Points

  • Cofactors are the non-protein part of an enzyme; they help in binding substrate, stabilizing structure and taking part in reactions.
  • Metal ions are loosely attached inorganic activators, e.g. Mg with hexokinase.
  • Coenzymes are loosely attached organic molecules, often from vitamins, e.g. NAD, NADH, NADPH and FADH₂.
  • Prosthetic groups are tightly and permanently bound, e.g. haeme.

mcqs.q: What is a cofactor and how does it help an enzyme?
options: A non-protein molecule or ion that helps the enzyme function, by binding the substrate, stabilizing the enzyme structure and participating in the chemical reactions
The protein part of an enzyme that contains the active site
A substrate that is permanently changed into product by the enzyme
A protein that inhibits the enzyme by blocking its active site
mcqs.why: Cofactors are the non-protein part of an enzyme; without them many enzymes cannot catalyse reactions. A cofactor can be an inorganic metal ion or an organic compound like flavin or haeme.

mcqs.q: How are inorganic metal ion cofactors attached, and what do they do?
options: They are tightly and permanently bound as a permanent part of the enzyme

They are loosely attached activators that are easily separated, such as Fe, Mg, Zn, Ca, Cu, K and Co ions, and they help make the enzyme-substrate complex by moulding the active site or the shape of the substrate
They are organic molecules derived from vitamins in the daily diet
They attach only to the allosteric site and switch the enzyme off
mcqs.why: Metal ions are loosely attached inorganic activators, easily separated; they help in making the enzyme-substrate complex by moulding the active site or the shape of the substrate.

mcqs.q: In the hexokinase reaction given in the notes, what is the role of the Mg ion?
options: Mg acts as the substrate that is converted into glucose 6-phosphate
Mg acts as a prosthetic group permanently bound to glucose
Mg acts as a metal ion activator of hexokinase in the reaction ATP + glucose -> ADP + glucose 6-phosphate
Mg acts as a competitive inhibitor that slows hexokinase down
mcqs.why: The book's example of a metal ion activator is: ATP + Glucose + Hexokinase + Mg -> ADP + Glucose 6-phosphate; the Mg ion activates the enzyme hexokinase.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes coenzymes correctly?
options: They are inorganic metal ions that are easily separated from the enzyme
They are tightly bound and form a permanent part of the enzyme structure
They are protein molecules that make up the apoenzyme part
They are organic, detachable and loosely attached, released from the active site during the reaction; examples are NADH, NADPH, FADH2 and ATP
mcqs.why: Coenzymes are organic and loosely attached like metal ions, but unlike prosthetic groups they detach; most vitamins are coenzymes or components of coenzymes, which is why vitamins are needed in the daily diet.
