In favourable conditions the spores germinate, releasing a haploid biflagellated or amoeboid cell; two such cells fuse into a diploid zygote, which feeds, grows and again forms a multinucleated plasmodium by mitosis.

b) Water Molds (Oomycota)

Oomycota consists of water molds, white rusts and downy mildews. All members are parasites or saprotrophs; most are aquatic and some live in soil. Their hyphae are aseptate and their walls contain cellulose, not chitin.

  • Asexual reproduction — Biflagellated zoospores are formed in a sporangium and, after release, give rise to a new body.
  • Sexual reproduction — The female gametangium is the oogonium and the male the antheridium; gametes are produced by meiosis. Antheridia contain several male nuclei; oogonia contain 2–8 eggs. Male gametes enter the oogonium and fuse with the eggs, forming zygotes that develop a thick wall — the oospore, which later gives rise to a new body.

8.3 Importance of Protists

  • Useful — protozoans and fungus-like protists: zooplanktons feed on phytoplankton and are important primary consumers in the food chain; fungus-like protists are used in genetics and other physiological research.
  • Useful — algae: euglenoids are used in research; dinoflagellates are food for small ocean animals; diatoms are an important source of food and oxygen for heterotrophs. Algin from brown algae is used in ice creams, toothpastes and shaving creams; brown algae also give vitamins A, C, D and E, serve as fertilizer, and kelps are human food in many countries. Agar from red algae is a culture medium for bacterial growth, used for capsules of vitamins and medicines and as a base of cosmetics. Green algae are important producers; Chlorella is used for photosynthesis research, in the synthesis of antibiotics, and as single cell protein (SCP) "health food", especially in Taiwan and Japan.
  • Harmful — protozoans: malaria (Plasmodium) is one of the most common infectious diseases — according to a WHO survey, 1 to 2 million people die from it every year. Acanthamoeba causes eye infections in contact lens users, Entamoeba histolytica causes amoebic dysentery, and Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness.
  • Harmful — plant-like and fungus-like: dinoflagellates sometimes produce a neurotoxin that kills fish and causes paralytic shellfish poisoning, and they sometimes block water pipes. Phytophthora infestans causes late blight of potato, responsible for the Irish potato famines of 1845 and 1847 (deaths from 250,000 to more than one million); white rusts and downy mildews are also important plant diseases.

Key Points

  • Fungus-like protists have hyphae but are not true fungi: they have centrioles, cellulose walls and motile sex cells.
  • Slime molds alternate between a mobile, multinucleated plasmodium and a stationary, spore-forming filamentous form.
  • Oomycota reproduce asexually by biflagellated zoospores and sexually by oogamy, forming thick-walled oospores.
  • Useful protists give food, oxygen, algin, agar and single cell protein; harmful ones cause malaria, dysentery, sleeping sickness and late blight of potato.

mcqs.q: Why are fungus-like protists not classified as true fungi?
options: They have chitin walls and no centrioles
They have centrioles, cellulose cell walls and motile sex cells, which fungi do not have
They are photosynthetic like algae
They lack hyphae in every phase
mcqs.why: Fungus-like protists have hyphae but differ from true fungi by having centrioles (absent in fungi), cellulose walls instead of chitin, and motile sex cells which fungi do not form.

mcqs.q: What is the plasmodium stage of a slime mold such as Physarum?
options: A haploid spore formed inside a sporangium
A biflagellated zoospore formed in water
The feeding stage: a diploid, multinucleated mass of cytoplasm covered by a slime sheath, up to 30 cm in diameter
A thick-walled oospore in an oogonium
mcqs.why: The mobile plasmodium is the feeding stage, a diploid multinucleated mass streaming over damp decaying logs and leaf litter, ingesting bacteria, yeast and decaying organic matter.

mcqs.q: How does a slime mold plasmodium return after forming spores?
options: Spores divide by binary fission directly into plasmodia
Zoospores enter an oogonium and form oospores
Conidia on conidiophores germinate into plasmodia
In unfavourable conditions it forms haploid spores by meiosis in sporangia; spores germinate to haploid cells that fuse into a diploid zygote, which forms a new plasmodium by mitosis
mcqs.why: The stationary form produces haploid spores by meiosis inside sporangia; germinating spores release haploid biflagellated or amoeboid cells, two fuse into a diploid zygote, and mitosis rebuilds the multinucleated plasmodium.

mcqs.q: Oomycota includes which organisms, and what are their hyphae and walls like?
options: Water molds, white rusts and downy mildews; hyphae are aseptate and walls contain cellulose, not chitin
Slime molds only; hyphae are septate with chitin walls
Mushrooms and bracket fungi; walls contain chitin
Yeast and truffles; walls contain silica
mcqs.why: Oomycota consists of water molds, white rusts and downy mildews, all parasites or saprotrophs, with aseptate hyphae and cellulose walls, not chitin.

mcqs.q: How does sexual reproduction occur in water molds?
options: Two gametangia conjugate and form a zygospore
Male nuclei from the antheridium enter the oogonium containing 2-8 eggs and fuse with them, forming thick-walled oospores
Ascospores form inside an ascus after karyogamy
Basidiospores form on gills under a cap
mcqs.why: In Oomycota the female gametangium is the oogonium and the male the antheridium; male gametes enter and fuse with the 2-8 eggs, forming zygotes that develop a thick wall, the oospore.

mcqs.q: What useful products come from brown and red algae respectively?
options: Agar from brown algae; algin from red algae
Both give only single cell protein
Algin from brown algae for ice creams, toothpastes and shaving creams; agar from red algae as a culture medium and for capsules and cosmetics
Algin for culture media; agar for ice creams only
mcqs.why: Algin from brown algae is used in ice creams, toothpastes and shaving creams, while agar from red algae is a culture medium for bacterial growth, used for capsules of vitamins and medicines and as a base of cosmetics.

mcqs.q: Chlorella is used for which purposes in the notes?
options: Making algin for shaving creams
Causing late blight of potato
Producing neurotoxin that kills fish
Photosynthesis research, synthesis of antibiotics, and as single cell protein (SCP) health food, especially in Taiwan and Japan
mcqs.why: Green algae are important producers and Chlorella is used for photosynthesis research, in synthesis of antibiotics, and as single cell protein health food especially in Taiwan and Japan.

mcqs.q: How many people die from malaria every year according to the WHO survey cited?
options: 1 to 2 million people every year
250,000 to 1 million people in total
About 5,000 people every year
More than 10 million people every year
mcqs.why: Malaria caused by Plasmodium is one of the most common infectious diseases; according to a WHO survey, 1 to 2 million people die from it every year.

mcqs.q: Phytophthora infestans causes which disaster-linked disease?
options: White rust of crops in wet soil
Late blight of potato, responsible for the Irish potato famines of 1845 and 1847
Paralytic shellfish poisoning in humans
Amoebic dysentery in the intestine
mcqs.why: Phytophthora infestans causes late blight of potato, responsible for the Irish potato famines of 1845 and 1847, with deaths from 250,000 to more than one million.

mcqs.q: Dinoflagellates can be harmful in which ways, per the notes?
options: They cause malaria and sleeping sickness
They cause eye infections in contact lens users
They sometimes produce a neurotoxin that kills fish and causes paralytic shellfish poisoning, and they sometimes block water pipes
They penetrate root cells and form mycorrhizae
mcqs.why: Harmful plant-like protists include dinoflagellates producing neurotoxin causing fish kills and paralytic shellfish poisoning and blocking water pipes; Acanthamoeba, a protozoan, causes eye infections in contact lens users.

lessons.title: Fungi: Zygomycota and Ascomycota
lessons.notes_html:
Fungi are a very large, diverse group of spore-producing thallophytes. They look like plants but do not have chlorophyll. They are heterotrophs, living as saprotrophs or parasites, contain chitin in their cell walls instead of cellulose, and store food as glycogen. The main body of a fungus is the mycelium, made of thin thread-like hyphae. Fungi are classified into four main groups: Zygomycota, Ascomycota, Basidiomycota and Deuteromycota.

1. Zygomycota (Zygomycetes)

This phylum has about 2000 species, called zygospore-producing fungi or conjugating fungi because of conjugation and zygospore formation. They are mainly saprophytes on dead, decomposing matter: moist stale bread, jelly, horse dung, decaying fruits, cheese, moist leather and soil humus. The hyphae are non-septate and the mycelium is well developed and branched. Examples: Rhizopus (black bread mold) and Pilobolus (spitting fungus).

  • Asexual reproduction — By conidia and spores. Spores form in a sporangium; it bursts, spores are dispersed by wind, and on a suitable place form a new mycelium.
  • Sexual reproduction (conjugation) — Between hyphae (stolons) of two strains, plus (+) and minus (-). Nuclei accumulate at each tip; the tip swells and a septum cuts it off as a gametangium. The (+) and (-) gametangia meet by hormonal action, their walls dissolve by enzymes, and the nuclei fuse into a diploid zygote. A thick wall forms around it: the zygospore, resistant to unfavourable conditions. After rest it germinates by meiosis: its wall splits, a vertical hypha (promycelium) emerges, and its tip forms a sporangium full of spores, which give new mycelia.

2. Ascomycota (Ascomycetes)

Ascomycota are called sac fungi because their sexual spores form in little sacs called asci (singular: ascus). They occur in many habitats all year, mostly terrestrial, some marine or fresh water. It is the largest group of fungi, about 32,000 species, unicellular (yeast) or multicellular (truffles). The mycelium has septate hyphae with porous septa, so cytoplasm moves between compartments, and the walls contain a large amount of chitin. Examples: morels, truffles, yeast and Neurospora.

  • Asexual reproduction — There are no sporangia in sac fungi. In budding (yeast), a small outgrowth (bud) forms on the parent, grows and separates as a new independent yeast. Conidia (naked spores) form at the tips of specialized hyphae called conidiophores, are dispersed by wind, and each forms a new mycelium on a suitable place.
  • Sexual reproduction — Two monokaryotic hyphae (n) grow together and their cytoplasm mingles (plasmogamy); the nuclei migrate but do not fuse, forming dikaryotic hyphae (n+n), which form a fruiting body, the ascocarp. In the ascus the two nuclei fuse (karyogamy) into a diploid zygote (2n); meiosis gives four haploid nuclei and mitosis in each gives eight haploid ascospores. The mature ascus swells and bursts, and air currents carry the ascospores to germinate into new mycelia.

Key Points

  • Fungi are heterotrophic thallophytes with chitin walls; they store glycogen and are classified into Zygomycota, Ascomycota, Basidiomycota and Deuteromycota.
  • Zygomycetes (about 2000 species) have non-septate hyphae and reproduce sexually by conjugation, forming a thick-walled zygospore. Example: Rhizopus.
  • Ascomycetes (about 32,000 species, the largest group) have septate hyphae and form eight ascospores inside each ascus.
  • Sac fungi reproduce asexually by budding (yeast) and by conidia formed on conidiophores.

mcqs.q: What food do fungi store, and what is in their cell walls?
options: They store starch and have cellulose in their walls
They store laminarin and have silica in their walls
They store food as glycogen and have chitin in their cell walls
They store oil and have peptidoglycan in their walls
mcqs.why: Fungi are heterotrophs without chlorophyll that contain chitin in their cell walls instead of cellulose and store food as glycogen; their body is a mycelium of hyphae.

mcqs.q: How many species does Zygomycota have, and what are its hyphae like?
options: About 32,000 species, with septate hyphae
About 22,300 species, with perforated septa
About 25,000 species, with no sexual stage
About 2000 species, with non-septate hyphae and a well developed branched mycelium
mcqs.why: Zygomycota has about 2000 species called zygospore-producing or conjugating fungi; the hyphae are non-septate, with examples Rhizopus (black bread mold) and Pilobolus (spitting fungus).

mcqs.q: Where are zygomycetes commonly found as saprophytes?
options: On moist stale bread, jelly, horse dung, decaying fruits, cheese, moist leather and soil humus
Only inside the human intestine
On gills under mushroom caps
In warm ocean water as seaweeds
mcqs.why: Zygomycetes are mainly saprophytes on dead decomposing matter including moist stale bread, jelly, horse dung, decaying fruits, cheese, moist leather and soil humus.

mcqs.q: In zygomycete conjugation, what forms after the + and - gametangia fuse?
options: An ascus containing eight ascospores
A diploid zygote around which a thick wall forms, making the resistant zygospore
A basidium bearing four basidiospores
An oospore inside an oogonium
mcqs.why: In conjugation the + and - gametangia meet, walls dissolve and nuclei fuse into a diploid zygote; a thick wall forms around it as the zygospore, resistant to unfavourable conditions.

mcqs.q: How does the zygospore germinate after its rest period?
options: By budding directly into yeast cells
By forming conidia on conidiophores only
By meiosis: its wall splits, a promycelium emerges and its tip forms a sporangium full of spores
By plasmogamy followed by karyogamy in an ascus
mcqs.why: After rest the zygospore germinates by meiosis, its wall splits, a vertical hypha called promycelium emerges, and its tip forms a sporangium whose spores give new mycelia.

mcqs.q: Why are Ascomycota called sac fungi, and how large is the group?
options: Their spores form on club-shaped basidia; about 22,300 species
Their spores form in sporangia; about 2000 species
They have no sacs; about 25,000 species with no sexual stage
Their sexual spores form in little sacs called asci; it is the largest group with about 32,000 species
mcqs.why: Ascomycota are sac fungi because sexual spores form in sacs called asci (singular ascus); with about 32,000 species including yeast, morels, truffles and Neurospora, it is the largest fungal group.

mcqs.q: How does asexual reproduction differ in sac fungi compared with zygomycetes?
options: Sac fungi have no sporangia; they reproduce by budding in yeast and by conidia formed on conidiophores
Sac fungi reproduce only by sporangium spores
Sac fungi reproduce by zoospores in sporangia
Sac fungi reproduce by basidiospores on gills
mcqs.why: There are no sporangia in sac fungi; budding forms a new yeast from a small outgrowth, and conidia (naked spores) form at tips of specialized hyphae called conidiophores and are dispersed by wind.

mcqs.q: What sequence leads to eight ascospores inside an ascus?
options: Karyogamy first, then plasmogamy, giving four ascospores
Plasmogamy forms dikaryotic hyphae (n+n); in the ascus karyogamy gives a diploid zygote, meiosis gives four haploid nuclei, and mitosis in each gives eight ascospores
Meiosis alone gives eight spores without mitosis
Two zygotes fuse to give sixteen ascospores
mcqs.why: Two monokaryotic hyphae undergo plasmogamy without nuclear fusion, forming dikaryotic hyphae and an ascocarp; in the ascus karyogamy, then meiosis (4 nuclei) and mitosis produce eight haploid ascospores.

mcqs.q: What are the hyphae and walls of ascomycetes like?
options: Non-septate hyphae with cellulose walls
Aseptate hyphae with silica walls
Septate hyphae with porous septa so cytoplasm moves between compartments, and walls with a large amount of chitin
Hyphae without any septa or chitin
mcqs.why: The ascomycete mycelium has septate hyphae with porous septa so cytoplasm moves between compartments, and the walls contain a large amount of chitin.

mcqs.q: Which set contains only ascomycete examples from the notes?
options: Rhizopus and Pilobolus
Mushrooms and bracket fungi
Pilobolus, bracket fungi and Aspergillus
Morels, truffles, yeast and Neurospora
mcqs.why: Examples of Ascomycota given are morels, truffles, yeast and Neurospora; Rhizopus and Pilobolus are zygomycetes and mushrooms are basidiomycetes.

lessons.title: Basidiomycota, Deuteromycota and Yeast
lessons.notes_html:
3. Basidiomycota (Basidiomycetes)

Basidiomycetes are also called club fungi, because they develop club-shaped reproductive structures called basidia; at the tip of each basidium, four basidiospores develop. Nearly 22,300 species have been discovered, e.g. mushrooms and bracket fungi. The hyphae are septate, with perforated septa, so cytoplasm moves among the cells.

  • Sexual reproduction — The +ve and -ve primary monokaryotic hyphae grow towards each other; their cytoplasm fuses (plasmogamy) through a bridge and nuclei migrate into the other hypha, forming a secondary, dikaryotic mycelium (n+n) whose cells each contain two haploid nuclei that do not fuse. This mycelium forms a fruiting body, the basidiocarp: a stalk and a cap, the lower surface of the cap bearing many thin plates called gills, radiating from the stalk to the edges.
  • In the gills, the two nuclei in each basidium fuse into a diploid zygote (2n), which immediately undergoes meiosis to produce four (+) and (-) haploid basidiospores. Released spores are carried by wind and animals to a moist habitat and germinate into +ve and -ve mycelia.

A mushroom (basidiocarp): basidia on the gills under the cap produce four basidiospores each.

4. Deuteromycota (Deuteromycetes)

This phylum includes about 25,000 species, e.g. Aspergillus and Penicillium. They are called imperfect fungi because no sexual stage has been observed in their life cycle. They live saprophytically or parasitically on plants, and their morphology and biochemistry show they are sac fungi that have lost the ability to reproduce sexually. Hyphae may be non-septate or septate. Asexual reproduction is by conidiospores formed on special hyphae called conidiophores; the non-motile conidia are dispersed by wind, water or animals, and each gives rise to a new mycelium.

8.5 Yeast — a Single-Celled Fungus

Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) is a unicellular fungus, round or oval and a few micrometers in diameter, heterotrophic, and naturally found on fruits and leaves. Its importance:

  • Food industry — Used commercially to prepare bread: mixed with flour, it ferments and the CO₂ formed is trapped as bubbles, so the dough rises with a light texture; alcohol and CO₂ evaporate during baking, making the bread porous. Different strains give different flavoured breads.
  • Beverages — Ethyl alcohol is prepared by fermentation of grapes, cereals, potatoes, fruits and sugar cane: C₆H₁₂O₆ + yeast —(enzymes)→ 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.
  • Vaccines and medicines — Yeast is the only organism used for the formation of the hepatitis B vaccine, and is used in medicines such as ergotine (for migraine) and lovastatin (for lowering blood cholesterol).
  • Research and gene vector — Used to study the effects of chemicals and medicines, in genetic recombination experiments and to study mutation; its plasmids can carry genes from one body to another (gene vector).

Key Points

  • Basidiomycetes (club fungi, about 22,300 species) form four basidiospores on each basidium; the basidiocarp has a stalk, cap and gills.
  • Deuteromycetes (imperfect fungi, about 25,000 species) have no observed sexual stage and reproduce by conidiospores. Examples: Aspergillus, Penicillium.
  • Yeast is a unicellular fungus used in bread making and alcohol production by fermentation, and for the hepatitis B vaccine, medicines, research and as a gene vector.

mcqs.q: Why are basidiomycetes called club fungi, and how many spores does each basidium bear?
options: They develop sac-shaped asci, each bearing eight spores
They develop sporangia, each bearing many conidia
They are club fungi bearing two spores per basidium
They develop club-shaped basidia, each bearing four basidiospores at its tip
mcqs.why: Basidiomycetes are club fungi because of club-shaped basidia; at the tip of each basidium, four basidiospores develop, and nearly 22,300 species are known, e.g. mushrooms and bracket fungi.

mcqs.q: What are the parts of a mushroom basidiocarp and where are the basidia found?
options: A stalk and a cap, with many thin plates called gills under the cap bearing the basidia
A blade, stipe and holdfast with air bladders
An oogonium and antheridium on the stalk
A promycelium and sporangium on the cap
mcqs.why: The basidiocarp is a stalk and a cap whose lower surface bears many thin plates called gills radiating from stalk to edges, where basidia produce the basidiospores.

mcqs.q: In basidiomycete sexual reproduction, what is the secondary mycelium?
options: A monokaryotic mycelium with one nucleus per cell only
A dikaryotic mycelium (n+n) formed after plasmogamy, whose cells each contain two haploid nuclei that do not fuse
A diploid mycelium formed immediately by karyogamy
A mycelium with no nuclei in its hyphae
mcqs.why: After plasmogamy between +ve and -ve primary hyphae, nuclei migrate without fusing, forming the secondary dikaryotic mycelium (n+n) that forms the basidiocarp.

mcqs.q: Why are deuteromycetes called imperfect fungi?
options: Their hyphae are imperfectly septate
They cannot form any spores at all
No sexual stage has been observed in their life cycle
They are imperfect parasites of humans only
mcqs.why: Deuteromycota, about 25,000 species e.g. Aspergillus and Penicillium, are called imperfect fungi because no sexual stage has been observed; they are sac fungi that have lost the ability to reproduce sexually.

mcqs.q: How do deuteromycetes reproduce asexually?
options: By budding only, like yeast
By biflagellated zoospores in a sporangium
By conjugation forming a zygospore
By conidiospores formed on special hyphae called conidiophores, dispersed by wind, water or animals
mcqs.why: Asexual reproduction in deuteromycetes is by conidiospores on conidiophores; the non-motile conidia are dispersed by wind, water or animals and each gives rise to a new mycelium.

mcqs.q: What is yeast, scientifically and in appearance?
options: Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a unicellular fungus, round or oval and a few micrometers in diameter, found on fruits and leaves
Rhizopus stolonifer, a multicellular mold on bread
Penicillium notatum, a septate sac fungus
Agaricus, an edible mushroom with gills
mcqs.why: Yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) is a unicellular heterotrophic fungus, round or oval, a few micrometers in diameter, naturally found on fruits and leaves.

mcqs.q: How does yeast make bread dough rise?
options: It releases oxygen that inflates the dough
It ferments and the CO2 formed is trapped as bubbles, so the dough rises with a light texture and becomes porous on baking
It produces alcohol that dissolves the flour
Its hyphae spread through the dough lifting it
mcqs.why: Mixed with flour, yeast ferments and CO2 is trapped as bubbles so dough rises; alcohol and CO2 evaporate during baking, making the bread porous, and different strains give different flavours.

mcqs.q: What is the fermentation equation for beverage alcohol production by yeast?
options: C6H12O6 -> C2H5OH + CO2 only, unbalanced
2H2S + CO2 -> (CH2O)n + H2O + S
C6H12O6 + yeast (enzymes) -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2
mcqs.why: Ethyl alcohol is prepared by fermentation of grapes, cereals, potatoes, fruits and sugar cane: C6H12O6 with yeast enzymes gives 2C2H5OH + 2CO2, as written in the notes.

mcqs.q: For which vaccine is yeast the only organism used, according to the notes?
options: The TB vaccine
The pneumonia vaccine
The typhoid vaccine
The hepatitis B vaccine
mcqs.why: Yeast is the only organism used for formation of the hepatitis B vaccine, and is also used in medicines such as ergotine for migraine and lovastatin for lowering blood cholesterol.

mcqs.q: How is yeast used as a gene vector in research?
options: Its plasmids can carry genes from one body to another
Its basidiospores carry human genes into mushrooms
Its cell wall chitin transfers DNA between bacteria
It conjugates with bacteria through a pilus
mcqs.why: In research yeast is used to study effects of chemicals and medicines, in genetic recombination experiments and to study mutation; its plasmids can carry genes from one body to another as a gene vector.

lessons.title: Antibiotics, Mutualism, Edible Fungi and the Roles of Fungi
lessons.notes_html:
8.6 Fungi from which Antibiotics are Obtained

Many antibiotics are prepared from fungi:

Name of AntibioticSpecies of Fungus
CyclosporinsTolypocladium inflatum
CephalosporinCephalosporin acremonum
PenicillinPenicillium notatum and P. crysogenum
GriseofulvinP. nigricans, P. griseofulvum
CitrininP. citrinum
PalutinP. palutum
Fusidic acidFusidium coccineum

8.7 Mutualism in Fungi

Mutualism is the association between two different organisms in which both partners get benefits. Fungi form two mutualistic associations:

  • Lichens — Made up of a fungus (mostly ascomycetes), a cyanobacterium (blue green algae) and a green alga (Chlorophyta). The fungus receives nutrients from the algal cells, and the algal cells get protection from desiccation. Lichens survive where there is low moisture, low temperature and even no soil at all. The body has three layers: an upper layer, thin and tough, of fungal hyphae; a middle layer of fungal hyphae interwoven with photosynthetic cells; and a bottom layer of loosely packed fungal hyphae.
  • Mycorrhizae — From Greek words meaning "fungal roots": a mutualistic relationship between soil fungi and the roots of most higher vascular plants, occurring in about 90–95% of all land plants; such plants show better growth. The fungus gets sugar, amino acids and other substances from the roots, and benefits the plant by decomposing organic matter in the soil and by increasing the absorptive surface for water and inorganic salts like K, Zn, Cu, P, etc. In endomycorrhizae the hyphae penetrate only the cell wall of the outer root cells, form coils, swellings and minute branches, and extend several centimeters into the soil; common with angiosperms. In ectomycorrhizae the hyphae form a dense net around the root, remain between the cells without penetrating them, and form no coils or swellings; mostly with pines and firs, and less beneficial than endomycorrhizae.

8.8 Edible Fungi

  • Yeast — A good source of vitamin B and protein; yeast is composed of 50% protein.
  • Morels and truffles — Morel (Morchella esculenata) and truffle (Tuber melanosporum) are used as proteinaceous food.
  • Mushrooms — More than 200 species are edible, e.g. Agaricus spp.; used in soups, to flavor cheeses and in pizzas. Warning: certain mushrooms are poisonous and can even cause death, e.g. Amanita phalloides (Death cap).

8.9 Ecological Importance of Fungi

  • Decomposers — Fungi decompose dead leaves, stems and animals; their potent enzymes break tough materials like lignin and cellulose that other organisms cannot digest, which is especially important in woodlands. They prevent the accumulation of dead organic matter on earth, so they are called scavengers.
  • Recyclers — Nutrients blocked in dead bodies are brought back into the soil for other organisms, and a large amount of CO₂ is released into the air, which photosynthetic organisms use to prepare food. Thus fungi maintain the ecological balance of the environment.

8.10 Pathogenic Role of Fungi

  • Plant diseases — Rusts of cereals by Puccinia and smuts of cereals by Ustilago (both Basidiomycota); sac fungi cause Dutch elm disease, chestnut blight, red rot of sugarcane, powdery mildews, potato wilt, cotton root wilt, apple scab and brown rot of stone fruits.
  • Animal diseases — Aspergillus spp. cause reproductive disorders (e.g. abortion); ringworm in dogs and horses by Trichophyton rubrum and Microsporum audovinii; carp and salmon are affected by Saprolegnia parasitica; Aspergillus causes lung infection of chickens.
  • Human diseases — Ringworm and athlete's foot; ergotism from purple ergot of rye (nervous spasm, convulsions, psychotic delusions, gangrene); candidiasis of mouth, throat and vagina by Candida spp.; Rhizopus and Mucor cause histoplasmosis (lung infection) and infections of the digestive tract and brain; Aspergillus flavus produces aflatoxin, a cancer-causing chemical in improperly stored grains; dandruff is caused by Microsporum furfur; Neurospora and Fusarium infect the cornea of the eye.

Key Points

  • Important antibiotics from fungi include penicillin (Penicillium), cephalosporin, griseofulvin, cyclosporins and fusidic acid.
  • Lichens are a mutualism of a fungus with an alga or cyanobacterium; mycorrhizae are a mutualism of fungi with plant roots, found in 90–95% of land plants.
  • Edible fungi include yeast, morels, truffles and more than 200 mushrooms; Amanita phalloides (Death cap) is poisonous.
  • Fungi are decomposers and recyclers maintaining ecological balance, but also cause diseases of plants, animals and humans.

mcqs.q: Which fungus produces penicillin, according to the antibiotic table?
options: Penicillium notatum and P. crysogenum (book spelling)
Tolypocladium inflatum
Cephalosporin acremonum
Fusidium coccineum
mcqs.why: The table lists penicillin from Penicillium notatum and P. crysogenum; Tolypocladium inflatum gives cyclosporins and Fusidium coccineum gives fusidic acid.

mcqs.q: Match the antibiotic to its fungus: griseofulvin.
options: Produced by Penicillium citrinum
Produced by P. nigricans and P. griseofulvum
Produced by Tolypocladium inflatum
Produced by Fusidium coccineum
mcqs.why: Griseofulvin is listed from P. nigricans and P. griseofulvum; P. citrinum gives citrinin and Tolypocladium inflatum gives cyclosporins.

mcqs.q: What organisms make up a lichen in the notes?
options: Two fungi and a moss
A fungus and the roots of a pine tree
A fungus (mostly ascomycetes), a cyanobacterium (blue green algae) and a green alga (Chlorophyta)
A bacterium and a green alga only
mcqs.why: Lichens are made up of a fungus, a cyanobacterium and a green alga; the fungus receives nutrients from algal cells and the algal cells get protection from desiccation.

mcqs.q: What are the three layers of the lichen body?
options: A cap, gills and a stalk
An upper algal layer, a middle root layer and a lower soil layer
A cortex, core and spore coat
An upper thin tough layer of fungal hyphae, a middle layer of hyphae interwoven with photosynthetic cells, and a bottom layer of loosely packed fungal hyphae
mcqs.why: The lichen body has three layers: upper thin and tough fungal hyphae, middle hyphae interwoven with photosynthetic cells, and a bottom layer of loosely packed fungal hyphae.

mcqs.q: In what proportion of land plants do mycorrhizae occur, and how do they benefit the plant?
options: In about 90-95% of all land plants; the fungus decomposes organic matter and increases absorptive surface for water and salts like K, Zn, Cu and P
In about 50-60% of land plants; by producing chlorophyll
In about 21% of land plants; by fixing nitrogen gas
In all aquatic plants only; by forming oospores
mcqs.why: Mycorrhizae occur in about 90-95% of all land plants, which show better growth; the fungus gets sugar and amino acids and benefits the plant by decomposition and increased absorption of water and inorganic salts.

mcqs.q: How do endomycorrhizae differ from ectomycorrhizae?
options: Ectomycorrhizae penetrate cells and form coils; endomycorrhizae stay outside

Endomycorrhizae hyphae penetrate only the cell wall of outer root cells, forming coils, swellings and minute branches; ectomycorrhizae form a dense net around the root, remain between cells without penetrating, and form no coils
Both penetrate the root cells and form coils
Endomycorrhizae occur mostly with pines and firs; ectomycorrhizae with angiosperms
mcqs.why: Endomycorrhizae, common with angiosperms, penetrate only the cell wall and form coils and swellings; ectomycorrhizae, mostly with pines and firs, form a net around the root without penetrating and are less beneficial.

mcqs.q: What is the protein content and vitamin value of yeast as food?
options: Yeast is 10% protein and a source of vitamin C
Yeast is 90% protein and a source of vitamin D
Yeast is composed of 50% protein and is a good source of vitamin B
Yeast has no protein but is rich in vitamin A
mcqs.why: Edible fungi include yeast, a good source of vitamin B and protein, with yeast composed of 50% protein; morels and truffles are also used as proteinaceous food.

mcqs.q: Which mushroom is poisonous and can cause death, and what is it called?
options: Agaricus species, called the Death cap
Morchella esculenata, the morel
Tuber melanosporum, the truffle
Amanita phalloides, called the Death cap
mcqs.why: More than 200 mushroom species are edible, e.g. Agaricus spp., but certain mushrooms are poisonous and can even cause death, e.g. Amanita phalloides (Death cap).

mcqs.q: Why are fungi called scavengers in their ecological role?
options: Their potent enzymes break tough materials like lignin and cellulose that other organisms cannot digest, preventing accumulation of dead organic matter
They hunt and kill living animals in woodlands
They produce antibiotics that clean the soil of bacteria
They fix nitrogen from dead bodies into the air
mcqs.why: As decomposers fungi break down dead leaves, stems and animals, digesting lignin and cellulose, preventing accumulation of dead matter, so they are called scavengers and act as recyclers releasing CO2.

mcqs.q: Which human fungal problems are correctly paired in the notes?
options: Aflatoxin is produced by Candida; dandruff by Aspergillus flavus
Aflatoxin, a cancer-causing chemical in improperly stored grains, is produced by Aspergillus flavus; dandruff is caused by Microsporum furfur
Ergotism is caused by Microsporum furfur in grains
Candidiasis of the eye cornea is caused by Neurospora only
mcqs.why: Human diseases listed include candidiasis by Candida spp., ergotism from purple ergot of rye, aflatoxin by Aspergillus flavus in improperly stored grains, and dandruff by Microsporum furfur; Neurospora and Fusarium infect the cornea.

lessons.title: Bryophytes and the Life Cycle of Polytrichum
lessons.notes_html:
Plants are multicellular, predominantly photosynthetic and eukaryotic organisms. They have well-defined body parts, cell walls of cellulose, develop from an embryo, store carbohydrate as starch, and are non-motile. It is the second largest kingdom, comprising over 3,60,000 species. The major groups are bryophytes (seedless, non-vascular), pteridophytes (seedless vascular plants) and the seeded plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms). Plants live in almost all habitats: deserts, mountains, tundra, tropical and subtropical regions, and water.

9.1 Bryophytes

Bryophytes are the first land plants, evolved from green algae; up to now 15,000 species have been discovered. They are homosporous, i.e. they produce one type of spores.

  • They grow mostly in damp, shady places near water. They have no vascular tissues, so transport of minerals and food takes place by diffusion.
  • They need water for fertilization, so they are called amphibious plants (the amphibians of the plant kingdom).
  • The gametophyte generation is dominant, green and photosynthetic, while the sporophyte is non-photosynthetic and dependent on the gametophyte. They are seedless and non-flowering.
  • The male sex organ is the antheridium (many sperms are formed in it); the female sex organ is the archegonium (a single egg is formed in it). They show alternation of generations: dominant gametophyte with reduced sporophyte.
  • Three major groups: Liverworts (Hepaticeae), e.g. Marchantia, Riccia, Pellia; Mosses (Musci), e.g. Funaria, Polytrichum, Sphagnum; Hornworts (Anthocerotae), e.g. Anthoceros, Notothylos, Megaceros. Liverworts are closely related to mosses.

9.2 Life Cycle of Polytrichum

Polytrichum (a moss) shows heteromorphic alternation of generations, because its gametophyte and sporophyte generations have different morphology.

  • Gametophyte generation — Dominant, autotrophic, independent and haploid: a leafy shoot bearing antheridia and archegonia intermixed with multicellular hair-like paraphyses. Many motile sperms form in the antheridium and a single non-motile egg in the archegonium. Water (rain or dew) is necessary: sperms swim in water by their cilia to the archegonium, and only one fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote (2n), retained inside the archegonium.
  • Sporophyte generation — The zygote is the first cell of the sporophyte (2n); it develops into an embryo and then a sporophyte plant, which is dependent on the gametophyte for nutrition. It has three parts: the foot, embedded in the gametophyte and absorbing nutrients from it; the long stalk or seta, which elevates the capsule and provides it food and water; and the capsule (sporangium), inside which spores are formed by meiosis. The haploid spores are unicellular with thick walls, are dispersed by wind, and germinate into a filamentous protonema with buds and branches, which gives rise to a leafy gametophyte again. (The book's exercise notes the ciliated sperms as the only positive evidence of the aquatic ancestry of bryophytes.)

The moss sporophyte: a capsule (sporangium) raised on a seta, with its foot embedded in the leafy gametophyte on which it depends.

Key Points

  • Plants are multicellular, photosynthetic eukaryotes with cellulose walls; they store starch and number over 3,60,000 species.
  • Bryophytes are seedless, non-vascular first land plants — the amphibians of the plant kingdom — with a dominant gametophyte.
  • Bryophytes have three groups: liverworts, mosses and hornworts.
  • In Polytrichum, the dependent sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule) grows on the gametophyte, and its spores germinate into a protonema.

mcqs.q: Which set of features best describes plants as given in the notes?
options: Multicellular eukaryotes with chitin cell walls that store carbohydrate as glycogen and are motile
Multicellular, predominantly photosynthetic eukaryotes with cellulose cell walls that store carbohydrate as starch and are non-motile
Unicellular photosynthetic prokaryotes with cellulose walls that store starch
Multicellular heterotrophic eukaryotes with cellulose walls that store fat
mcqs.why: The notes define plants as multicellular, predominantly photosynthetic and eukaryotic, with cellulose walls, starch storage and a non-motile habit.

mcqs.q: Why are bryophytes called the amphibians of the plant kingdom?
options: They spend half their life in water as fish-like swimmers
They have lungs for breathing on land and gills in water
They need water for fertilization although they live on land
They produce seeds only when flooded with water
mcqs.why: The notes state bryophytes grow in damp places, have no vascular tissue and need water for fertilization, so they are called amphibious plants.

mcqs.q: In bryophytes, which generation is dominant?
options: The sporophyte, which is green and photosynthetic
Both generations are equally dominant and independent
The sporophyte, which is dependent on the gametophyte
The gametophyte, which is green and photosynthetic
mcqs.why: According to the notes the gametophyte generation is dominant, green and photosynthetic, while the sporophyte is non-photosynthetic and dependent on it.

mcqs.q: Bryophytes are described as homosporous. What does this mean?
options: They produce only one type of spore
They produce two types of spores, microspores and megaspores
They produce spores and seeds of the same type
They produce no spores at all
mcqs.why: The notes say bryophytes are homosporous, i.e. they produce one type of spores, unlike heterosporous plants that make two types.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of a bryophyte group with its example is correct?
options: Liverworts (Hepaticeae) — Funaria and Polytrichum
Mosses (Musci) — Funaria, Polytrichum and Sphagnum
Hornworts (Anthocerotae) — Marchantia and Riccia
Mosses (Musci) — Anthoceros and Notothylos
mcqs.why: The notes list mosses as Musci with examples Funaria, Polytrichum and Sphagnum; liverwort examples are Marchantia, Riccia and Pellia, hornworts are Anthoceros, Notothylos and Megaceros.

mcqs.q: In Polytrichum, the sporophyte part that is embedded in the gametophyte and absorbs nutrients from it is the:
options: Seta
Capsule
Foot
Protonema
mcqs.why: The notes describe the foot as embedded in the gametophyte and absorbing nutrients from it; the seta elevates the capsule and the capsule forms spores.

mcqs.q: Put the Polytrichum sequence in the correct order after spore dispersal:
options: Spores germinate directly into a capsule, which then forms a leafy gametophyte
Spores first form a zygote, which then becomes a protonema
Spores form an embryo inside the archegonium and then a protonema
Spores germinate into a filamentous protonema, which bears buds and branches and gives rise to a leafy gametophyte
mcqs.why: The notes state haploid spores are dispersed by wind and germinate into a filamentous protonema with buds and branches, which gives rise to a leafy gametophyte again.

mcqs.q: How do sperms reach the egg in Polytrichum?
options: They swim in water (rain or dew) by their cilia to the archegonium
They are carried by wind inside a pollen tube to the archegonium
They are carried by insects to the archegonium
They move through vascular tissue to the archegonium
mcqs.why: The notes say water is necessary, sperms swim in water by their cilia to the archegonium, and only one fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote.

mcqs.q: The capsule of the Polytrichum sporophyte is important because:
options: Fertilization takes place inside it
Spores are formed inside it by meiosis
It photosynthesises to feed the gametophyte
It anchors the gametophyte in the soil
mcqs.why: The notes call the capsule the sporangium, inside which spores are formed by meiosis; those haploid spores are unicellular with thick walls.

mcqs.q: According to the book's exercise note in this lesson, the only positive evidence of the aquatic ancestry of bryophytes is:
options: The dominant gametophyte
The presence of a protonema
The ciliated sperms
The absence of vascular tissue
mcqs.why: The notes explicitly state the book's exercise notes the ciliated sperms as the only positive evidence of the aquatic ancestry of bryophytes.

lessons.title: Vascular Plants, Their Division and Pteridophytes
lessons.notes_html:
9.3 General Features of Vascular Plants (Tracheophytes)

Vascular plants are the largest and most successful group of land plants. They have vascular tissues: xylem, which gives support and conducts water and dissolved salts from roots to leaves, and phloem, which transports organic food from leaves to other parts. Their xylem has special conducting cells called tracheids, so they are called tracheophyta. They have a diploid (2n) dominant sporophyte and a haploid (n) reduced gametophyte, stomata, well-protected sporangia, true roots, stem and leaves, and heteromorphic alternation of generations. They fall into two major groups:

  • Seedless vascular plants — No seeds are produced, e.g. ferns. Four subgroups: i) Psilopsida, e.g. Psilotum; ii) Lycopsida, e.g. Lycopodium; iii) Sphenopsida, e.g. Horse tail; iv) Pteropsida, e.g. Ferns.
  • Seeded vascular plants — Seeds are produced: i) Gymnosperms, e.g. Pines; ii) Angiosperms, e.g. Rose.

9.4 Division among Pteridophytes, Gymnosperms and Angiosperms

FeaturePteridophytesGymnospermsAngiosperms
Seeds and flowersSeedless, flowerlessSeeded, flowerlessSeeds and flowers present
Vessels in xylemAbsentAbsentPresent
Companion cells in phloemAbsentPresentPresent
Dominant generationSporophyteSporophyteSporophyte
ReproductionBy sporesBy seedsBy seeds
Spores / seedsSpores in sporangiaSeeds on surface of scale leavesSeeds in fruits
Sperms reach eggThrough waterBy pollen tubeBy pollen tube
OriginFirst vascular plants on landEvolved from pteridophytesEvolved from gymnosperms
SporophyllsPresentPresentAbsent
Sporophylls formCone or strobilusCone or strobilusCones absent
ExamplesFernsPine, CycadsRose, Grasses

9.5 General Characters of Pteridophytes

Pteridophytes (Greek: Pteron = feather, Phyton = plant) are seedless, flowerless and fruitless vascular plants with true roots, stems and leaves. The xylem is without vessels and the phloem without companion cells. They show heteromorphic alternation of generations, with a dominant diploid (2n) sporophyte (the main plant body) and a reduced haploid (n) gametophyte.

  • Sporangia burst and spores are dispersed by wind; the spores germinate into gametophytes that are independent from the sporophyte. (A fern differs from a moss in having an independent sporophyte.)
  • The sex organs are multicellular: sperms form in antheridia and eggs in archegonia. Sperms swim in a film of water (rain, dew) to the archegonia, so pteridophytes are water-dependent for fertilization.
  • Examples in the book: Psilotum, Lycopodium, Equisetum and Nephrolepis.

Key Points

  • Vascular plants (tracheophytes) have xylem with tracheids and phloem, true roots, stem and leaves, and a dominant sporophyte.
  • Seedless vascular plants have four subgroups: Psilopsida, Lycopsida, Sphenopsida and Pteropsida; seeded plants are gymnosperms and angiosperms.
  • Pteridophytes are seedless, flowerless and fruitless, with no vessels in xylem and no companion cells in phloem.
  • Pteridophyte gametophytes are independent, but fertilization still needs water for the sperms to swim.

mcqs.q: Xylem and phloem have which respective functions in vascular plants?
options: Xylem transports organic food from leaves; phloem conducts water from roots
Both xylem and phloem conduct only water from roots to leaves
Xylem conducts water and dissolved salts from roots to leaves and gives support; phloem transports organic food from leaves to other parts
Xylem stores food in leaves; phloem gives only mechanical support
mcqs.why: The notes state xylem gives support and conducts water and dissolved salts from roots to leaves, while phloem transports organic food from leaves to other parts.

mcqs.q: Vascular plants are called tracheophytes because their xylem contains:
options: Vessels only, with no tracheids
Companion cells next to sieve tubes
Stomata in the xylem walls
Special conducting cells called tracheids
mcqs.why: The notes say their xylem has special conducting cells called tracheids, so they are called tracheophyta or tracheophytes.

mcqs.q: Which subgroup of seedless vascular plants is correctly matched with its example?
options: Lycopsida — Lycopodium
Psilopsida — Ferns
Sphenopsida — Lycopodium
Pteropsida — Psilotum
mcqs.why: The notes list Psilopsida with Psilotum, Lycopsida with Lycopodium, Sphenopsida with Horse tail and Pteropsida with Ferns.

mcqs.q: Compared with gymnosperms, angiosperms differ in the table by having:
options: No vessels in xylem and seeds on the surface of scale leaves
Vessels in xylem and seeds enclosed in fruits
No companion cells in phloem and reproduction by spores
Sporophylls forming a cone or strobilus
mcqs.why: The comparison table shows angiosperms have vessels present, companion cells present and seeds in fruits, whereas gymnosperms lack vessels and bear seeds on scale leaves.

mcqs.q: In pteridophytes, sperms reach the egg:
options: By a pollen tube, as in gymnosperms
By a pollen tube, as in angiosperms
Through water, by swimming in a film of water
By wind, inside dry pollen grains
mcqs.why: The table and text state pteridophyte sperms reach the egg through water; in both gymnosperms and angiosperms they reach it by a pollen tube.

mcqs.q: Which statement about pteridophytes is correct?
options: They are seeded, flowering plants without true roots
They are non-vascular plants with a dominant gametophyte
They have vessels in xylem and companion cells in phloem
They are seedless, flowerless and fruitless vascular plants with true roots, stems and leaves
mcqs.why: The notes define pteridophytes as seedless, flowerless and fruitless vascular plants with true roots, stems and leaves, without vessels or companion cells.

mcqs.q: A fern differs from a moss in having:
options: An independent sporophyte
A dependent sporophyte
No sporophyte generation
A dominant gametophyte only
mcqs.why: The notes point out a fern differs from a moss in having an independent sporophyte, and pteridophyte gametophytes are also independent from the sporophyte.

mcqs.q: The dominant generation in vascular plants is the:
options: Haploid (n) gametophyte, with a reduced diploid sporophyte
Diploid (2n) sporophyte, with a reduced haploid (n) gametophyte
Diploid gametophyte, with a dominant haploid sporophyte
Haploid sporophyte, with no gametophyte
mcqs.why: The notes state vascular plants have a diploid dominant sporophyte and a haploid reduced gametophyte, with heteromorphic alternation of generations.

mcqs.q: Which origin sequence is given in the comparison table?
options: Angiosperms were first, then gymnosperms, then pteridophytes
Gymnosperms were the first vascular plants and pteridophytes evolved from them
Pteridophytes were the first vascular plants on land, gymnosperms evolved from pteridophytes, and angiosperms evolved from gymnosperms
Pteridophytes evolved from angiosperms and gymnosperms from pteridophytes
mcqs.why: The table lists origin as: pteridophytes first vascular plants on land, gymnosperms evolved from pteridophytes, angiosperms evolved from gymnosperms.

mcqs.q: In pteridophytes, the spores are produced in and dispersed as follows:
options: Seeds are produced in cones and dispersed by wind
Spores are produced in fruits and dispersed by water
Seeds are produced in sporangia and dispersed by insects
Spores are produced in sporangia, the sporangia burst and spores are dispersed by wind
mcqs.why: The notes say reproduction is by spores in sporangia; sporangia burst and spores are dispersed by wind and germinate into independent gametophytes.

lessons.title: Life Cycle of a Fern
lessons.notes_html:
Adiantum (an example of a fern) shows heteromorphic alternation of generations, in which the dominant sporophyte alternates with a reduced gametophyte.

A. Sporophyte Generation

  • The main plant body, in the form of a herb: the dominant, diploid (2n) generation. Its stem is a rhizome — short and underground — from which roots arise, and special large leaves or fronds arise from its upper side.
  • On the underside of the leaflets of fronds, groups of sporangia or sori (singular: sorus) are formed, first green, then dark brown or black when mature. The sporangia-bearing leaves are called sporophylls.
  • Each sporangium is a flattened biconvex capsule with a multicellular stalk, in which many haploid spores are formed by meiosis. Each spore is a simple cell of cytoplasm and a nucleus, with an outer wall called exine and an inner wall called intine.
  • The mature sporangium bursts; spores are dispersed by wind, and a spore falling on moist soil germinates into a small haploid gametophyte, the prothallus.

A fern sporophyte: fronds bear sori (groups of sporangia) on the underside of their leaflets; the short underground stem is the rhizome.

B. Gametophyte Generation

  • The gametophyte or prothallus is heart-shaped and autotrophic, about 1/3 of an inch in size, with many rhizoids on its lower side that anchor it in the soil and absorb water and minerals.
  • It is monoecious (bisexual), containing both sex organs. The antheridium produces a large number of flagellated sperms (antherozoids). The archegonium is flask-shaped: the upper, enlarged part is the neck and the broad lower part is the venter, which contains an egg or oosphere.
  • Water is necessary for fertilization. The antheridium bursts, sperms swim by their flagella towards the archegonium (archegonia secrete a sweet substance that attracts them), and one sperm enters the venter through the neck and unites with the egg to form a zygote or oospore. After many divisions the zygote forms an embryo inside the archegonium, which develops into a sporophyte — at first attached to the gametophyte, later independent.

Key Points

  • The fern sporophyte is dominant and diploid, with a rhizome, roots and fronds bearing sori on the underside of leaflets.
  • Spores formed by meiosis in the sporangia germinate into a small, heart-shaped, independent gametophyte — the prothallus.
  • The prothallus is monoecious, bearing antheridia and flask-shaped archegonia, and its rhizoids anchor it and absorb water and minerals.
  • Flagellated sperms swim in water to the egg; the young sporophyte starts attached to the prothallus and later becomes independent.

mcqs.q: In Adiantum (fern), the stem of the sporophyte is:
options: A tall woody trunk bearing fronds along its length
A prothallus bearing rhizoids on its lower side
A seta elevating a capsule above the fronds
A rhizome — short and underground, from which roots arise and fronds arise from its upper side
mcqs.why: The notes describe the fern sporophyte stem as a rhizome, short and underground, with roots arising from it and large fronds from its upper side.

mcqs.q: Sori on a fern frond are:
options: Groups of sporangia formed on the underside of the leaflets, first green then dark brown or black when mature
Single spores formed on the upper side of the leaflets
Groups of archegonia on the prothallus
Roots arising from the rhizome
mcqs.why: The notes state groups of sporangia or sori (singular sorus) form on the underside of leaflets, first green, then dark brown or black when mature.

mcqs.q: The leaves of a fern that bear sporangia are called:
options: Fronds without sori
Sporophylls
Prothalli
Rhizoids
mcqs.why: The notes say the sporangia-bearing leaves are called sporophylls; the large leaves themselves are fronds.

mcqs.q: The wall layers of a fern spore are:
options: An outer wall called intine and an inner wall called exine
A single wall called the testa
An outer wall called exine and an inner wall called intine
Two walls both called exine
mcqs.why: Each spore is described as a simple cell with an outer wall called exine and an inner wall called intine.

mcqs.q: The fern gametophyte (prothallus) is best described as:
options: Filamentous and non-photosynthetic, several inches long
Heart-shaped and dependent on the sporophyte for nutrition
Monoecious only in the sporophyte generation
Heart-shaped and autotrophic, about 1/3 of an inch in size, with many rhizoids on its lower side
mcqs.why: The notes describe the prothallus as heart-shaped, autotrophic, about 1/3 of an inch, with rhizoids below that anchor it and absorb water and minerals. Working: the size is given directly as 1/3 inch in the notes.

mcqs.q: Monoecious in the fern prothallus means it:
options: Contains both sex organs, antheridia and archegonia
Contains only antheridia
Contains only archegonia
Has separate male and female prothalli
mcqs.why: The notes say the prothallus is monoecious (bisexual), containing both sex organs on the same gametophyte.

mcqs.q: The archegonium of a fern is flask-shaped with:
options: A broad upper venter and a narrow lower neck containing sperms
An upper enlarged neck and a broad lower venter containing an egg (oosphere)
Two necks and no venter
A venter containing many flagellated sperms
mcqs.why: The notes state the archegonium's upper enlarged part is the neck and the broad lower part is the venter, which contains an egg or oosphere.

mcqs.q: How are fern sperms attracted to the archegonium?
options: The prothallus secretes a bitter substance that repels them
Rhizoids guide the sperms through the soil
Archegonia secrete a sweet substance that attracts the flagellated sperms
The sorus releases a substance that attracts them
mcqs.why: The notes say sperms swim by their flagella towards the archegonium and archegonia secrete a sweet substance that attracts them.

mcqs.q: After fertilization in a fern, the zygote develops as follows:
options: It immediately disperses by wind as a spore
It forms a protonema that stays dependent forever
It becomes a seed enclosed in a fruit
It divides many times to form an embryo inside the archegonium, which develops into a sporophyte at first attached to the gametophyte and later independent
mcqs.why: The notes state after many divisions the zygote forms an embryo inside the archegonium, developing into a sporophyte at first attached, later independent.

mcqs.q: Spores in the fern sporangium are haploid because they are formed by:
options: Meiosis
Mitosis
Fertilization
Binary fission of the zygote
mcqs.why: The notes say each sporangium is a capsule in which many haploid spores are formed by meiosis, then dispersed by wind.

lessons.title: Gymnosperms and the Life Cycle of Pinus
lessons.notes_html:
9.7 Gymnosperms

The word gymnosperm is derived from two Greek words: Gymnos = naked and sperma = seed. They are commonly called evergreen plants, are found worldwide, and make up one third of the world's forest. They are woody plants — shrubs, trees or rarely vines (in some Gnetophytes) — with about 700 living species.

  • The main plant body is the sporophyte; the gametophyte is reduced. They are flowerless and fruitless and usually bear cones; the seeds are born on the exposed surface of fertile leaves, mostly combined to form a cone.
  • Leaves are of two types, foliage and scale. Foliage leaves are evergreen with xerophytic features like a thick, tough cuticle and sunken stomata (needle-shaped foliage leaves are found in gymnosperms).
  • The xylem consists of tracheids and xylem parenchyma. Two spore types form: microspores (male) on microsporophylls and megaspores (female) on megasporophylls; the female gametophyte is retained in the ovule permanently. Alternation is heteromorphic, with an independent dominant sporophyte and a dependent reduced gametophyte. Polyembryony is common, but usually a single embryo matures.
  • Important genera: cycads (Cycas spp.), pines (Pinus spp.), hemlock (Conium maculatum), deodar (Cedrus deodara), maidenhair tree (Ginkgo biloba), joint pine (Ephedra sinica) and Himalayan spruce (Picea smithiane).

9.8 Classification of Gymnosperms

There are four main groups of gymnosperms: i) Conifers, ii) Ginkgos, iii) Cycads, iv) Gnetophytes. Cycads belong to the non-flowering seed plants.

9.9 Life Cycle of Pinus

Pinus is a conifer. Its dominant, diploid sporophyte alternates with a small, dependent haploid gametophyte, and there is no vegetative reproduction in Pinus.

  • Sporophyte — A tall evergreen tree, up to 36 meters, with roots, a woody stem, branches, needle-like green leaves and brown scale-like leaves. It bears cones or strobili of two types, male and female, on separate branches of the same plant, so Pinus is monoecious.
  • Male cone — Smaller, in clusters, with many microsporophylls spirally arranged on a central axis; each has a stalk (filament) and a terminal leafy expansion (anther), and two pouch-like microsporangia (pollen sacs) on its underside. Each microspore mother cell produces four haploid microspores (pollen grains) by meiosis. Each pollen grain has an outer coat (exine), an inner coat (intine) and two air-filled, balloon-like wings, so it can float in air and travel long distances.
  • Female cone — Larger, formed from one to three at a point, with many megasporophylls spirally arranged on a central axis. Each megasporophyll has two scales: a small, thin, dry bract scale below, and a larger, thicker, woody ovuliferous scale above it, bearing two sessile ovules (megasporangia) on its upper surface. Each ovule has a mass of tissue called the nucellus, a single integument with an opening, the micropyle. The megaspore mother cell produces four haploid megaspores by meiosis; three degenerate and one becomes functional.
  • Male gametophyte — The microspore nucleus forms a small prothelial cell (which degenerates) and a sister cell, which gives a second prothelial cell and an antheridial cell; the antheridial cell divides into a generative nucleus and a tube nucleus. Released microspores reach the female cone by wind (pollination); the exine bursts and the intine forms a pollen tube carrying both nuclei. The tube nucleus degenerates; the generative nucleus divides into a stalk cell (which degenerates) and a body cell, which forms two sperms. The pollen tube with two gametes is the male gametophyte.
  • Female gametophyte and seed — It develops during the year following pollination. The functional megaspore (n) divides by mitosis inside the megasporangium and is never set free; many free nuclei form, then walls form between them, making gametophytic tissue called endosperm. At the micropyle end, two archegonia form, each flask-shaped with a neck of eight cells, a ventral canal cell and the egg. The pollen tube enters an archegonium and bursts near the egg, releasing the sperms; one sperm unites with the egg to form a zygote, which divides repeatedly into an embryo. The integument becomes the seed coat and the ovule is now a seed with a wing. Seeds are dispersed when the ovuliferous scales open apart, and germinate into a new young sporophyte. The life cycle of Pinus is completed in about three years.

Key Points

  • Gymnosperms are naked-seeded, evergreen, woody plants with cones, no flowers and no fruits; about 700 living species in four groups: conifers, ginkgos, cycads and gnetophytes.
  • Pinus is monoecious: smaller male cones in clusters and larger female cones with bract and ovuliferous scales, each bearing two ovules.
  • Pinus pollen grains have two air-filled wings, so they float in air and travel long distances to the female cone.
  • The female gametophyte (endosperm) stays inside the ovule and forms archegonia; the fertilized ovule becomes a winged seed, and the whole life cycle takes about three years.

mcqs.q: The word gymnosperm means:
options: Naked seed — from Gymnos = naked and sperma = seed
Enclosed seed — from Angion = enclosed and sperma = seed
Flowerless fruit — from Gymnos = flower and sperma = fruit
Evergreen leaf — from Gymnos = green and sperma = leaf
mcqs.why: The notes derive gymnosperm from Greek Gymnos = naked and sperma = seed, because seeds are born on the exposed surface of fertile leaves.

mcqs.q: Which is a correct general feature of gymnosperms?
options: They are flowering and fruit-bearing, with about 700 living species
They are flowerless and fruitless, usually bear cones, and have about 700 living species
They are herbaceous annuals with vessels in their xylem
They make up one third of the world's desert herbs
mcqs.why: The notes state gymnosperms are evergreen woody plants, flowerless and fruitless, usually bearing cones, with about 700 living species and making up one third of the world's forest.

mcqs.q: The four main groups of gymnosperms are:
options: Conifers, Ferns, Cycads and Mosses
Ginkgos, Lycopsida, Cycads and Pteropsida
Conifers, Ginkgos, Cycads and Gnetophytes
Conifers, Ginkgos, Horsetails and Gnetophytes
mcqs.why: The classification in the notes lists four main groups: i) Conifers, ii) Ginkgos, iii) Cycads, iv) Gnetophytes.

mcqs.q: Pinus is monoecious because:
options: Male and female cones occur on separate plants
Only male cones are produced on the plant
Only female cones are produced on the plant
Male and female cones occur on separate branches of the same plant
mcqs.why: The notes say Pinus bears cones of two types, male and female, on separate branches of the same plant, so Pinus is monoecious.

mcqs.q: A Pinus pollen grain can travel long distances because it has:
options: Two air-filled, balloon-like wings
A sticky secretion holding it to insects
Flagella for swimming in air
A single large wing and a tail
mcqs.why: Each pollen grain is described with exine, intine and two air-filled balloon-like wings, so it can float in air and travel long distances.

mcqs.q: On a female Pinus megasporophyll, the two scales are:
options: A large woody bract scale above and a small ovuliferous scale below bearing one ovule
A small, thin, dry bract scale below and a larger, thicker, woody ovuliferous scale above bearing two sessile ovules
Two equal ovuliferous scales each bearing four ovules
A single bract scale bearing seeds inside a fruit
mcqs.why: The notes state each megasporophyll has a bract scale below and an ovuliferous scale above it, bearing two sessile ovules on its upper surface.

mcqs.q: In the Pinus ovule, meiosis of the megaspore mother cell produces:
options: Four haploid megaspores, all of which become functional
Two haploid megaspores, both functional
Four haploid megaspores, of which three degenerate and one becomes functional
One diploid megaspore that becomes the seed
mcqs.why: The notes say the megaspore mother cell produces four haploid megaspores by meiosis; three degenerate and one becomes functional. Working: 4 produced - 3 degenerate = 1 functional megaspore.

mcqs.q: The tissue called endosperm in the Pinus female gametophyte is formed when:
options: Two sperms fuse with the egg inside the ovule
The integument hardens into a seed coat
The pollen tube bursts inside the archegonium
The functional megaspore divides by mitosis inside the megasporangium, many free nuclei form, then walls form between them
mcqs.why: The notes describe the functional megaspore dividing by mitosis, never set free, forming many free nuclei then walls, making gametophytic tissue called endosperm.

mcqs.q: Polyembryony in gymnosperms means:
options: Many embryos may form, but usually a single embryo matures
Many seeds form inside a single fruit
A single embryo always produces many mature plants
No embryo matures inside the ovule
mcqs.why: The notes state polyembryony is common in gymnosperms, but usually a single embryo matures.

mcqs.q: The life cycle of Pinus is completed in about:
options: One year
Three years
Three months
Ten years
mcqs.why: The notes state the life cycle of Pinus is completed in about three years, with the female gametophyte developing during the year following pollination.

lessons.title: Angiosperms and Their Classification
lessons.notes_html:
9.10 Angiosperms

The word angiosperm is derived from two Greek words: Angion = enclosed and sperma = seed. Rose (Rosa spp.), apple (Malus domestica), mango (Mangifera indica) and sheesham (Dalbergia sissoo) are examples of angiosperms — the group of flowering and seeded plants.

  • It is believed that angiosperms diverged from gymnosperms about 300–350 million years ago (Triassic period). It is the most diverse group of plants, with approximately 416 families, 13,164 genera and 295,383 species.
  • Angiosperms are flowering plants and contain their seeds in fruits. The main plant body is the dominant sporophyte, while the gametophyte generation is reduced.
  • The sporophyte is heterosporous (it produces microspores and megaspores) and varies greatly in size: duckweed is about one mm long, while Eucalyptus is about 100 m high.
  • They have well-developed xylem and phloem, and form pollen tubes to transport sperms towards the egg in the ovules. They show heteromorphic alternation of a dominant sporophyte with a reduced gametophyte, and resemble gymnosperms in the presence of ovules.

9.11 Classification of Angiosperms

According to the number of cotyledons in the embryo, angiosperms are divided into two classes: Liliopsida (monocot) and Magnoliopsida (dicot).

  • Monocotyledons (Liliopsida) — A single cotyledon in the seed; mostly herbaceous plants; leaves usually long and narrow with parallel veins; flowers usually with three or a multiple of three petals and six stamens; mature seeds usually contain endosperm (nutritive tissue). Examples: wheat, sugarcane, orchids, rice, bamboo, grasses, maize, lilies, palm.
  • Dicotyledons (Magnoliopsida) — Two cotyledons in the seed; herbaceous (tomato) or woody (apple tree); leaves broader than monocot leaves, with veins in a network; sepals and petals usually in fours or fives, or multiples of these; the mature seed usually lacks endosperm, which is absorbed by the two cotyledons before germination. Examples: apples, guava, roses, sunflower, sheesham, oak, cacti.
FeatureMonocotDicot
Pollen grainsOne pore or furrowThree pores or furrows
SeedsOne cotyledonTwo cotyledons
FlowersThree floral parts (or multiples)Four or five floral parts (or multiples)
LeavesNarrow, parallel veinsOval or palmate, net-like veins
Vascular bundlesSmall, spread throughout the stemArranged in a ring around the stem
RootsFibrous rootsTap roots

Difference between monocot and dicot, as shown in the book (Fig. 9.7).

Key Points

  • Angiosperms are flowering plants with enclosed seeds in fruits — the most diverse plant group, with about 416 families and 295,383 species.
  • The sporophyte is dominant and heterosporous; the gametophyte is much reduced, and sperms reach the egg by a pollen tube.
  • Monocots (Liliopsida) have one cotyledon, parallel leaf veins, fibrous roots and floral parts in threes.
  • Dicots (Magnoliopsida) have two cotyledons, net-like leaf veins, tap roots and floral parts in fours or fives.

mcqs.q: Angiosperms differ from gymnosperms in that their seeds are:
options: Naked on the surface of scale leaves, with no flowers
Enclosed in fruits, and the plants bear flowers
Formed in cones without fruits
Produced without any ovules
mcqs.why: The notes derive angiosperm from Angion = enclosed and sperma = seed, and state angiosperms are flowering plants containing their seeds in fruits.

mcqs.q: The size range in angiosperms given in the notes is:
options: Duckweed about one cm long to Eucalyptus about 10 m high
Duckweed about one mm long to mango about 100 m high
Duckweed about one mm long to Eucalyptus about 100 m high
Rose about one mm long to Eucalyptus about 100 m high
mcqs.why: The notes say the sporophyte varies greatly: duckweed is about one mm long, while Eucalyptus is about 100 m high.

mcqs.q: Monocotyledons (Liliopsida) are recognised by:
options: Two cotyledons, broad leaves with net veins, and floral parts in fours or fives
A single cotyledon, tap roots, and floral parts in fives
Two cotyledons, parallel veins, and fibrous roots
A single cotyledon, long narrow leaves with parallel veins, and floral parts in threes or multiples of three
mcqs.why: Monocots in the notes have one cotyledon, usually long narrow leaves with parallel veins, and flowers with three or a multiple of three petals.

mcqs.q: Which example list belongs only to dicotyledons as given in the notes?
options: Apples, guava, roses, sunflower, sheesham, oak and cacti
Wheat, sugarcane, orchids, rice and bamboo
Grasses, maize, lilies and palm
Rice, bamboo, grasses and maize
mcqs.why: Dicot examples in the notes are apples, guava, roses, sunflower, sheesham, oak and cacti; wheat, rice, maize and grasses are listed as monocots.

mcqs.q: In the monocot–dicot table, pollen grains differ as:
options: Monocot: three pores or furrows; Dicot: one pore or furrow
Monocot: one pore or furrow; Dicot: three pores or furrows
Monocot: no pores; Dicot: one pore
Both have three pores or furrows
mcqs.why: The book's table (Fig. 9.7) shows monocot pollen with one pore or furrow and dicot pollen with three pores or furrows.

mcqs.q: Vascular bundles and roots differ between monocots and dicots as:
options: Monocot bundles are in a ring with tap roots; dicot bundles are spread with fibrous roots
Both have bundles in a ring and tap roots
Monocot bundles are small and spread throughout the stem with fibrous roots; dicot bundles are arranged in a ring with tap roots
Both have bundles spread throughout and fibrous roots
mcqs.why: The table states monocot vascular bundles are small and spread throughout the stem with fibrous roots, while dicot bundles are arranged in a ring with tap roots.

mcqs.q: Mature dicot seeds usually lack endosperm because:
options: The endosperm is converted into the seed coat
Dicot seeds never form endosperm at any stage
The endosperm is dispersed with the pollen
The endosperm is absorbed by the two cotyledons before germination
mcqs.why: The notes say the mature dicot seed usually lacks endosperm, which is absorbed by the two cotyledons before germination; monocot seeds usually contain endosperm.

mcqs.q: Angiosperms are described as heterosporous, meaning the sporophyte produces:
options: Two types of spores — microspores and megaspores
Only one type of spore
Spores and seeds of one type only
No spores, only gametes directly
mcqs.why: The notes state the angiosperm sporophyte is heterosporous, producing microspores and megaspores, with a dominant sporophyte and reduced gametophyte.

mcqs.q: Angiosperms resemble gymnosperms in:
options: The presence of flowers
The presence of ovules
Seeds enclosed in fruits
Vessels absent from xylem
mcqs.why: The notes say angiosperms show heteromorphic alternation and resemble gymnosperms in the presence of ovules, while differing in flowers and enclosed seeds.

mcqs.q: How diverse are angiosperms according to the notes?
options: Approximately 92 families and 250 species in Pakistan only
About 700 living species in four groups
Approximately 416 families, 13,164 genera and 295,383 species — the most diverse group of plants
About 15,000 species discovered so far
mcqs.why: The notes give approximately 416 families, 13,164 genera and 295,383 species for angiosperms, the most diverse group of plants.

lessons.title: Life Cycle of a Flowering Plant: Double Fertilization, Seed and Fruit
lessons.notes_html:
Like all other vascular plants, angiosperms show heteromorphic alternation of generations, in which a diploid, dominant sporophyte alternates with a reduced gametophyte.

A. Sporophyte Generation

The main plant body is the diploid, dominant sporophyte. Flowers are the reproductive parts: a flower contains the male reproductive part, the anther, and the female reproductive part, the carpel. Angiosperms are heterosporous, producing two types of haploid spores in the flowers. (Gametes differ from spores: gametes fuse in fertilization to form a zygote, while spores germinate directly into a new gametophyte.)

  • Microspores (male spores) — Formed in the anther (microsporangium) of the stamen, which usually has four elongated pollen sacs. Mitotic divisions produce diploid microspore mother cells; each divides by meiosis into four haploid microspores. The microspore nucleus then divides by mitosis into a vegetative or tube nucleus and a generative nucleus, and the thick-walled microspore becomes a pollen grain with a double folded wall.
  • Megaspores (female spores) — Produced by meiosis in the ovule (megasporangium), an integumented, oval female sporangium attached to the inner wall of the ovary by a short stalk; an ovary may contain one, two, or several thousand ovules. A megaspore mother cell (megasporocyte) undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid cells; only one survives and the other three degenerate — the survivor is the megaspore.
  • Pollination — Binucleate pollen grains are carried by wind, insects or other means to the stigma of carpels.

Parts of a flower: the carpel (stigma, style, ovary with ovule) and the stamen (anther and filament), with petals and sepals on the thalamus.

B. Gametophyte Generation

The gametophyte generation is much reduced: the male gametophyte is just a three-celled structure and the female gametophyte a seven-celled structure.

  • Male gametophyte — The pollen grain is held on the stigma by a sticky secretion and germinates to form a pollen tube, which grows down the style into the ovary. The two nuclei move down into the tube; the generative nucleus divides by mitosis to form two sperms, while the tube nucleus stays near the tip. The pollen tube with its two sperms is the male gametophyte.
  • Female gametophyte — Inside the ovule, the megaspore nucleus divides by mitosis three times to produce eight haploid nuclei in the embryo sac, the microscopic structure at the centre of the ovule, surrounded by integuments that leave a small opening, the micropyle. Walls form around the nuclei, giving a seven-celled structure: the egg apparatus near the micropyle (two synergids, which guide the pollen tube and then degenerate, plus the egg); three antipodal cells at the opposite side (functionless, later disorganized); and the fusion nucleus, formed when the two central polar nuclei fuse into a diploid endosperm mother cell.
  • Double fertilization — The pollen tube enters the embryo sac through the micropyle; the tube nucleus degenerates, the tube tip ruptures and releases the two sperms. One sperm fuses with the egg to form a zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus (2n) to form the triploid (3n) endospermic nucleus. This is double fertilization, found only in angiosperms.
  • Seed and fruit — The zygote develops into an embryonic plant (embryo: one or more cotyledons, an epicotyl and a hypocotyl on a rod-like axis), and the endospermic nucleus develops into triploid (3n) endosperm tissue, rich in starch that is broken down to glucose when the seed germinates. As the ovule matures into a seed, the micropyle closes and the integuments become the seed coat or testa, protecting the embryo. Most flower parts die, but the ovary enlarges into the fruit; the ripe fruit releases seeds, which are dispersed and germinate into new sporophyte plants.

Key Points

  • In flowering plants the flower is the reproductive part: microspores (pollen) form in the anther and the megaspore forms in the ovule.
  • The male gametophyte is the pollen tube with a tube nucleus and two sperms; the female gametophyte is the seven-celled embryo sac.
  • The embryo sac contains the egg apparatus (egg and two synergids), three antipodal cells and a fusion nucleus formed from two polar nuclei.
  • Double fertilization — one sperm fuses with the egg (zygote) and the other with the fusion nucleus (triploid endosperm) — occurs only in angiosperms.
  • After fertilization the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.

mcqs.q: Gametes differ from spores in flowering plants because:
options: Gametes germinate directly into a gametophyte, while spores fuse to form a zygote
Gametes are diploid and spores are triploid
Gametes fuse in fertilization to form a zygote, while spores germinate directly into a new gametophyte
There is no difference given in the notes
mcqs.why: The notes explicitly contrast them: gametes fuse in fertilization to form a zygote, while spores germinate directly into a new gametophyte.

mcqs.q: Microspores in a flowering plant are formed in:
options: The ovule inside the ovary
The stigma of the carpel
The embryo sac at the centre of the ovule
The anther (microsporangium) of the stamen, which usually has four elongated pollen sacs
mcqs.why: The notes state microspores are formed in the anther of the stamen, which usually has four elongated pollen sacs.

mcqs.q: Of the four haploid cells produced by meiosis of a megaspore mother cell:
options: Only one survives as the megaspore and the other three degenerate
All four survive as megaspores
Two survive and two degenerate
None survives; a new cell forms the megaspore
mcqs.why: The notes say a megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to produce four haploid cells; only one survives and the other three degenerate. Working: 4 - 3 degenerate = 1 surviving megaspore.
