lessons.notes_html:
The kingdom Animalia includes all animals. The word animal is derived from the Latin word anima, which means breath or soul. Animals are multicellular, ingestive, heterotrophic organisms, and they originated from animal-like protists. The branch of biology that deals with the study of animals is called Zoology.

11.1 Two Subkingdoms: Parazoa and Eumetazoa

Kingdom Animalia is divided into two subkingdoms, Parazoa and Eumetazoa, on the basis of the presence or absence of cellular organization.

  • Parazoa (para = beside, zoon = animal) — The simplest multicellular animals, believed to have evolved from protozoans. The body is just a collection of cells not differentiated into tissues or organs; there is some division of labour among the cells, but they are not strongly associated to perform a specific collective function. The only surviving Parazoans are the sponges, phylum Porifera (cellular level of organization).
  • Eumetazoa — Animals in which body cells are arranged into tissues, tissues into organs and organs into organ systems. Their cells are arranged into germinal layers: diploblastic (two germ layers) or triploblastic (three germ layers), present during the development of the embryo.

Symmetry: Grade Radiata and Grade Bilatera

The geometrical view of an organism is called symmetry; asymmetrical animals do not exhibit symmetry. On the basis of body symmetry, Eumetazoa is classified into grade Radiata and grade Bilatera.

Grade RadiataGrade Bilatera
Body organs arranged around a central axis; the body can be cut into two identical halves from any plane passing through the central axis.The body can be cut into two identical halves from a single longitudinal plane running down the middle line.
No right and left side.Right and left sides, anterior and posterior ends, dorsal and ventral surfaces.
Mostly sessile animals; an adaptation for a sessile life.Mostly motile animals; an adaptation to motility.
Radially symmetrical animals, e.g. coelenterates and adult echinoderms.Bilaterally symmetrical animals, from phylum Platyhelminthes to Chordata.

Diploblastic and Triploblastic Animals

  • Diploblastic — Two germ layers, ectoderm and endoderm, with a non-cellular jelly-like mesoglea between them. Mostly without specialized organs; no specialized nervous system, only a network of neurons with few ganglia. A gastrovascular cavity with a single opening acts as both mouth and anus, e.g. Coelenterata (Cnidaria).
  • Triploblastic — Three germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, visible only during embryonic development and later transformed into organs. Specialized organs, organ systems and a nervous system with ganglia or a brain are present. Bilaterally symmetrical, with a tubular digestive system having an anterior mouth and a posterior anus or cloaca, e.g. from Platyhelminthes to Chordata.

Classification According to Coelom (Body Cavity)

The coelom is a fluid-filled cavity between the outer body wall and the alimentary canal, lined by mesodermal membranes. Grade Bilatera is divided into three groups on the basis of the kind of coelom:

AcoelomatesPseudocoelomatesCoelomates
No body cavity; found only in Platyhelminthes. Between the digestive tract and the body wall, the mesoderm forms a loose cellular tissue called parenchyma or mesenchyma.A false coelom (pseudocoelom); found only in nematodes (Aschelminthes). It lies between mesoderm and endoderm, is not covered by coelomic epithelium, and is the remnant of the blastocoel.A true coelom; found from annelids to chordates. The mesoderm splits into outer parietal and inner visceral layers, and the cavity is filled with coelomic fluid.

The three kinds of body cavity: acoelomate, pseudocoelomate and coelomate (centre circle = gut).

Protostomes and Deuterostomes

Coelomates are classified into two groups on the basis of early development. In Protostomes (mollusks, annelids, arthropods) the mouth develops from the blastopore. In Deuterostomes (echinoderms, chordates) the anus develops from the blastopore and the mouth forms later. (Cleavage is the division of the zygote in which the number of cells increases but the size of cells hardly increases; cleavage is either radial or spiral.)

Key Points

  • Animalia is divided into Parazoa (cellular level, sponges only) and Eumetazoa (tissue, organ and organ-system levels).
  • Radiata are radially symmetrical and mostly sessile; Bilatera are bilaterally symmetrical and mostly motile.
  • Diploblastic animals have ectoderm and endoderm with mesoglea; triploblastic animals also have mesoderm.
  • On the basis of coelom, Bilatera are acoelomates, pseudocoelomates or coelomates; coelomates are protostomes or deuterostomes.

lessons.title: Invertebrates and Vertebrates, and Phylum Porifera (Sponges)

Absent, with only neurosensory cells
A ventral, solid tube

mcqs.why: The lesson states Porifera, from poros meaning channels and ferre meaning to bear, was named by Robert E. Grant in 1836.

Guanine
Urea crystals
Ammonia

options: Internal budding, a type of asexual reproduction
External budding only
Sexual reproduction with internal fertilization
Fission followed by regeneration in flatworms
mcqs.why: Sponges reproduce asexually by external budding or internal budding called gemmule formation, and regeneration is also common.

mcqs.q: Which sponge example given in the notes is a fresh water sponge?
options: Sycon
Spongilla
Euplectella
Leucosolenia
mcqs.why: The examples list Spongilla as the fresh water sponge, while Sycon is a marine sponge, Leucosolenia is erect and tube-shaped, and Euplectella has a glassy framework.

lessons.notes_html:
Most biologists have divided animals into two major groups on the basis of the presence or absence of a vertebral column (backbone): invertebrates, which lack a vertebral column, and vertebrates, which possess one. Invertebrates account for more than 95% of known animal species and are divided into eight major phyla: Porifera, Coelenterata, Platyhelminthes, Nematodes, Annelids, Mollusca, Arthropoda and Echinodermata.

11.3 Differences Between Invertebrates and Vertebrates

InvertebratesVertebrates
Vertebral column (backbone) is absent.Vertebral column is present.
Mostly small in size, slowly moving or sessile.Large in size and mostly fast moving.
About 95% of all animal species.Only 5% of all animal species.
No pharyngeal gill cleft.Pharyngeal gill cleft increases the efficiency of breathing.
Ventral, solid tube of nervous system.Hollow, fluid-filled dorsal central nervous system.
Endoskeleton absent; if present, non-living.All possess a living endoskeleton (skull and vertebral column).
Heart, if present, is dorsal or lateral; mostly an open blood vascular system.Heart is ventrally located; closed blood vascular system.
May have more than two pairs of limbs; compound eyes present; tail usually absent.Not more than two pairs of limbs; no compound eyes; tail usually present.

11.4 Phylum Porifera — the Sponges

Porifera (Greek: poros = channels; Latin: ferre = to bear). The name Porifera was given by Robert E. Grant in 1836. Sponges are the simplest multicellular animals.

  • Habit and habitat — The larval stage is motile while the adult is sessile; about 10,000 species have been recorded. Their size ranges from a few millimetres wide to more than a metre long (e.g. Scolymastra joubini from Antarctica).
  • Body — No tissues and no organ organization; either asymmetrical or radially symmetrical. The body wall has an outer dermal layer, the pinacoderm, made of pinacocytes, and an inner layer, the choanoderm, containing flagellated collar cells called choanocytes. Between the two layers is a gelatinous matrix, the mesenchyma, containing many kinds of wandering amoeboid cells; amoeboid cells store food and give colour, while scleroblasts are the spicule and spongin fibre forming cells.
  • Canal system — The body has a single body cavity, the spongocoel, divided into canals. Water enters through numerous incoming pores, the ostia, and leaves through a single large outgoing pore, the osculum.
  • Nutrition — Heterotrophic: food comes in with the water current through the ostia, moved by the flagella of choanocytes, and intracellular digestion takes place. Digested food is transported by mesenchymal cells. Waste diffuses out through the body wall or the osculum; the nitrogenous product is ammonia, removed from each body cell by diffusion.
  • Nervous system and skeleton — The nervous system is absent, but neuron and neurosensory cells help to coordinate the water flow. The skeleton is mostly formed of needle-like spicules (calcareous or siliceous), while some sponges, like the bath sponge, possess spongin fibres.
  • Reproduction — Both asexual and sexual. Asexual reproduction is by external budding or internal budding (gemmule formation); regeneration is also common. Sponges are mostly hermaphrodite (bisexual) and protandrous (male gametes develop before the female). Fertilization is internal and occurs in the mesenchyma.
  • Examples — Sycon (marine sponge), Leucosolenia (erect, tube-shaped), Euplectella (glassy frame work) and Spongilla (fresh water sponge).

Anatomy of a sponge: water enters through the ostia into the spongocoel and leaves through the osculum.

Importance of Sponges

  • Bath sponges are used for washing and bathing by humans.
  • Sponges greatly absorb water, so they are used in surgical operations for absorbing fluid and blood.
  • In large buildings, sponges are used for sound absorption, to prevent echo.
  • They are also used for decorative purposes and in shoe or vehicle polishing.

Key Points

  • Invertebrates lack a backbone and make up more than 95% of animal species; vertebrates have a backbone and a closed blood vascular system.
  • Sponges (Porifera) are the simplest animals: cellular organization, no tissues, no nervous system.
  • Water enters a sponge through ostia and leaves through the osculum; choanocytes move the water and capture food.
  • The sponge skeleton is made of spicules or spongin fibres; gemmules are internal buds.

lessons.title: Phylum Cnidaria and Phylum Platyhelminthes

mcqs.q: Cnidarians are named for specialized stinging cells called cnidocytes, which give rise to:
options: Flame cells, used for excretion in flatworms
Nematocysts, capsules with paralyzing venom for offence and defence
Choanocytes, used to move water in sponges
Gemmules, used for internal budding in sponges
mcqs.why: The phylum name Cnidaria comes from cnidocytes, which produce nematocysts, a capsule with paralyzing venom acting as an offensive and defensive organ.

options: A mouth at the anterior end and a separate anus posteriorly
No opening, with digestion entirely intracellular

mcqs.q: The body wall of a cnidarian consists of outer ectoderm and inner endoderm with what between them?
options: Cellular mesoderm
Parenchyma tissue
A true coelom filled with fluid
Gelatinous mesoglea
mcqs.why: Cnidarians are mostly diploblastic and radially symmetrical, with gelatinous mesoglea between the outer ectoderm and inner endoderm layers.

mcqs.q: In polymorphic colonial cnidarians, polyps or hydrozooids are the:
options: Cylindrical feeding zooids
Umbrella-shaped reproductive zooids
Larval stage that develops into medusae
Stinging cells covering the body
mcqs.why: Polymorphism means two or more structural forms with division of labour: polyps are cylindrical feeding zooids and medusae are umbrella-shaped reproductive zooids.

options: The medusa asexually produces polyps that directly become adults
The polyp asexually produces medusae, which sexually produce larvae that develop into new polyps
Both polyp and medusa reproduce only by budding and regeneration
Larvae develop into medusae without a polyp stage

mcqs.why: The notes state a coral reef is a colony of coral polyps held by calcium carbonate, and the Great Barrier Reef stretches over 2,300 km in warm shallow tropical water.

mcqs.q: Flatworms (Platyhelminthes) are correctly described as:
options: Diploblastic, radially symmetrical and pseudocoelomate
Triploblastic, segmented and truly coelomate
Diploblastic with a gastrovascular cavity and nematocysts
Triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical, dorsoventrally flattened and acoelomate
mcqs.why: Platyhelminthes means flat worm; the body is triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical, soft, dorsoventrally flattened and acoelomate, hence acoelomate worms.

mcqs.q: Excretion in flatworms is carried out by a protonephridial system containing:
options: Flame cells
Nephridia
Malpighian tubules
Green glands
mcqs.why: Flatworms possess a well developed protonephridial excretory system containing flame cells, distinct from the nephridia of annelids and mollusks.

mcqs.q: Special parasitic features of parasitic flatworms include:
options: A complete digestive tube with separate anus
Suckers and hooks for attachment and enormous egg production
Parapodia and chaetae for locomotion
A mantle that secretes a calcareous shell
mcqs.why: Parasitic flatworms show suckers and hooks for attachment, tapeworms have no digestive system of their own, and they produce enormous numbers of eggs.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of flatworm example and habit is correct from the notes?
options: Planaria is parasitic; Fasciola and Taenia are free-living
Planaria lives in the human liver; Taenia is free-living in water
Planaria is free-living; Fasciola (liver fluke) and Taenia (tapeworm) are parasitic
Fasciola is free-living; Planaria and Taenia are both parasitic
mcqs.why: The examples given are Planaria (Dugesia) as the free-living form, with liver fluke Fasciola and tapeworm Taenia as the parasitic flatworms.

lessons.notes_html:
After the sponges, the next two phyla are the cnidarians, the first animals with true tissues and a gastrovascular cavity, and the flatworms, the first triploblastic and bilaterally symmetrical animals.

11.5 Phylum Cnidaria (Coelenterata)

The name Cnidaria is given to this phylum because of the specialized stinging cells called cnidocytes, present all over the body, which give rise to nematocysts. The nematocyst is a capsule with paralyzing venom which acts as an offensive and defensive organ.

  • Habit and habitat — Either sessile (e.g. Hydra) or free-living and motile (e.g. jellyfish); many are colonial (e.g. Obelia). Most are carnivores. All cnidarians are aquatic, both marine and fresh water. Size ranges from microscopic (Hydra) to very large (e.g. Brachioceranthus, up to two metres in length).
  • Body — Radially symmetrical and mostly diploblastic: an outer ectoderm and an inner endoderm, with a gelatinous substance, mesoglea, between the two layers. A single hollow internal cavity, the enteron or gastrovascular cavity, has a single opening, the mouth, which acts both as mouth and anus. The mouth is surrounded by tentacles.
  • Nervous system — An irregularly placed network of neurons with few ganglia. Some colonial cnidarians exhibit polymorphism: a species has two or more very different structural forms, with division of labour among units called zooids — polyps or hydrozooids (cylindrical feeding zooids) and medusae (umbrella-shaped reproductive zooids).
  • Reproduction — Both asexual and sexual. Asexual reproduction is by budding and regeneration (as in Hydra). In sexual reproduction gametes are formed. Alternation of generation is shown by some cnidarians (like Obelia): the polyp asexually produces male or female medusae, which undergo sexual reproduction to produce larvae that develop into new polyps.
  • Importance — Coral reefs protect the shores from erosion by tidal waves; many jewellery items are made from corals; cnidarians are used as decoration in aquariums and rock gardens; but some cnidarians sting humans (jellyfish and sea anemone). In Pakistan they are common at the sea shores of Mekran and Karachi. A coral reef is made up of a colony of coral polyps held together by calcium carbonate and is found in the warm shallow water of tropical oceans; the Great Barrier Reef, off the coast of Queensland, Australia, is the largest coral reef system in the world, stretching over 2,300 km.

11.6 Phylum Platyhelminthes — the Flatworms

Platyhelminthes (Greek: platy = flat, helminth = worm) are also called flatworms or acoelomate worms.

  • Habit and habitat — Either free-living (e.g. Planaria) or parasitic (e.g. tapeworm). They are found in both fresh water and marine water, while parasitic worms are also found in the liver and gut of human beings.
  • Body — Triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical and soft-bodied; the body is dorsoventrally flattened and acoelomate. They possess an incomplete digestive system, with a single opening, the mouth, which is less developed or absent in parasitic forms. The excretory system is a well developed protonephridial system containing flame cells.
  • Nervous system and locomotion — The nervous system consists of a network of nerves, with two longitudinal nerves and an anterior cerebral ganglion. Locomotion occurs by means of cilia located on the underside of the body.
  • Reproduction — Asexual reproduction by fission (regeneration) and sexual reproduction are both present. These worms are bisexual (hermaphrodite) with well developed gonads, ducts and accessory organs; fertilization is internal and development may be direct or indirect. Parasitic forms show special parasitic features: suckers and hooks for attachment, no digestive system of their own in tapeworms, and enormous egg production.
  • Examples — Planaria (Dugesia), liver fluke (Fasciola) and tapeworm (Taenia).

Key Points

  • Cnidarians are diploblastic and radially symmetrical, with stinging cnidocytes and nematocysts for offence and defence.
  • The gastrovascular cavity of cnidarians has one opening that serves as both mouth and anus; Obelia shows alternation of generation between polyp and medusa.
  • Flatworms are triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical and acoelomate, with flame cells for excretion.
  • Planaria is free-living; liver fluke and tapeworm are parasitic flatworms with suckers and hooks.

lessons.title: Phylum Aschelminthes and Phylum Mollusca

Absent, with parenchyma filling the space instead

No digestive tube, absorbing food through the body wall
A gastrovascular cavity surrounded by tentacles
A single tube with a mouth at the anterior end and an anus at the posterior end
mcqs.why: Nematodes are the first animals in this sequence with a complete digestive tube, with mouth anteriorly and anus posteriorly, and a cylindrical body pointed at both ends.

mcqs.why: The lesson quotes the World Health Organization that 24% of the world population is infected with soil-transmitted helminths (worms).

mcqs.q: Ascaris lumbricoides, a human intestinal parasite, is described as causing:
options: Itching of the anus, insomnia and loss of appetite only
Anaemia, abdominal pain and fever, and it also migrates to the lungs
Bleeding from the intestine as its only effect
Disease of potato, onion, cotton and apple roots
mcqs.why: The importance section states Ascaris causes anaemia, abdominal pain and fever and migrates to the lungs; the itching symptoms belong to pinworm.

mcqs.q: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) lives in which part of the human body?
options: The small intestine only
The liver and bile duct
The caecum, appendix and colon
The lungs and blood
mcqs.why: Pinworm lives in the caecum, appendix and colon of man and causes itching of the anus, inflammation of the colon and appendix, insomnia and loss of appetite.

mcqs.q: In mollusks, the mantle is:
options: A muscular organ used only for locomotion on land
A tongue-like rasping organ with horny teeth
A pair of gills used only for respiration
An envelope of glandular epithelial tissue covering the whole body, which in many cases secretes a calcareous shell
mcqs.why: The mollusk body of head, visceral region and muscular foot is covered by the mantle, a glandular epithelial envelope that secretes the shell in many cases.

mcqs.q: Which shell arrangement in mollusks is correct?
options: Internal in cuttlefish, external in snail, absent in octopus
External in cuttlefish, internal in snail, external in octopus
Absent in cuttlefish, external in snail, internal in octopus
External in all three: cuttlefish, snail and octopus
mcqs.why: The notes give exactly this sequence for the mantle-secreted calcareous shell: internal in cuttlefish, external in snail and absent in octopus.

mcqs.q: The radula of mollusks is:
options: An excretory organ present as one, two or six units
A tongue-like rasping structure provided with horny teeth
A larval stage through which development occurs
A glandular envelope that secretes the shell
mcqs.why: Mollusks have a radula, the rasping tongue, a tongue-like structure with horny teeth used in feeding; nephridia, not the radula, are excretory.

mcqs.q: The excretory organs of mollusks are the:
options: Flame cells of the protonephridial system
Malpighian tubules and green glands
Nephridia, present as one, two or six
A glomerulus in the proboscis
mcqs.why: The lesson states nephridia are the excretory organs of mollusks, numbering one, two or six, while respiration is through gills or the mantle.

mcqs.q: The largest invertebrate named in the mollusk lesson is the squid, reaching:
options: 2 metres long including tentacles
More than 1 metre long in Antarctica
30 to 50 feet long including fins
15 metres long including tentacles
mcqs.why: About 50,000 mollusk species are recorded, and the notes identify the squid as the largest invertebrate at 15 metres long including tentacles.

lessons.notes_html:
The roundworms are the first animals with a false body cavity and a complete digestive tube, while the mollusks are soft-bodied coelomates with a mantle, a muscular foot and, in most, a shell.

11.7 Phylum Aschelminthes — Nematodes or Roundworms

Aschelminthes (Greek: askos = cavity, helminthes = worms) are the nematodes or roundworms.

  • Habit and habitat — Parasitic or free-living. Some are intestinal parasites of humans and other animals, but most are free-living in soil and in the roots of plants. Size varies from microscopic to large, such as Ascaris, more than one foot in length. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 24% of the world population is infected with soil-transmitted helminths (worms).
  • Body — Triploblastic and bilaterally symmetrical; segmentation is absent; the body is cylindrical and pointed at both ends. The body cavity is a pseudocoel.
  • Digestive system — Complete: a single tube with a mouth at the anterior end and an anus at the posterior end. The muscular layer is not continuous; it is divided into four longitudinal quadrants (two dorsolateral and two ventrolateral).
  • Nervous system — A nerve ring from which the nerve cord and fibres extend in various directions. Sensory papillae are present on the front part of the body, especially on the lips.
  • Reproduction — Sexual; sexes are mostly separate, some are hermaphrodite; fertilization is internal. Circulatory and respiratory systems are absent.
  • Importance — Nematodes cause many serious parasitic diseases: Ascaris lumbricoides, a human intestinal parasite, causes anaemia, abdominal pain and fever, and also migrates to the lungs. Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) lives in the caecum, appendix and colon of man and causes itching of the anus, inflammation of the colon and appendix, insomnia and loss of appetite. Hookworms are also parasites of the human intestine and cause bleeding. Free roundworms in soil cause disease to potato, onion, cotton and apple. Beneficial nematodes are used in biological pest control against insect pests in their larval and pupal stages.

11.8 Phylum Mollusca — Soft-Bodied Animals

Mollusca (Latin: mollis = soft). The term mollusk was introduced in 1650; about 50,000 species are recorded. The squid is the largest invertebrate, 15 metres long including tentacles.

  • Habit and habitat — Mostly free-living; some are attached (sessile). Found in fresh water, marine water, moist soil and on mountain rocks, all over the world.
  • Body — Soft-bodied and triploblastic. They are mostly haemocoelomate: the coelom is divided into blood spaces. The body contains a head, a visceral region and a muscular foot.
  • Mantle and shell — The whole body is covered by an envelope of glandular epithelial tissue called the mantle. The mantle in many cases secretes a calcareous shell, which may be internal (cuttlefish), external (snail), or absent (octopus).
  • Systems — Most body systems are well developed (digestive, circulatory, respiratory, nervous and reproductive). Respiration is through gills or the mantle. The blood circulatory system is of the open type, except in class Cephalopoda. They have a tongue-like structure provided with horny teeth called the radula (the rasping tongue). Nephridia are the excretory organs (one, two or six). The nervous system consists of a collection of ganglia in the head region forming a ganglionic mass, connected with the ganglia of the foot and visceral mass.
  • Reproduction — Mostly unisexual, a few bisexual; development is indirect through the trochophore larva.
  • Economic importance — Useful: some oysters make precious pearls (pearl oyster); shells of fresh water mussels are used in the button industry; oyster shells are mixed with tar in road building; mollusks are used for making ornaments and are a source of food in many countries (oyster, mussel, clam). Pearl culture (pearl farming) induces pearl formation in oysters by surgically implanting a nucleus and mantle tissue; the oyster secretes nacre, layer by layer, around the nucleus, forming a pearl over several years. Harmful: Teredo, a shipworm, destroys the wood of ships; some mollusks destroy plants by cutting up their roots and stems.
  • Examples — Snail, mussel (Unio), octopus and chiton.

Key Points

  • Roundworms (nematodes) are pseudocoelomates with a complete digestive tube — separate mouth and anus.
  • Ascaris lives in the human small intestine; pinworm lives in the caecum, appendix and colon.
  • Mollusks are soft-bodied animals with a head, visceral mass and muscular foot, covered by a mantle that secretes the shell.
  • The radula is the rasping, tongue-like feeding organ of mollusks; nephridia are their excretory organs.

lessons.title: Phylum Annelida and Phylum Arthropoda

mcqs.q: Metamerism in annelids means the body is:
options: Divided only externally into rings with no internal partitions
Unsegmented and cylindrical, pointed at both ends
Divided into head, thorax and abdomen only
Divided into segments both internally and externally, with a transverse partition called a septum between segments
mcqs.why: Annelids are metamerically segmented internally and externally by septa, possess a true coelom divided by septa, and the coelomic fluid acts as a hydrostatic skeleton.

mcqs.q: The coelomic fluid in annelids also functions as:
options: A hydrostatic skeleton, making the body hard by fluid pressure
A respiratory pigment carrying oxygen in closed vessels
An excretory fluid discharged through flame cells
A digestive fluid filling the alimentary canal
mcqs.why: The notes state the annelid coelom is divided into compartments by septa and its fluid acts as a hydrostatic skeleton, working with muscles for locomotion.

mcqs.q: Which combination is correct for annelids?
options: Open circulatory system and Malpighian tubules as excretory organs
Closed circulatory system and segmentally arranged nephridia as excretory organs
No circulatory system and flame cells as excretory organs
Closed circulatory system and green glands as excretory organs
mcqs.why: Annelids have a straight complete gut, a closed circulatory system, segmental nephridia, and gaseous exchange through the skin.

mcqs.q: Locomotory organs differ among annelids as follows:
options: Earthworm has parapodia, Nereis has setae, and the leech has chaetae
All three move only by cilia on the underside
Earthworm has chitinous chaetae or setae, Nereis has parapodia, and the leech has none
Earthworm and leech both use tube feet for locomotion
mcqs.why: The lesson gives chaetae or setae for the earthworm, parapodia for Nereis, and states the leech has no locomotory organs.

mcqs.q: Phylum Arthropoda, named by Ernst Von Siebold in 1845, comprises about what share of the animal kingdom?
options: About 5%, making it a small phylum
About 24%, as the second largest phylum
About 95%, including all invertebrates
About 75%, making it the biggest phylum
mcqs.why: Arthropoda means jointed foot, was named by Ernst Von Siebold in 1845, and is the biggest phylum comprising about 75% of the animal kingdom.

mcqs.q: In arthropods the reduced coelom containing blood is called the:
options: Haemocoel, connected with an open blood vascular system
Pseudocoel, a remnant of the blastocoel
Spongocoel, the central cavity of the body
Enteron, the gastrovascular cavity
mcqs.why: Arthropods have a reduced coelom called the haemocoel containing blood, linked to an open blood vascular system, and their blood contains haemocyanin.

mcqs.q: Nitrogenous wastes in arthropods, uric acid and guanine, are removed through:
options: Segmental nephridia only
Malpighian tubules or green glands
Flame cells of a protonephridial system
The skin by diffusion as ammonia
mcqs.why: The notes list Malpighian tubules or green glands as the unique excretory organs of arthropods removing uric acid and guanine wastes.

mcqs.q: Incomplete metamorphosis in arthropods, as in the cockroach, is characterized by:
options: Four stages of egg, larva, pupa and adult
No larval stage and direct development only
A larval stage called a nymph that is similar to the adult
A trochophore larva that settles and transforms
mcqs.why: Incomplete metamorphosis has a nymph resembling the adult, e.g. cockroach, while complete metamorphosis in the butterfly passes through egg, larva, pupa and adult.

mcqs.q: The periodic shedding of the chitinous exoskeleton during arthropod metamorphosis is called:
options: Metamerism
Polymorphism
Regeneration
Ecdysis or moulting
mcqs.why: Arthropods are covered by a chitinous exoskeleton for muscle attachment and protection, and its periodic shedding is termed ecdysis or moulting.

mcqs.q: Which harmful arthropod pairing is correct from the notes?
options: Mosquito carries malaria and the tsetse fly carries sleeping sickness
Mosquito carries sleeping sickness and the tsetse fly carries malaria
Cyclops carries malaria directly to humans
Silverfish carries sleeping sickness to humans
mcqs.why: Harmful insects listed include mosquito for malaria and tsetse fly for sleeping sickness, while Cyclops acts as an intermediate host carrying nematode larvae.

lessons.notes_html:
Annelids are the first truly segmented coelomate worms, and arthropods — with jointed legs and a chitinous exoskeleton — form the biggest phylum of the animal kingdom.

11.9 Phylum Annelida — Segmented Worms

Annelida (Latin: annulus = a little ring; Greek: eidos = form).

  • Habit and habitat — Free-living, found in soil (earthworm), fresh water and marine water (Nereis); some are ectoparasites (leech).
  • Body and metamerism — Triploblastic and metamerically segmented: in metamerism the body is divided into segments both internally and externally, by a transverse partition called a septum between segments. Annelids possess a true coelom, divided into compartments by septa; the coelomic fluid also acts as a hydrostatic skeleton (the body becomes hard by fluid pressure).
  • Systems — A straight alimentary canal with mouth and anus at opposite ends (a complete digestive system). The circulatory system is closed. Segmentally arranged nephridia are the excretory organs. The nervous system has a dorsal pair of cerebral ganglia and a ventral double ganglionated nerve cord. Gaseous exchange is through the skin. Muscles with the hydrostatic skeleton help in locomotion. Chitinous chaetae or setae are the locomotory organs in the earthworm, while Nereis has parapodia; the leech has no locomotory organs.
  • Reproduction — Most annelids are bisexual (e.g. leeches, earthworm), some are unisexual (Nereis). Development is either direct or indirect through the trochophore larva. They also exhibit regeneration.
  • Economic importance — Earthworms burrow in the soil, which permits great penetration of air into the soil, improves the drainage capacity of the soil, makes the soil soft and increases fertility. Many worms are used as food by fishes.

11.10 Phylum Arthropoda — Joint-Footed Animals

Arthropoda (Greek: arthron = jointed, pous = foot). The name was given by Ernst Von Siebold in 1845.

  • Habit and habitat — Free-living or parasitic, found in almost all habitats. It is the biggest phylum, comprising about 75% of the animal kingdom.
  • Body — (i) A segmented body, the segments attached to one another by a thin, flexible cuticle. (ii) Several pairs of jointed limbs (appendages). (iii) The body is usually divided into head, thorax and abdomen. (iv) The body is covered with a chitinous cuticle. The reduced coelom contains blood and is called the haemocoel, connected with an open blood vascular system.
  • Systems — The digestive system is well developed, with mouth and anus or cloaca. The nervous system consists of paired ganglia forming a simple brain and a central ganglionated nerve cord. Sensory receptors, especially eyes, are present, along with cuticular hairs and antennae. Uric acid and guanine are the nitrogenous wastes, removed through unique excretory organs called Malpighian tubules or green glands. Respiration is through tracheae, gills or book lungs. The blood circulatory system is of the open type; the blood is colourless, without haemoglobin, but haemocyanin (a copper-containing protein) is present. A chitinous exoskeleton is present for the attachment of muscles.
  • Reproduction and metamorphosis — All are unisexual; fertilization is internal or external. Development is mostly indirect, accompanied by metamorphosis of two types: (a) Incomplete metamorphosis — the larval stage, called a nymph, is similar to the adult, e.g. cockroach. (b) Complete metamorphosis — through egg, larva, pupa and adult, e.g. butterfly. The periodic shedding of the exoskeleton during metamorphosis is called ecdysis or moulting.
  • Examples — Wasp, scorpion, centipede, crab, millipede.
  • Why arthropods are successful — They possess jointed feet and a segmented body, which provides great mobility. The chitinous exoskeleton protects the body and makes it light. Internal fertilization and development within an egg case (cocoon) help them, and appendages perform various functions such as quick movement, defence and offence, so they live in a variety of habitats — for example, the legs and mouth parts of the cockroach.

11.11 Economic Importance of Arthropods

  • Crustaceans — Provide food directly and indirectly to humans (prawn, crab, lobster). Some are harmful because they act as intermediate hosts for human parasites (larvae of nematodes are carried by Cyclops).
  • Beneficial insects — Help in pollination (bee, butterfly, ants); used as food in some parts of the world (grasshopper, cricket); many are scavengers. Commercial substances such as honey, beeswax, silk and shellac are produced by honey bees, silkworms and lac insects. Some insects eat other harmful insects, e.g. the dragonfly feeds on mosquitoes. Several insects are used for scientific studies, such as cockroach, fruit fly and grasshopper.
  • Harmful insects — Destroy stored foods and grains (ants, weevils); carry parasitic diseases (mosquito: malaria; tsetse fly: sleeping sickness); damage crops, fruit and timber trees (grasshoppers, locusts, beetles); damage books (silverfish) and furniture (white ants); some sting (bee) or suck blood (louse).
  • Arachnida — Poisonous arachnids like the scorpion and certain spiders sting humans; ticks and mites are parasitic disease carriers, and mites also destroy crops. Beneficial arachnids like scorpions and spiders feed on injurious insects.

Key Points

  • Annelids show true metamerism and a true coelom; nephridia are their excretory organs and setae or parapodia help in locomotion.
  • Earthworms improve soil aeration, drainage and fertility.
  • Arthropods are the largest phylum (about 75% of the animal kingdom): jointed legs, segmented body, chitinous exoskeleton shed by ecdysis.
  • Arthropods are both useful (pollination, honey, silk, food) and harmful (crop pests and disease carriers such as the mosquito).

lessons.title: Echinodermata, Hemichordata and Phylum Chordata

mcqs.q: Phylum Echinodermata, named by Leuckert in 1847, has how many known species recorded in the notes and what habitat?
options: More than 5,000 species, exclusively marine
About 70 species, marine and fresh water
About 10,000 species, marine and fresh water
About 50,000 species, in all habitats
mcqs.why: Echinodermata means spiny skin, was named by Leuckert in 1847, has more than 5,000 known species and is exclusively marine.

mcqs.q: Symmetry in echinoderms changes during life as:
options: Adults are bilaterally symmetrical while larvae are radially symmetrical
Adults are radially symmetrical while larvae are bilaterally symmetrical
Both adults and larvae are radially symmetrical
Both adults and larvae are asymmetrical
mcqs.why: Echinoderms are triploblastic coelomates whose adults are radially symmetrical but whose Bipinnaria and Brachiolaria larvae are bilaterally symmetrical.

mcqs.q: In the echinoderm water vascular system, water enters through:
options: The ostia on the body wall, and locomotion is by parapodia
The mouth on the oral surface, and locomotion is by setae
The madreporite, a sieve-like plate on the aboral surface, and locomotion is by tube feet
The osculum at the top, and locomotion is by cilia
mcqs.why: Water enters the ambulacral system through the madreporite on the aboral surface, circulates through tubes to the arms and tube feet, which perform locomotion.

mcqs.q: The hemichordate body is distinguished into three parts:
options: Head, thorax and abdomen
Head, visceral region and foot
Prothorax, collar and abdomen
Proboscis, collar and trunk
mcqs.why: Hemichordates are soft, unsegmented, worm-like animals with only about 70 species recorded, and their body is divided into proboscis, collar and trunk.

mcqs.q: Hemichordates are grouped with echinoderms and chordates because only these three groups are:
options: Deuterostomes
Protostomes
Acoelomates
Pseudocoelomates
mcqs.why: The notes say hemichordates resemble both echinoderms and chordates because only these three groups are deuterostomes, sharing deuterostome development and gill slits.

mcqs.q: The three basic characteristics every chordate possesses at some stage of life are:
options: Vertebral column, cranium, and paired appendages
Notochord, dorsal hollow nervous system, and pharyngeal gill slits and pouches
Mantle, muscular foot, and radula
Proboscis, collar, and trunk
mcqs.why: All chordates have a notochord, a dorsal hollow fluid-filled non-ganglionated nerve cord, and pharyngeal gill slits at some stage or throughout life.

mcqs.q: In vertebrate chordates, the notochord is:
options: Retained unchanged throughout life in all cases
Present only in the tail of the larva and lost in the adult
Replaced by the vertebral column, serving as the axial endoskeleton
Converted into the dorsal hollow nerve cord
mcqs.why: The notochord appears in the embryo of all chordates; in lower chordates it persists for life, but in vertebrates it is replaced by the vertebral column.

mcqs.q: In terrestrial vertebrates, the pharyngeal gill slits are replaced by structures including:
options: Gills that persist and function in respiration
The madreporite and tube feet
The mantle and the radula
The Eustachian or auditory tube, parathyroid, tonsils and thymus
mcqs.why: In aquatic chordates gill slits persist for respiration, while in terrestrial vertebrates they are replaced by the Eustachian tube, parathyroid, tonsils and thymus.

mcqs.q: In Urochordata such as Ascidia and Herdmania, the notochord is:
options: Present only in the tail of the larva and disappears in the adult, and the body is covered with a tunic
Present throughout life running mid-dorsally through the body
Replaced by a vertebral column with a cranium in the adult
Absent even in the larval stage
mcqs.why: Urochordates are tunicates: the larva is free-swimming with a tail notochord, but the adult is non-motile, loses the notochord and nerve cord except a dorsal ganglion.

mcqs.q: Cephalochordata, exemplified by Amphioxus (Branchiostoma), are characterized by:
options: The notochord present only in the larval tail and a tunic covering the adult
The notochord runs mid-dorsally through the body and persists, with the nerve cord, throughout life
A vertebral column, brain, cranium, jaws and red blood cells
No notochord at any stage of life
mcqs.why: In Cephalochordata the notochord and nerve cord persist throughout life, unlike Urochordata, and like other Acrania they have no skull, jaws or paired appendages.

lessons.notes_html:
The echinoderms are spiny-skinned marine deuterostomes with a water vascular system. The hemichordates stand between invertebrates and chordates, and the chordates are defined by three basic characters: a notochord, a dorsal hollow nervous system and pharyngeal gill slits.

11.12 Phylum Echinodermata — Spiny-Skinned Animals

Echinodermata (Greek: echinos = spine, derma = skin). The phylum name was given by Leuckert in 1847.

  • Habit and habitat — Mostly free-living, some attached to the substratum; exclusively marine. More than 5,000 known species are recorded.
  • Body — Triploblastic and coelomate. The adult is radially symmetrical while the larvae are bilaterally symmetrical. A delicate epidermis covers a firm mesodermal calcareous exoskeleton. The mouth is on the lower (oral) surface and the anus on the upper (aboral) surface. Arms radiate from a central disc; the body may be biscuit-shaped (cake urchin), star-shaped (starfish, brittle star), globular (sea urchin) or elongated (sea cucumber).
  • Water vascular system (ambulacral canal) — Water circulates through coelomic channels, entering through a sieve-like plate called the madreporite on the aboral body surface. It is a system of complex tubes and spaces surrounding the mouth and passing into the arms and tube feet. Locomotion occurs through the tube feet.
  • Other systems — The digestive and reproductive systems are well developed. There are no specialized organs for respiration or excretion. The nervous system is poorly developed and consists only of a pharyngeal nerve ring; the circulatory system is also less developed.
  • Reproduction — Mostly sexual; fertilization is external and the animals are unisexual. Development is indirect, through complex, bilaterally symmetrical larvae named Bipinnaria and Brachiolaria. Echinoderms also exhibit regeneration.
  • Examples and importance — Starfish, sea cucumber, sea lily, brittle star and sea urchin. Many are used as food; starfish act as scavengers and clean sea water; dried skeletons are used as fertilizer (rich in calcium and nitrogenous compounds). Some are poisonous (sea urchin stings humans) and they damage oyster beds.

11.13 Phylum Hemichordata — the Tongue Worms

Hemichordates resemble both echinoderms and chordates, because only these three groups are deuterostomes. Only 70 species are recorded. They were earlier placed in the chordates, but are now a separate phylum: they have some chordate-like characters (deuterostome development, pharyngeal gill slits, a dorsal nerve cord that is sometimes hollow), but lack a complete notochord, and their dorsal heart and epidermal nervous system are non-chordate characters.

  • The body is soft, unsegmented and mostly worm-like, distinguished into proboscis, collar and trunk.
  • The epidermis contains mucus-secreting cells; the animals are bilaterally symmetrical and triploblastic.
  • Gills are the respiratory organs; the blood is colourless and without cells; a dorsal heart has invertebrate-like blood vessels.
  • The excretory system is well developed (a glomerulus is present in the proboscis, where the excretory pore also opens); the nervous system is epidermal.
  • They are either unisexual or bisexual; fertilization is external and development indirect. They are marine, solitary or colonial, free-living or sessile, and feed on microliving things. Examples: Balanoglossus and Saccoglossus.

11.14 Phylum Chordata: Basic and General Characteristics

All chordates possess three basic or fundamental characteristics, during some stage or in the whole of life:

  • Notochord — An unjointed, solid skeleton placed above the alimentary canal and below the dorsal body wall and central nervous system; it appears in the embryo of all chordates. In lower chordates it is present throughout life, but in vertebrate chordates it is replaced by the vertebral column; in vertebrates it serves as the axial endoskeleton and gives support to the body.
  • Dorsal hollow nervous system — The central nervous system is dorsally placed, located above the notochord; the nerve cord is hollow, fluid-filled and non-ganglionated.
  • Pharyngeal gill slits and gill pouches — Paired openings in the pharyngeal region. In aquatic chordates they persist and function as respiratory organs, while in terrestrial vertebrates they are replaced by the Eustachian or auditory tube, parathyroid, tonsils and thymus.

General characteristics: bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic body; coelomate body cavity; a complete digestive system with digestive glands; a closed blood vascular system with a ventral heart; a well developed hepatic portal system; organ-system level of organization; a post-anal tail in most chordates; and kidneys (proto-, meso- or meta-nephric) as excretory organs.

The basic characteristics of chordates: dorsal hollow nerve cord, notochord, pharyngeal slits and a post-anal tail.

Acrania and Craniata

Phylum Chordata has two groups. (i) Acrania (invertebrate chordates) — "without skull": no brain or cranium, no jaws, RBCs or paired appendages, and the notochord never changes into a vertebral column. Its two subphyla are: Urochordata — the notochord is present only in the tail of the larva and disappears in the adult, as does the nerve cord (only a dorsal ganglion remains); larvae are free-swimming, adults non-motile, and the body is covered with a tunic, so they are called tunicates, e.g. Ascidia, Herdmania, Molgula; and Cephalochordata — the notochord runs mid-dorsally through the body and persists, with the nerve cord, throughout life, e.g. Amphioxus (Branchiostoma). (ii) Craniata (vertebrate chordates) — one subphylum, Vertebrata: the notochord is replaced by a vertebral column; they have a brain and cranium, paired appendages, teeth, jaws and RBCs, and kidneys. So all vertebrates are chordates, but all chordates are not vertebrates.

Key Points

  • Echinoderms are marine, radially symmetrical as adults, with a water vascular system entering through the madreporite and locomotion by tube feet.
  • Hemichordates (Balanoglossus) have proboscis, collar and trunk, with some chordate-like and some non-chordate characters.
  • Every chordate has, at some stage, a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord and pharyngeal gill slits.
  • Acrania (Urochordata and Cephalochordata) have no skull; Craniata (Vertebrata) replace the notochord with a vertebral column.

lessons.title: Vertebrate Classes: Fishes, Amphibians, Reptiles, Birds and Mammals

mcqs.q: Superclass Agnatha, class Cyclostomata, are the most primitive living vertebrates because they lack:
options: A vertebral column and a cranium
True jaws and paired appendages, and have a circular suctorial mouth
Gills for respiration in water
A cartilaginous skeleton
mcqs.why: Cyclostomata means circular mouth; these eel-shaped fishes have no true jaws or paired appendages, no scales, a cartilaginous skeleton and 6 to 14 pairs of gills.

mcqs.q: Class Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fishes) can be recognized by:
options: Cycloid scales, 4 pairs of gills covered by an operculum and a swim bladder present
A bony endoskeleton and a terminal mouth
Placoid scales, 5 to 7 pairs of gills not covered by an operculum, a completely cartilaginous endoskeleton and no swim bladder
Smooth scaleless skin and a suctorial circular mouth
mcqs.why: Chondrichthyes are exclusively marine with tough placoid scales, uncovered gills, cartilaginous skeleton, a J-shaped stomach and a cloaca, and no swim bladder.

mcqs.q: The largest of all fishes, the whale shark at 30 to 50 feet long, belongs to:
options: Class Osteichthyes
Class Cyclostomata
Class Amphibia
Class Chondrichthyes
mcqs.why: The notes place the whale shark, 30 to 50 feet long, in the cartilaginous fishes Chondrichthyes, whose liver oil is a source of vitamins A and D.

mcqs.q: Class Osteichthyes (bony fishes) differ from cartilaginous fishes in having:
options: Four pairs of gills covered by an operculum, a mostly bony endoskeleton and usually a swim bladder for buoyancy
Five to seven pairs of uncovered gills and no swim bladder
Placoid scales and a completely cartilaginous skeleton
A cloaca and a J-shaped stomach as diagnostic features
mcqs.why: Bony fishes have ganoid, cycloid or ctenoid scales, four gill pairs under an operculum, a bony skeleton and a swim bladder that helps them stay at a chosen depth.

mcqs.q: Amphibians, believed to have originated from Dipnoi the lobe-finned lung fishes, have a heart with:
options: A single auricle and a single ventricle only
Right and left auricles and a single ventricle, with sinus venosus and truncus arteriosus
Two auricles and two completely divided ventricles
Two atria and two ventricles with one left aorta
mcqs.why: Amphibia are the first land vertebrates; larvae respire by gills, adults by lungs and skin, and the heart has two auricles and one ventricle.

mcqs.q: In reptiles, the heart has a partly divided ventricle except in which animal, where ventricles and atria are completely divided?
options: Snake
Wall lizard
Crocodile
Tortoise
mcqs.why: Reptiles are the first successful terrestrial group with dry scaly skin; their heart has a partly divided ventricle, except the crocodile which has completely divided ventricles and atria.

mcqs.q: The Jurassic fossil birds providing a connecting link between birds and reptiles are:
options: Kiwi and ostrich, preserved as running birds
Penguin and emu, preserved as aquatic birds
Archaeopteryx, preserved in Berlin, and Archaeornis in London
Archaeopteryx, preserved in the British Museum London, and Archaeornis, preserved in Berlin Museum Germany
mcqs.why: Birds evolved from ancient running reptiles; Archaeopteryx in London and Archaeornis in Berlin, from the Jurassic 144 to 208 million years ago, evidence the link.

mcqs.q: Which set lists only flight adaptations of birds from the notes?
options: Streamlined body, wings, hollow bones, keeled sternum, air sacs, beak and no urinary bladder
Feathers, four-chambered heart, teeth in the beak and a urinary bladder
Scales on the whole body, solid bones and two functional ovaries
Gizzard, syrinx and uric acid as the only adaptations
mcqs.why: Flight adaptations given are streamlined body, forelimbs as wings, light hollow endoskeleton, keeled sternum, air sacs with double respiration, a toothless beak and no urinary bladder to reduce weight.

mcqs.q: The diagnostic character of Mammalia, whose name was given by Linnaeus, is:
options: Presence of feathers and a keeled sternum
Presence of mammary glands by which females nurse their young
Presence of a swim bladder and an operculum
Presence of mammary glands only inside an abdominal pouch
mcqs.why: Mammals are diagnosed by mammary glands, and also have hair or fur, a diaphragm, sweat and sebaceous glands, two occipital condyles and non-nucleated mature RBCs.

mcqs.q: Subclass Eutheria, the placental mammals and largest mammalian group, are truly viviparous because:
options: Females rear immature young in an abdominal pouch or marsupium
They lay eggs and have a cloaca like reptiles
The young develop inside the mother and are nourished through the placenta
They nurse young only with glands inside a pouch
mcqs.why: Eutheria nourish young through a placenta with anus and urinogenital openings completely separated; the pouch description belongs to Metatheria and egg laying to Prototheria.

lessons.notes_html:
The vertebrate chordates (Craniata) are divided into two superclasses: Agnatha, without true jaws and paired appendages, and Gnathostomata, with true jaws and paired appendages. Gnathostomata has six classes: Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes, Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves and Mammalia. The two fish classes are sometimes together placed in a division known as Pisces.

Superclass Agnatha: Class Cyclostomata

Cyclostomata (cyclo = circular, stoma = mouth, because their mouth is circular). These fishes are without true jaws and form the most primitive group of living vertebrates. The body is eel-shaped, scales are absent, the skin is smooth and soft, the skeleton is cartilaginous and the mouth is suctorial; there are no paired appendages. The heart is a two-chambered venous heart with many aortic arches; the digestive system lacks a stomach; there are 6–14 pairs of gills for respiration. They are unisexual (lamprey) or bisexual (hagfish), with a single testis or a single ovary and no accessory ducts; fertilization is external, and development is direct or indirect (the lamprey has a prolonged larval period). Examples: Myxine (hagfish) and Lamprey (Petromyzon).

Class Chondrichthyes — Cartilaginous Fishes

  • Habit and habitat — Exclusively marine and free-living.
  • Body — Spindle-shaped; the mouth is ventral and semi-circular, and the nasal sacs do not open into the oral cavity. The skin is tough, covered with sandpaper-like placoid scales. Respiration is through 5–7 pairs of gills, not covered by an operculum (lid). The endoskeleton is completely cartilaginous and the swim bladder is absent.
  • Systems and reproduction — The digestive system has a cloaca (a common opening acting as the urinogenital opening) and a J-shaped stomach. The heart is a venous, single-circuit heart with a single auricle and a single ventricle, and 5–7 pairs of aortic arches. Sexes are separate with paired gonads; fertilization is internal; oviparous or ovoviviparous. The largest of all fishes, the whale shark (30–50 feet long), belongs to this group. Examples: skate, rays, sting ray, electric ray and dog fish (sharks).
  • Economic importance — Beneficial: a great source of food; shark liver oil is a source of vitamin A and D; shark skin leather is used for bags and shoes. Harmful: sharks feed on sea food used by humans, like prawn, crab and lobster. In fishes, gills take oxygen from water and fins give balance, steering and propulsion.

Class Osteichthyes — Bony Fishes

  • Habit and body — They live in both marine and fresh water. The body is spindle-shaped and the mouth is terminal. Most have dermal, non-placoid scales: ganoid, cycloid or ctenoid. There are four pairs of gills, supported by bony arches and covered with a lid called the operculum. The endoskeleton is mostly bony, and a swim bladder is usually present, which helps in buoyancy (staying at a chosen depth without spending energy).
  • Systems and reproduction — The heart has two chambers (an auricle and a ventricle) and four pairs of aortic arches; the brain has ten pairs of cranial nerves. Sexes are separate with paired gonads; fertilization is mostly external; most are oviparous, some ovoviviparous. Examples: trout, cod, carp and catfish.
  • Economic importance — Fresh water and marine bony fishes are an important food source (cod, herring, salmon, trout, carp, catfish, mullet). Fish oil, fish meat and liquid glue are made from bony fish, and cod liver oil is the source of vitamin A and D.

Class Amphibia — the First Land Vertebrates

Amphibia (Greek: amphi = both, bios = life) are the first land vertebrates, i.e. the transition from aquatic to land habitat; they probably originated from Dipnoi, the lobe-finned lung fishes.

  • Body — The skin is smooth, scaleless and with many mucus glands (some also have poisonous glands and chromatophores). The body is divided into head, trunk, and tail or no tail. There are usually two pairs of legs, but some are legless (caecilians). Larvae respire through gills; adults mostly through lungs and skin. The heart has right and left auricles and a single ventricle, with sinus venosus and truncus arteriosus.
  • Reproduction — Unisexual, with paired sex organs; fertilization is usually external. Most are oviparous and show indirect development through metamorphosis. They are anamniotes (the embryo lacks a protective membrane) and poikilothermic (cold-blooded), so they hibernate in winter. Examples: frogs and toads (tailless), salamanders (tailed), caecilians (limbless).

Class Reptilia

Reptilia (Latin: repere = to crawl) are the first successful terrestrial group.

  • Skin and body — Dry, non-glandular, scaly skin (snakes and lizards) or bony plates (tortoise and crocodile). The body is divided into head, trunk and tail; appendages are tetrapod and pentadactyl, but some reptiles are legless (snakes). The skull has one occipital condyle. All are cold-blooded, so they hibernate in winter.
  • Heart and reproduction — The heart has right and left auricles and a partly divided ventricle, except in the crocodile, which has completely divided ventricles and atria. Fertilization is internal; mostly oviparous, laying amniotic, large, yolky, shelled eggs. They respire through lungs. Examples: snakes (cobra), lizards (wall lizard), turtles, tortoises and crocodiles.

Class Aves — Birds

Aves (Latin: avis = bird). Birds evolved from ancient running reptiles; the Jurassic (144–208 million years ago) birds Archaeopteryx (preserved in the British Museum, London) and Archaeornis (preserved in Berlin Museum, Germany) provided evidence of a connecting link between birds and reptiles.

  • Diagnostic characters — The body is streamlined, covered with feathers, and the forelimbs are modified into wings. The mouth contains a beak without teeth, and the sternum is modified into a keel. They have a single occipital condyle and are warm-blooded (homeothermic). The body is divided into head, neck, trunk and tail. Locomotion is bipedal; the hind limbs are modified for perching and bear scales and claws. The endoskeleton is light and hollow.
  • Systems — A four-chambered heart (two auricles and two ventricles); only the right aorta is present. The lungs are supplemented with air sacs and show double respiration. The voice box is the syrinx. There is a pair of kidneys but no urinary bladder (to reduce weight); the nitrogenous waste is uric acid, removed as crystals through the faeces. The gizzard is the grinding organ.
  • Reproduction — All are unisexual; fertilization is internal; birds lay eggs (oviparous); the left ovary is functional. These are the flight adaptations of birds: streamlined body, wings, hollow bones, keeled sternum, air sacs, beak and no urinary bladder. Some birds have lost flight and are called running birds (kiwi, ostrich, emu, rhea, cassowary); flying birds include parrot, crow, pigeon, sparrow and kite. The penguin is an aquatic bird whose forelimbs are modified into paddles.

Class Mammalia

The name Mammalia was given by Linnaeus. The diagnostic character of mammals is the presence of mammary glands, by which females nurse their young ones.

  • General characters — The body is mostly covered with hairs or fur. The central nervous system is highly developed; the lungs possess numerous alveoli and bronchioles. The diaphragm is a muscular partition between the chest and abdomen. Most have external ears (pinnae), and sweat and sebaceous (oil) glands. Mammals are warm-blooded (homeotherms, like birds; reptiles and amphibians are poikilotherms). They have two pairs of pentadactyl limbs, two occipital condyles and a large cranium. The buccal cavity has two sets of teeth in the life span (milk teeth and permanent teeth); dentition is heterodont. The heart has two atria and two ventricles, with one left aorta. Mature RBCs are non-nucleated. Fertilization is internal and they are mostly viviparous.
  • Subclass Prototheria (egg-laying mammals) — A connecting link between reptiles and mammals. Mammalian characters: mammary glands, hair, diaphragm and left aorta. Reptilian characters: cloaca, egg laying and some reptilian skeleton. They have one living order, the monotremes, found only in Australia. Examples: Echidna (spiny ant eater) and duck-billed platypus.
  • Subclass Metatheria (pouched mammals, marsupials) — Females possess an abdominal pouch (marsupium) in which they rear their immature young; the mammary glands are inside the pouch. Generally burrowing and herbivorous; found in Australia and America. Examples: opossum, kangaroo and Tasmanian wolf.
  • Subclass Eutheria (placental mammals) — True mammals and the largest group: the young develop inside the mother's body and are nourished through the placenta, so they are truly viviparous. The anus and urinogenital openings are completely separated. In some forms hair is modified into spines (porcupine, hedgehog) or scales (pangolin). Examples: goat, dog, horse, elephant, seal, whale, dolphin, man and monkey.

Key Points

  • Agnatha (Cyclostomata: hagfish, lamprey) have no true jaws; Gnathostomata have jaws and paired appendages.
  • Chondrichthyes have a cartilaginous skeleton, placoid scales and no swim bladder; Osteichthyes have a bony skeleton, an operculum and usually a swim bladder.
  • Amphibians are cold-blooded anamniotes with metamorphosis; reptiles are the first successful terrestrial group, laying shelled amniotic eggs.
  • Birds are homeothermic, feathered, with wings, hollow bones, a keeled sternum, air sacs and a syrinx.
  • Mammals have mammary glands, hair and a diaphragm: Prototheria lay eggs, Metatheria carry young in a pouch, Eutheria nourish young through a placenta.

lessons.title: Chromosomes: Structure, Types and Ultra-Structure
lessons.notes_html:
Chromosomes (Chromo — colored; soma — body) are compact coils of thread-like structure, clearly visible only during cell division. In interphase they uncoil into a fine chromatin network (DNA and proteins) and carry the information the cell needs to exist. They were first recorded by Walther Fleming in 1882 in rapidly dividing cells of salamander larvae; Waldeyer assigned the name chromosome. They are linear in eukaryotes and circular in prokaryotes.

Chromosome Number and Karyotype

Number varies between species but stays constant in a species, generation after generation. Most animals and plants are diploid (two sets), many plants are polyploid (more than two sets), bryophytes and many fungi are monoploid, and haploid (half the somatic number) applies to gametes and most spores. Book examples (pairs): Penicillium 1, mosquito 3, fruit fly 4, lettuce 9, corn 10, frog 13, honey bee 16, mouse 20, human 23, monkey 24, camel 35, sugarcane 40, some ferns more than 500. The particular array of chromosomes an individual possesses is its karyotype.

Structure of a Chromosome

  • Monad and diad — A monad (unduplicated) chromosome has one strand, a chromatid; a diad (duplicated) has two sister chromatids, each a long DNA molecule tightly coiled with histone proteins.
  • Centromere (primary constriction) — The narrowed point of union. On both sides are disc-shaped proteins, the kinetochore, where spindle microtubules attach to move the chromosome during division.
  • Secondary constriction (nuclear organizer) — A second point of union on some chromosomes; it gives rise to nucleoli in interphase. The part beyond it is a knob-like satellite. DNA with useless sequences is junk DNA.
  • Telomeres — The terminal ends; they prevent chromosomes attaching to each other at their ends, and are made of repeated DNA with the sequence 5' TTAGGG-3'.

A duplicated (diad) chromosome: two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, telomeres at the ends.

Types on the Basis of Centromere Position

  • Metacentric — Centromere in the centre.
  • Submetacentric — Centromere below or above the centre.
  • Acrocentric — Arms on one side very short, on the other side very long.
  • Telocentric — Centromere at the tip, at one end.

Chemical Composition and Ultra-Structure

Chromosomes are nucleoprotein: about 60% proteins, 40% DNA and a significant amount of RNA. An average human chromosome has about 140 million nucleotides in about 5 cm of DNA. Under the electron microscope, DNA is packed in repeated nucleosomes: about 146–147 nucleotides coiled around a core of eight histones (an octamer: two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4). Histones are positively charged (rich in arginine and lysine) and are attracted to the negatively charged phosphate groups of DNA. DNA between nucleosomes is linker DNA, with linker histone H1. Packing levels: 2 nm DNA → 10 nm nucleosome string → 30 nm chromatin solenoid → 300 nm fibres → 700 nm supercoils → 1400 nm chromatid. In interphase, highly condensed heterochromatin is mostly not expressed, while less condensed euchromatin condenses during division and its genes can be expressed after division.

Key Points

  • Chromosomes are DNA coiled with histones, visible only during division; number is fixed for each species.
  • Diad = two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, with kinetochore, satellite and telomeres.
  • Four types by centromere position: metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric, telocentric.
  • Nucleosome = 146–147 nucleotides around a histone octamer (H2A, H2B, H3, H4 x 2).

mcqs.q: Chromosomes were first recorded by Walther Fleming in 1882 in:
options: Gametes of the fruit fly
Root tip cells of corn
Rapidly dividing cells of salamander larvae
Bacterial cells of E. coli
mcqs.why: The notes state Fleming first recorded chromosomes in 1882 in rapidly dividing salamander larva cells, and Waldeyer assigned the name chromosome.

mcqs.q: Which chromosome number pairing is correct from the book examples given?
options: Human 20 pairs, fruit fly 9 pairs, mosquito 16 pairs
Human 24 pairs, fruit fly 13 pairs, mosquito 1 pair
Human 23 pairs, fruit fly 10 pairs, mosquito 40 pairs
Human 23 pairs, fruit fly 4 pairs, mosquito 3 pairs
mcqs.why: Book examples in pairs are Penicillium 1, mosquito 3, fruit fly 4, lettuce 9, corn 10, frog 13, honey bee 16, mouse 20 and human 23.

mcqs.q: The particular array of chromosomes an individual possesses is called its:
options: Karyotype
Chromatin network
Nucleosome
Chromatid
mcqs.why: Chromosome number is constant for a species generation after generation, and the particular array an individual possesses is defined as its karyotype.

mcqs.q: A diad (duplicated) chromosome differs from a monad because a diad has:
options: One single chromatid strand only
Two sister chromatids, each a long DNA molecule coiled with histone proteins
Four chromatids joined at two centromeres
No centromere or kinetochore at all
mcqs.why: A monad has one chromatid, while a diad has two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, each made of DNA tightly coiled with histones.

mcqs.q: The kinetochore, found on both sides of the centromere, is:
options: A knob-like satellite beyond the secondary constriction
A terminal end that prevents chromosomes attaching to each other
A disc-shaped protein where spindle microtubules attach to move the chromosome during division
A repeated DNA sequence at the chromosome tip
mcqs.why: The centromere is the primary constriction; its disc-shaped kinetochore proteins are the attachment sites for spindle microtubules during division.

mcqs.q: The secondary constriction (nuclear organizer) gives rise to what in interphase, and the part beyond it is called a:
options: Spindle fibres; the part beyond is a telomere
Histones; the part beyond is a chromatid
Nucleosomes; the part beyond is linker DNA
Nucleoli; the part beyond is a knob-like satellite
mcqs.why: Some chromosomes have a secondary constriction that gives rise to nucleoli in interphase, and the region beyond it is the knob-like satellite.

mcqs.q: Telomeres, the terminal ends of chromosomes, are made of repeated DNA with the sequence:
options: 5 prime TTAGGG 3 prime, and they prevent chromosomes attaching to each other at their ends
5 prime AAAAAA 3 prime, and they attach spindle fibres
3 prime TTAGGG 5 prime, and they form the centromere
5 prime CCAATT 3 prime, and they give rise to nucleoli
mcqs.why: The notes give the telomere repeat as 5' TTAGGG-3' and state telomeres prevent chromosomes from attaching to each other at their ends.

mcqs.q: A telocentric chromosome is one in which the centromere is:
options: Exactly in the centre of the chromosome
At the tip, at one end of the chromosome
Below or above the centre of the chromosome
Absent, so arms form on both sides equally
mcqs.why: By centromere position: metacentric is central, submetacentric is off-centre, acrocentric has very short and very long arms, and telocentric is at the tip.

mcqs.q: A nucleosome consists of:
options: About 500 nucleotides coiled around a single H1 histone only
About 60 nucleotides coiled around four histones in total
About 146 to 147 nucleotides coiled around a core of eight histones, two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4
About 140 million nucleotides coiled around a centromere
mcqs.why: DNA packing uses nucleosomes of 146-147 nucleotides around a histone octamer of two each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4, with linker DNA and H1 between nucleosomes.

mcqs.q: Chromosomes are nucleoprotein with an approximate composition of:
options: About 40 percent proteins and 60 percent DNA only
About 90 percent DNA and 10 percent proteins
Equal parts DNA, protein and RNA at one third each
About 60 percent proteins, 40 percent DNA and a significant amount of RNA
mcqs.why: The chemical composition given is about 60% proteins and 40% DNA plus significant RNA, and packing proceeds 2 nm DNA to 10, 30, 300, 700 and 1400 nm chromatid.

lessons.title: DNA as the Hereditary Material: Griffith, Avery and Hershey–Chase
lessons.notes_html:
Chromosomes contain both DNA and protein, so it was not confirmed which one carries hereditary information. Three classic experiments settled the question.

Griffith's Experiment (1928)

Fredrick Griffith gave the first evidence while working with Streptococcus pneumoniae: the S-type has a polysaccharide capsule, smooth and shiny colonies, and is virulent; the R-type has no capsule, rough colonies, and is non-virulent. S-type killed mice by blood poisoning; R-type caused no ill effects. Heat-killed S-type alone left mice healthy, but a mixture of dead S-type and live R-type — each harmless alone — killed the mice, and live virulent S-type bacteria were recovered from their blood. The information for the coat had passed from dead S-type to live R-type, permanently transforming it. This transfer of genetic material that alters the recipient cell is called transformation.

Avery, Macleod and McCarty (1944)

Oswald Avery, with Colin Macleod and Maclyn McCarty, identified the transforming principle. To mixtures of dead S- and live R-Streptococcus they added proteinase, RNase and DNase in separate tubes. Proteinase and RNase did not affect transformation — S-cells appeared. DNase destroyed all transforming activity and no S-cells appeared. They confirmed DNA is the hereditary material, while protein and RNA have no hereditary role.

Hershey and Chase Experiment (1952)

Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase used bacteriophage T₂, which infects Escherichia coli and, like a chromosome, is made of DNA and protein only (linear double-stranded DNA). They labelled phage DNA with radioactive 32P in one experiment and the protein coats with radioactive 35S (present only in protein) in another. Separate bacterial cultures were exposed to each type, then agitated violently in a blender to remove the protein coats from the bacterial surfaces. Bacteria lost nearly all the 35S label, because it stayed in the coats outside; the 32P label was found inside the bacteria. When new viruses were released, those from the 32P culture were labelled and those from the 35S culture were unlabelled — proving the hereditary information injected into bacteria was DNA, not protein.

Key Points

  • Griffith (1928): dead S + live R killed mice — transformation showed a hereditary principle passes between cells.
  • Avery, Macleod and McCarty (1944): only DNase destroyed transformation, so the principle is DNA.
  • Hershey and Chase (1952): 32P (DNA) entered bacteria and labelled the next phage generation; 35S (protein) stayed outside.

mcqs.q: In Griffith's 1928 experiment, the S-type Streptococcus pneumoniae was virulent because it had:
options: No capsule, forming rough colonies
A protein capsule, forming rough colonies
No capsule, but it killed mice by blood poisoning alone
A polysaccharide capsule, forming smooth and shiny colonies
mcqs.why: Griffith's S-type has a polysaccharide capsule, smooth shiny colonies and is virulent, while the R-type has no capsule, rough colonies and is non-virulent.

mcqs.q: The R-type bacteria in Griffith's experiment were:
options: Non-virulent, with no capsule and rough colonies, causing no ill effects in mice
Virulent, killing mice by blood poisoning
Virulent only after being heated and killed
Smooth and shiny because of their capsule
mcqs.why: The R-type lacks a capsule, forms rough colonies, is non-virulent and caused no ill effects, unlike the S-type which killed mice by blood poisoning.

mcqs.q: Griffith found that a mixture of heat-killed S-type and live R-type, each harmless alone:
options: Left the mice healthy with only R-type recovered
Killed the mice, and live virulent S-type bacteria were recovered from their blood
Killed the mice but only dead S-type was recovered
Left the mice healthy because transformation cannot occur
mcqs.why: This result showed information for the coat passed from dead S to live R, permanently transforming it; this transfer altering the recipient is called transformation.

mcqs.q: Avery, Macleod and McCarty (1944) proved DNA was the transforming principle because:
options: Only proteinase destroyed transformation and no S-cells appeared
Only RNase destroyed transformation and no S-cells appeared
Only DNase destroyed all transforming activity and no S-cells appeared
All three enzymes destroyed transformation equally
mcqs.why: Proteinase and RNase did not affect transformation, but DNase destroyed it completely, confirming DNA is the hereditary material and protein and RNA have no hereditary role.

mcqs.q: In the Avery experiment, when proteinase or RNase was added to the mixture:
options: Transformation stopped and no S-cells appeared
Only R-cells appeared because DNA was destroyed
The bacteria were killed by the enzymes
Transformation still occurred and S-cells appeared
mcqs.why: The notes state proteinase and RNase did not affect transformation so S-cells appeared, isolating DNase as the only enzyme that blocked the principle.

mcqs.q: Hershey and Chase (1952) used bacteriophage T2, which infects E. coli and is made of:
options: DNA and protein only, with linear double-stranded DNA
DNA, protein and RNA in equal parts
Protein and RNA only, with no DNA
A polysaccharide capsule and protein only
mcqs.why: Phage T2, like a chromosome, consists only of DNA and protein, which allowed Hershey and Chase to label each part separately and test which enters bacteria.

mcqs.q: In Hershey and Chase's labelling, radioactive 32P was used for DNA and 35S was used for protein because:
options: 32P is present only in protein coats
35S is present only in protein, so it labels the protein coats specifically
35S is present only in DNA bases
Both isotopes label DNA and protein equally
mcqs.why: They labelled phage DNA with 32P in one experiment and protein coats with 35S, present only in protein, in another, then separated coats in a blender.

mcqs.q: After agitation in a blender, bacteria lost nearly all the 35S label because:
options: It had entered the bacteria and been converted to DNA
It was destroyed by the agitation in the blender
It stayed in the protein coats outside the bacterial surfaces
It passed into the next generation of viruses
mcqs.why: The blender removed protein coats from bacterial surfaces; 35S stayed outside in the coats while the 32P DNA label was found inside the bacteria.

mcqs.q: When new viruses were released in Hershey and Chase's experiment:
options: Those from the 35S culture were labelled and 32P ones were unlabelled
Both cultures produced fully labelled viruses
Neither culture produced labelled viruses at all
Those from the 32P culture were labelled and those from the 35S culture were unlabelled
mcqs.why: This proved the hereditary information injected into bacteria was DNA, not protein, because only the DNA-labelled parent produced labelled progeny phages.

mcqs.q: Taken together, the three experiments in this lesson established that:
options: DNA, not protein, is the hereditary material carried by chromosomes
Protein, not DNA, carries hereditary information
RNA is the main hereditary material in phages
The polysaccharide capsule is the hereditary material
mcqs.why: Griffith showed transformation, Avery identified the principle as DNA using DNase, and Hershey and Chase showed only DNA enters bacteria and labels the next generation.

lessons.title: DNA Replication: Models, Meselson–Stahl and the Mechanism
lessons.notes_html:
DNA replication copies a double-stranded DNA molecule to produce two identical molecules, so that daughter cells get the same genetic information as the parent cell. It occurs in the S-phase of interphase.

Three Models of Replication

  • Conservative — Both parental strands stay intact: one daughter molecule is wholly parental, the other wholly new.
  • Dispersive — Both daughter molecules are mixtures; each strand is a patchwork of original and new DNA.
  • Semiconservative — Parental strands separate, each is a template for a new strand; each daughter has one original and one new strand.

Meselson and Stahl Experiment (1958)

Mathew Meselson and Franklin Stahl grew E. coli for many generations in heavy nitrogen (15N) so the DNA became fully labelled, then shifted them to light nitrogen (14N). Samples after each replication round were centrifuged in cesium chloride (CsCl); heavier DNA settled lower. After the first generation in 14N the DNA was intermediate (hybrid) density, 14N–15N, rejecting the conservative model. After the second generation two bands appeared, one light and one hybrid — proving semiconservative replication.

Mechanism of Replication

  • 1. Initiation — Begins at origins of replication, forming replication bubbles and a Y-shaped replication fork. Helicase unwinds the helix; topoisomerase relieves tension ahead of the fork by cutting and rejoining strands; single-strand binding proteins (SSBs) stop the strands re-annealing; primase synthesizes a short RNA primer (a few nucleotides) as the starting point for DNA polymerase.
  • 2. Elongation — DNA polymerase III (prokaryotes; similar enzymes in eukaryotes) adds complementary nucleotides to the 3' end of the primer. The leading strand is made continuously, 5' to 3', toward the fork. The lagging strand is made discontinuously away from the fork in Okazaki fragments, each needing a new primer. A subunit of polymerase III also does proof reading, removing mismatched nucleotides.
