  • 3. Termination — DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primers and replaces them with DNA; DNA ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments. Replication ends when forks meet, or at termination sequences (especially in prokaryotes).

Replication at a fork: the leading strand grows continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments away from it.

Stability and Variability of DNA

Stability depends on hydrogen bonds between bases and water molecules and base-stacking interactions between adjacent bases, plus accurate replication and repair systems; DNA polymerase adds about 1000 nucleotides per second. Genetic variation is the difference in DNA sequences between individuals, in germ cells (sperm and egg) and somatic cells. It creates new alleles and occurs mostly by random mating, random fertilization, mutation, recombination between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, and genetic drift — change in allelic frequencies of a small population by chance.

Key Points

  • Replication is semiconservative (S-phase); Meselson and Stahl proved it with 15N/14N and CsCl centrifugation.
  • Helicase unwinds, topoisomerase relieves tension, SSBs hold strands apart, primase lays an RNA primer.
  • Leading strand continuous toward the fork; lagging strand in Okazaki fragments; polymerase I replaces primers, ligase seals gaps.

mcqs.q: DNA replication occurs during which phase and produces:
options: The S-phase of interphase, producing two identical DNA molecules from one double-stranded molecule
The G1 phase, producing one new molecule from two parental ones
Mitosis itself, producing four different molecules
The G0 phase, producing RNA from a DNA template
mcqs.why: Replication copies a double-stranded DNA molecule into two identical molecules in the S-phase of interphase so daughter cells receive the same genetic information.

mcqs.q: In the conservative model of replication:
options: Each daughter has one original and one new strand
Both parental strands stay intact, so one daughter molecule is wholly parental and the other wholly new
Each strand is a patchwork of original and new DNA
Parental strands are destroyed after copying
mcqs.why: The three models are conservative (wholly old versus wholly new), dispersive (patchwork mixtures) and semiconservative (one old plus one new strand per daughter).

mcqs.q: In semiconservative replication, each daughter molecule contains:
options: Two original parental strands only
Two newly synthesized strands only
One original parental strand and one newly synthesized strand
Strands that are each a mixture of old and new pieces
mcqs.why: In the semiconservative model parental strands separate and each acts as a template for a new strand, giving each daughter one original and one new strand.

mcqs.q: Meselson and Stahl (1958) grew E. coli in heavy nitrogen 15N, shifted them to 14N, and separated DNA by:
options: Agitation in a blender to remove protein coats
Electrophoresis through a nucleosome gel
Heating to separate the two strands by density of bases
Centrifugation in cesium chloride (CsCl), where heavier DNA settled lower
mcqs.why: After labelling DNA fully with 15N and shifting to light 14N, samples from each round were centrifuged in CsCl and heavier DNA settled lower in the tube.

mcqs.q: After the first generation in 14N, Meselson and Stahl found DNA of intermediate hybrid 14N-15N density, which rejected:
options: The conservative model
The semiconservative model
The dispersive model only, proving conservative replication
All three models of replication
mcqs.why: A conservative first generation would give separate heavy and light bands, not a single intermediate hybrid band, so the hybrid result rejected the conservative model.

mcqs.q: After the second generation in 14N, two bands appeared, one light and one hybrid, proving:
options: Conservative replication
Semiconservative replication
Dispersive replication
That replication had stopped after one round
mcqs.why: One light and one hybrid band in the second generation matches semiconservative replication, where hybrid molecules produce one hybrid and one light daughter each.

mcqs.q: At initiation of replication, the roles of the enzymes and proteins are:
options: Ligase unwinds, polymerase relieves tension, helicase lays the primer, and SSBs seal gaps
Primase unwinds, helicase synthesizes the primer, and ligase holds strands apart
Helicase unwinds, topoisomerase relieves tension, SSBs stop re-annealing, and primase synthesizes a short RNA primer
Topoisomerase synthesizes the primer and primase unwinds the helix
mcqs.why: Initiation at origins forms bubbles and a Y-shaped fork: helicase unwinds, topoisomerase cuts and rejoins to relieve tension, SSBs hold strands apart and primase lays the RNA primer.

mcqs.q: DNA polymerase III adds complementary nucleotides to which end of the primer, and the leading strand is made:
options: To the 5 prime end; the leading strand is made discontinuously away from the fork
To the 3 prime end; the leading strand is made in Okazaki fragments away from the fork
To both ends equally; the leading strand is made 3 prime to 5 prime
To the 3 prime end; the leading strand is made continuously 5 prime to 3 prime toward the fork
mcqs.why: Elongation by polymerase III proceeds 5' to 3' from the primer's 3' end; the leading strand grows continuously toward the fork, and a subunit also proofreads mismatches.

mcqs.q: The lagging strand is synthesized:
options: Discontinuously away from the fork in Okazaki fragments, each needing a new primer
Continuously toward the fork as a single long strand
Discontinuously toward the fork without any primers
Continuously away from the fork in one fragment
mcqs.why: Because polymerase only works 5' to 3', the lagging strand is built away from the fork in short Okazaki fragments, each started by its own RNA primer.

mcqs.q: At termination of replication, DNA polymerase I and DNA ligase respectively:
options: Polymerase I seals gaps; ligase removes the primers and replaces them
Polymerase I removes RNA primers and replaces them with DNA; ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments
Polymerase I unwinds the helix; ligase synthesizes new primers
Both enzymes only proofread and remove mismatched nucleotides
mcqs.why: Termination involves polymerase I replacing RNA primers with DNA and ligase sealing the remaining gaps, ending when forks meet or at termination sequences.

lessons.title: Genetic Code, Codons and Transcription
lessons.notes_html:
A gene is the specific sequence of nucleotides in DNA which determines the amino acid sequence of a protein. The genetic code is the combination of three nucleotides which specifies a particular amino acid.

Code, Codon and Anticodon

The code lies on the sense or coding strand of DNA (5' to 3'); the other strand is the antisense / non-coding / template strand (3' to 5'). The alphabet is four nucleotides — A, G, C, T — arranged in code words of three bases. In transcription the codes pass to mRNA as codons. Of 64 codons, 61 are sense codons and 3 are stop (non-sense) codons: UGA, UAG, UAA. AUG is the start codon (methionine). The triplet on DNA is the code, its complement on mRNA the codon, and its complement on tRNA the anticodon (book example: codon GGU = glycine; DNA code CCA; anticodon CCA). Mitochondrial DNA is an exception to universality: there UGA codes tryptophan, AUA codes methionine, and AGA, AGG act as stop codons.

Characteristics of Codons

  • Triplet — Three nucleotides code for one amino acid.
  • Degenerate — Some amino acids have one codon (AUG = methionine, UGG = tryptophan); others have several, e.g. isoleucine (AUU, AUC, AUA) and leucine (six codons). This is degeneracy.
  • Universal — The same in most organisms, e.g. AUU for isoleucine, UUU for phenylalanine.
  • No punctuation — No punctuation between successive codons on mRNA.
  • Non-overlapping — AUGGUAGCG is read as AUG/GUA/GCG, not AUG/UGG/GUA.

Transcription

Gene expression is DNA to RNA (transcription) and RNA to protein (translation). Transcription copies a gene's DNA sequence into RNA by RNA polymerase, during interphase (G₁, G₀, G₂), in three phases:

  • Initiation — RNA polymerase binds the promoter (the gene's regulatory region) and synthesizes RNA 5' to 3'. Prokaryotes have one RNA polymerase for all RNAs; eukaryotes have three: polymerase-I for rRNA, polymerase-II for mRNA, polymerase-III for tRNA. The bacterial core enzyme (two alpha, one beta, one beta prime subunits) plus the sigma factor makes the holoenzyme; sigma is removed after binding. Binding sites: prokaryotes TATAAT (-10), TTGACA (-35); eukaryotes TATA box (-25), CAAT box (-70). Binding forms a transcription bubble.
  • Elongation — The core enzyme extends the RNA chain from ribonucleoside triphosphates, moving 5' to 3' toward the terminator and copying the DNA accurately.
  • Termination — The terminator has a series of GC pairs followed by AT pairs; the mRNA forms a GC hairpin followed by a poly U tail, and the hairpin makes RNA polymerase stop.

Transcription differs in eukaryotes: three polymerases (not one) and starts from many points, forming many transcription bubbles.

Post-Transcriptional Modification of mRNA

Newly made primary (immature) mRNA is changed into mature (functional) mRNA. Prokaryotes need no such process (no introns, no nucleus). In eukaryotes a cap — GTP (7-methyl triphosphate guanosine), linked 5' to 5' — and a poly A tail (about 30–500 adenine nucleotides at the 3' end) are added, keeping the mRNA stable against nucleases and phosphatases on its journey to the ribosomes. Primary mRNA contains non-coding introns and coding exons; in RNA splicing the spliceosome (small nuclear RNAs and about 80 proteins) removes introns and RNA ligase joins the exons — so the mature mRNA is shorter than the primary transcript.

Key Points

  • Genetic code: triplet, degenerate, universal, non-overlapping, no punctuation; AUG start, UAA/UAG/UGA stop.
  • Code on DNA, codon on mRNA, anticodon on tRNA.
  • Transcription: promoter binding, 5' to 3' elongation, GC hairpin termination.
  • Eukaryotic mRNA is capped, tailed and spliced, so it shortens before translation.

mcqs.q: The genetic code is a combination of how many nucleotides specifying one amino acid, giving how many total codons from four bases?
options: Two nucleotides; working: 4 to the power 2 = 16 codons in total
Three nucleotides; working: 4 to the power 3 = 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 codons in total
Three nucleotides; working: 3 to the power 4 = 81 codons in total
Four nucleotides; working: 4 to the power 4 = 256 codons in total
mcqs.why: Verified by Python: 4**3 = 64. With four bases A, G, C, T in words of three, there are 64 codons, of which 61 are sense and 3 are stop codons, and 61 + 3 = 64.

mcqs.q: The three stop (non-sense) codons listed in the notes are:
options: AUG, UGG and AUU
UAA, UAC and UGU
UGA, UAG and UAA
AGA, AGG and AUA in all organisms
mcqs.why: Of 64 codons, 61 are sense codons and 3 are stop codons UGA, UAG and UAA; AUG is the start codon for methionine, and mitochondrial exceptions are noted separately.

mcqs.q: AUG functions in the genetic code as:
options: A stop codon that ends translation
A codon for tryptophan only
An anticodon found on tRNA
The start codon, coding for methionine
mcqs.why: AUG is stated as the start codon (methionine), and together with UGG for tryptophan it is an example of an amino acid having only one codon.

mcqs.q: In the book example, codon GGU for glycine corresponds to:
options: DNA code CCA and anticodon CCA
DNA code GGU and anticodon GGU
DNA code CCT and anticodon GGU
DNA code CCA and anticodon GGU
mcqs.why: The triplet on DNA is the code, its complement on mRNA is the codon and its complement on tRNA is the anticodon; the book example gives GGU codon, CCA code and CCA anticodon.

mcqs.q: Degeneracy of the genetic code means:
options: Every amino acid has exactly one codon with no exceptions
Some amino acids have several codons, e.g. leucine has six codons and isoleucine has AUU, AUC and AUA
Codons overlap each other when read along mRNA
The code differs completely between all organisms
mcqs.why: Degeneracy is illustrated by leucine with six codons and isoleucine with three, while methionine (AUG) and tryptophan (UGG) each have only one codon.

mcqs.q: The non-overlapping nature of the code means the sequence AUGGUAGCG is read as:
options: AUG / UGG / GUA
AUG / GGU / AGC
AUG / GUA / GCG
AUGG / UUAG / CG as four-base words
mcqs.why: Codons are read in successive non-overlapping triplets with no punctuation between them, so AUGGUAGCG divides cleanly as AUG, GUA and GCG.

mcqs.q: Transcription begins (initiation) when RNA polymerase:
options: Binds the terminator and synthesizes RNA 3 prime to 5 prime
Binds an Okazaki fragment and removes a primer
Attaches to a ribosome at the P-site codon
Binds the promoter, the gene's regulatory region, and synthesizes RNA 5 prime to 3 prime
mcqs.why: In initiation RNA polymerase binds the promoter and forms a transcription bubble; prokaryotes have one polymerase for all RNAs while eukaryotes have three.

mcqs.q: The three eukaryotic RNA polymerases are matched correctly as:
options: Polymerase I for rRNA, polymerase II for mRNA, polymerase III for tRNA
Polymerase I for mRNA, polymerase II for tRNA, polymerase III for rRNA
Polymerase I for tRNA, polymerase II for rRNA, polymerase III for mRNA
One polymerase only, making all three RNA types
mcqs.why: Eukaryotes use three polymerases with this exact division of labour, contrasting with the single RNA polymerase used for all RNAs in prokaryotes.

mcqs.q: Promoter binding sites given in the notes are:
options: Prokaryotes TATA box at minus 25; eukaryotes TATAAT at minus 10 only
Prokaryotes TATAAT at minus 10 and TTGACA at minus 35; eukaryotes TATA box at minus 25 and CAAT box at minus 70
Both groups use only a single GC hairpin site
Prokaryotes CAAT box at minus 70; eukaryotes TTGACA at minus 35 only
mcqs.why: These exact sequences and positions are listed for promoter binding, after which the sigma factor in the bacterial holoenzyme is removed following binding.

mcqs.q: Post-transcriptional modification makes mature eukaryotic mRNA shorter than the primary transcript because:
options: DNA polymerase removes the exons and keeps only introns
The poly A tail deletes the coding regions of the mRNA
The spliceosome removes introns and RNA ligase joins the exons during RNA splicing
The cap removes the exons before export from the nucleus
mcqs.why: Primary mRNA contains non-coding introns and coding exons; splicing by the spliceosome of small nuclear RNAs and about 80 proteins removes introns, and a cap and poly A tail of about 30 to 500 adenines are also added.

lessons.title: Translation: Protein Synthesis, Prokaryote–Eukaryote Differences and Uses of Proteins
lessons.notes_html:
Translation is the formation of protein with the help of RNA — the second stage of gene expression. The ribosome decodes mRNA to produce a polypeptide that folds into an active protein. In prokaryotes it occurs freely in the cytoplasm; in eukaryotes across the membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum. It has four phases.

Phases of Translation

  • i) Activation — Inactive cytoplasmic amino acids are activated by aminoacyl tRNA synthetase with ATP: AA + ATP + Enzyme → AA.AMP.Enzyme Complex + 2Pi. The enzyme then attaches the amino acid to its specific tRNA at the 3' end, forming aminoacyl-tRNA.
  • ii) Initiation — The ribosomal subunits separate; mRNA binds an rRNA in the small subunit with initiation factor IF₃. A tRNA carrying N-formyl methionine binds at the P-site (peptidyl site), controlled by IF₁ and IF₂. The A-site (aminoacyl site) receives successive amino-acid tRNAs and the E-site (exit site) lets empty tRNA exit. The large subunit binds, exposing the codon next to AUG, and IF₁, IF₂, IF₃ are released.
  • iii) Elongation — Elongation factors bring the tRNA with the matching anticodon to the A-site codon. The large subunit catalyses a peptide bond: the first amino acid is released from its tRNA and attached to the second, in the presence of peptidyl synthetase. The ribosome then translocates three nucleotides along mRNA (5' to 3'): the empty tRNA moves to the E-site and leaves, the growing chain moves to the P-site, and the next codon is exposed at the A-site. The cycle repeats.
  • iv) Termination — When a non-sense (stop) codon reaches the A-site, no tRNA binds it; releasing factors (RF/TF) terminate translation, the polypeptide and tRNA are released, and the ribosomal subunits separate from the mRNA.

Protein Synthesis: Prokaryotes vs Eukaryotes

FeatureProkaryotesEukaryotes
Ribosomes70S (30S + 50S)80S (40S + 60S)
SiteCytosolCytosol, RER and outer nuclear membrane
Initiating amino acidN-formyl methionineMethionine
mRNAPolycistronic (many proteins)Monocistronic (one protein)
Initiation factorsSingle (as printed)More than one
Releasing factorsTwoOnly one

Uses of Synthesized Proteins

Proteins made in ribosomes are processed in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi bodies and packed in lysosomes. They work inside the cell (respiratory proteins; enzymes like DNase, RNase) or outside the cell (antibodies in blood, digestive enzymes in the digestive tract, many hormones in blood), and also give structural support, movement and enzymatic activity — their functions are as varied as their amino acid sequences and three-dimensional structures.

Key Points

  • Translation: activation, initiation (P, A, E sites), elongation (peptide bonds, translocation), termination (releasing factors).
  • Prokaryotes: 70S ribosomes, N-formyl methionine, polycistronic mRNA. Eukaryotes: 80S, methionine, monocistronic mRNA.
  • Proteins work inside cells (enzymes) or outside them (antibodies, digestive enzymes, hormones).

mcqs.q: Activation, the first phase of translation, involves:
options: Releasing factors binding a stop codon at the A-site
The ribosome translocating three nucleotides along mRNA
Aminoacyl tRNA synthetase activating amino acids with ATP and attaching each amino acid to its specific tRNA at the 3 prime end
Peptide bond formation between two amino acids at the P-site
mcqs.why: Activation follows AA + ATP + Enzyme forming an AA.AMP.Enzyme complex plus 2Pi, then the enzyme attaches the amino acid to its specific tRNA to form aminoacyl-tRNA.

mcqs.q: During initiation in prokaryotes, the tRNA carrying N-formyl methionine binds at:
options: The A-site (aminoacyl site), controlled by releasing factors
The E-site (exit site), after the large subunit has bound
The promoter site on the DNA template strand
The P-site (peptidyl site), controlled by initiation factors IF1 and IF2, after mRNA binds the small subunit with IF3
mcqs.why: Initiation places the N-formyl methionine tRNA at the P-site; the A-site receives successive amino acid tRNAs and the E-site lets empty tRNA exit.

mcqs.q: The A-site and E-site of the ribosome during translation function respectively to:
options: A-site receives successive amino-acid tRNAs; E-site lets empty tRNA exit
A-site lets empty tRNA exit; E-site receives amino-acid tRNAs
Both sites hold the growing polypeptide chain permanently
A-site binds the promoter; E-site binds the terminator
mcqs.why: The notes define P as peptidyl, A as aminoacyl receiving site and E as exit site, with the large subunit binding after initiation factors are released.

mcqs.q: During elongation, after a peptide bond is formed, the ribosome translocates:
options: One nucleotide along the mRNA in the 3 prime to 5 prime direction
Three nucleotides along the mRNA in the 5 prime to 3 prime direction, moving the empty tRNA to the E-site
Six nucleotides at a time, skipping one full codon
Along the DNA template strand to the next promoter
mcqs.why: Elongation uses peptidyl synthetase in the large subunit to form peptide bonds, then translocation by one codon (three nucleotides) repeats the cycle at the A-site.

mcqs.q: Translation terminates when:
options: AUG reaches the A-site and a new tRNA binds it
The last Okazaki fragment is sealed by DNA ligase
A non-sense stop codon reaches the A-site, no tRNA binds it, and releasing factors release the polypeptide and separate the subunits
RNA polymerase forms a GC hairpin and poly U tail
mcqs.why: Termination is driven by releasing factors (RF/TF) at a stop codon in the A-site, ending protein synthesis and freeing the polypeptide, tRNA and ribosomal subunits.

mcqs.q: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, made up of subunits:
options: 40S plus 60S
30S plus 60S
40S plus 50S
30S plus 50S
mcqs.why: The comparison table gives prokaryotic ribosomes as 70S (30S + 50S) in the cytosol, while eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S (40S + 60S).

mcqs.q: Eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S, made up of subunits:
options: 40S plus 60S, working in the cytosol, rough endoplasmic reticulum and outer nuclear membrane
30S plus 50S, working freely only in the cytoplasm
40S plus 50S, working only in the nucleus
30S plus 60S, working only on the Golgi bodies
mcqs.why: Eukaryotic translation uses 80S ribosomes (40S + 60S) at the cytosol, RER and outer nuclear membrane, with methionine (not N-formyl methionine) as initiator.

mcqs.q: mRNA type differs between the two groups as:
options: Monocistronic in prokaryotes and polycistronic in eukaryotes
Polycistronic (many proteins) in prokaryotes and monocistronic (one protein) in eukaryotes
Polycistronic in both groups without exception
Without codons in prokaryotes and with codons in eukaryotes
mcqs.why: The table states prokaryotic mRNA is polycistronic coding for many proteins, whereas eukaryotic mRNA is monocistronic coding for one protein.

mcqs.q: The initiating amino acid in protein synthesis is:
options: Methionine in prokaryotes and N-formyl methionine in eukaryotes
Tryptophan in both groups
N-formyl methionine in prokaryotes and methionine in eukaryotes
Glycine in prokaryotes and valine in eukaryotes
mcqs.why: This is a direct row of the comparison table, linked to the P-site initiation step where the formylated initiator tRNA binds in bacteria.

mcqs.q: Proteins that work outside the cell, as given in the uses section, include:
options: Only respiratory proteins locked inside mitochondria
Only structural proteins that never leave the ribosome
DNase and RNase acting in the blood as hormones
Antibodies in blood, digestive enzymes in the digestive tract, and many hormones in blood
mcqs.why: Synthesized proteins are processed in the ER and Golgi; inside-cell examples are respiratory proteins and enzymes like DNase and RNase, while antibodies, digestive enzymes and hormones work outside cells.

lessons.title: Regulation of Gene Expression and the Lac Operon
lessons.notes_html:
Regulation of gene expression is the control of the amount and timing of appearance of a gene (genotype to phenotype). Genes turn on or off in response to internal or external signals. An adult human has more than 37 trillion cells with the same genome, yet only some genes are on in each cell, giving about 200 types of cells by differential gene expression.

Importance

Regulation increases the adaptability and versatility of prokaryotes and eukaryotes, helps cells fulfil their protein needs, and drives differentiation, morphogenesis (shaping of the organism by differentiation of cells, tissues and organs according to the genetic blueprint and environment) and physiology. If regulation is disturbed, serious diseases such as cancer may occur.

Positive and Negative Control

  • Positive regulation — Gene expression is increased by activator proteins.
  • Negative regulation — Gene expression is stopped by a repressor protein.

The Lac Operon

In bacteria and viruses, a cluster of genes with related functions regulated as a unit is an operon: structural genes (direct synthesis of related enzymes), a promoter (starting point for transcription) and an operator (an on/off switch within or overlapping the promoter). In E. coli, without lactose the bacterium has very few lactose enzymes; fed lactose, it quickly makes them. The lac operon has three genes: lac-Z encodes beta-galactosidase (breaks lactose into glucose and galactose), lac-Y encodes lactose permease (transports lactose into the cell), and lac-A encodes thiogalactoside transacetylase (detoxification of lactose metabolism byproducts).

Negative and Positive Control of the Lac Operon

Negative control: the operon is on until switched off. The lac repressor, produced by a regulatory site, fits the operator like a key in a lock and blocks RNA polymerase from attaching to the promoter, so transcription cannot occur. When lactose is present, it binds the repressor and changes its shape; the repressor can no longer bind the operator, and the lactose enzymes are produced. Positive control: some operons must be switched on by activators such as catabolic activator protein (CAP), which bind at or within the promoter and stimulate transcription. Operons with both activators and repressors have both controls; regulatory sites code for both kinds of protein.

Regulation Through Introns and Exons (Eukaryotes)

In eukaryotes, primary mRNA is processed in the nucleus before mature mRNA is exported, giving regulation opportunities not available in prokaryotes — for example alternative RNA splicing, in which different mRNAs are produced from the same primary transcript depending on which segments are treated as exons and which as introns. Cell-type-specific regulatory proteins control this intron–exon choice by binding regulatory sequences in the primary transcript.

Key Points

  • One genome in all cells; differential expression makes about 200 cell types; disturbed regulation can cause cancer.
  • Activators = positive control; repressors = negative control.
  • Lac operon: lac-Z, lac-Y, lac-A; the repressor blocks the operator until lactose removes it; CAP activates.
  • Eukaryotes also regulate gene expression by alternative RNA splicing.

mcqs.q: An adult human has more than 37 trillion cells with the same genome, yet about 200 cell types exist because of:
options: Each cell having a completely different genome
Mutation changing the genome in every cell type
Alternative proteins replacing DNA in most cells
Differential gene expression, with only some genes on in each cell
mcqs.why: Regulation controls amount and timing of gene appearance; the same genome in all cells produces about 200 types by differential expression, driving differentiation and morphogenesis.

mcqs.q: If regulation of gene expression is disturbed, the serious disease specifically named in the notes may occur:
options: Cancer
Phenylketonuria
Sickle cell anaemia
Down's syndrome
mcqs.why: The importance section states regulation increases adaptability, fulfils protein needs and drives differentiation, and if disturbed, serious diseases such as cancer may occur.

mcqs.q: Positive and negative regulation of gene expression are correctly paired as:
options: Positive: expression stopped by repressors; Negative: expression increased by activators
Positive: expression increased by activator proteins; Negative: expression stopped by a repressor protein
Both controls work only through activator proteins
Both controls work only through the operator sequence
mcqs.why: The lesson defines activator proteins as positive control increasing expression and a repressor protein as negative control stopping expression.

mcqs.q: An operon in bacteria and viruses consists of:
options: Only structural genes with no regulatory regions
Introns, exons and a spliceosome acting as a unit
Structural genes, a promoter as the starting point for transcription, and an operator as an on/off switch within or overlapping the promoter
A repressor, a ribosome and a terminator only
mcqs.why: An operon is a cluster of genes with related functions regulated as a unit, comprising structural genes, promoter and operator as defined in the notes.

mcqs.q: In the lac operon, lac-Z encodes beta-galactosidase, which:
options: Transports lactose into the cell
Detoxifies byproducts of lactose metabolism
Blocks RNA polymerase at the operator
Breaks lactose into glucose and galactose
mcqs.why: lac-Z makes beta-galactosidase splitting lactose to glucose and galactose; lac-Y makes permease for transport and lac-A makes transacetylase for detoxification.

mcqs.q: lac-Y and lac-A encode respectively:
options: Lactose permease, which transports lactose into the cell, and thiogalactoside transacetylase, for detoxification of lactose metabolism byproducts
Beta-galactosidase and the lac repressor protein
Lactose permease and beta-galactosidase
The repressor and the catabolic activator protein
mcqs.why: The three lac genes have distinct roles: Z for breakdown, Y for transport into the cell by permease, and A for detoxification by transacetylase.

mcqs.q: In the absence of lactose, negative control of the lac operon works because the lac repressor:
options: Binds the promoter and stimulates transcription strongly
Fits the operator like a key in a lock and blocks RNA polymerase from attaching to the promoter, so transcription cannot occur
Breaks lactose into glucose and galactose at the operator
Removes the operator so polymerase can start freely
mcqs.why: The repressor, produced by a regulatory site, blocks the operator and prevents polymerase attachment, keeping the operon off until lactose is present.

mcqs.q: When lactose is present, lactose enzymes are produced because lactose:
options: Binds the operator directly and destroys the repressor gene
Acts as RNA polymerase at the promoter site
Binds the repressor and changes its shape, so the repressor can no longer bind the operator
Converts the repressor into beta-galactosidase
mcqs.why: Lactose binding alters the repressor's shape and releases the operator, allowing transcription of lac-Z, lac-Y and lac-A to make the lactose enzymes.

mcqs.q: Positive control of operons can be exerted by catabolic activator protein (CAP), which:
options: Binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase
Binds lactose and changes the repressor shape
Removes introns from the primary transcript
Binds at or within the promoter and stimulates transcription
mcqs.why: CAP is given as an activator example for positive control, binding at or within the promoter to stimulate transcription, while repressors provide negative control.

mcqs.q: Alternative RNA splicing as a eukaryotic regulation mechanism means:
options: Different mRNAs are produced from the same primary transcript depending on which segments are treated as exons and which as introns
The same mRNA is always produced from every primary transcript
Introns are translated into different proteins directly
Prokaryotes process mRNA in a nucleus before export
mcqs.why: Eukaryotes process primary mRNA in the nucleus, and cell-type-specific regulatory proteins control the intron-exon choice, producing different mature mRNAs from one transcript.

lessons.title: Mutation: Types, Chromosomal Disorders and Gene Disorders
lessons.notes_html:
Mutation is an alteration in the genetic material (genome) that can be transmitted to descendants, from a single nucleotide change to a whole set of chromosomes. Agents causing it are mutagens; the organism carrying it is a mutant. Mutagenesis is the formation of a mutation.

Causes of Mutation

  • Physical mutagens — UV, gamma rays, X-rays, radioactive radiation and high temperature, which damage DNA structure and break its bonds.
  • Chemical mutagens — Nitrosomethylurea, nitrous gas, mustard gas, pesticides, food preservatives, acridine orange, colchicines, caffeine, nicotine and radioactive isotopes; most resemble DNA bases.
  • Biological mutagens — Viruses, bacteria, and transposons (jumping DNA) that jump to a new place and influence the gene, plus errors in meiosis or replication.

Types of Mutation

  • Spontaneous (natural) — Occurs naturally from internal or external factors, e.g. replication errors. Induced — Caused by external factors (ionizing radiation, UV, base analogs, transposing) and used to establish new varieties.
  • Point mutation — Change of one or a few nucleotides (a base replaced by the same type or the opposite type), e.g. sickle cell anaemia, phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria (enzyme deficiency; urine turns black in air).
  • Frameshift mutation — One or more nucleotides inserted or deleted, giving a completely new codon sequence and a non-functional protein; thus fatal.
  • Chromosomal structure changes — Deletion (loss of a segment), duplication (segment repeated, in excess), inversion (segment inverted; genetic map altered), translocation (segment transferred to a non-homologous chromosome), insertion (segment reinserted into another chromosome or another region of the same one).
  • Chromosome number changes — From non-disjunction in meiosis. Aneuploidy: monosomy (2n - 1, Turner's), nullisomy (2n - 2, fatal), trisomy (2n + 1, Down's, Klinefelter's), tetrasomy (2n + 2, fatal). Euploidy: whole sets change (monoploidy, triploidy, tetraploidy, pentaploidy); favourable in plants, rare in animals.

Harmful Aspects and Evolution

Harmful mutations decrease fitness and cause cancer, cleft palate, microcephaly, the syndromes below, sickle cell anaemia and haemophilia, reducing survival or fertility. But mutation is also fundamental to evolution as a primary source of genetic variation; accumulated mutations may lead to evolution. Only germline mutations (in eggs and sperms) pass to offspring.

Chromosomal Disorders

  • Down's syndrome (mongolism) — Extra autosome 21 (trisomy, 2n + 1; 47 chromosomes), described by J. Langdon Down in 1866; cause is non-disjunction of chromosome 21 in gamete formation. Symptoms: short stature, poor muscle tone, mental retardation, protruding tongue, flat broad face, small ears and mouth, short hands and fingers, squint eyes; book life expectancy about 16 years. No cure; managed by regular check-up and screening, medications, surgery, counselling and support.
  • Klinefelter's syndrome — Sex chromosome non-disjunction in males only (XXY), described by Dr Henry Klinefelter in 1942, about 1/600 male births. Sterile male with some female characters (breasts, high pitched voice), small testes with no sperm, poorly developed male secondary characters, wide hips, tallness, long legs; some have lower intelligence. Treatment: Testosterone Replacement Therapy (TRT) from puberty, continued for life; it does not restore fertility. Other trisomies: XYY, XXX.
  • Turner's syndrome — Monosomy in females, 2n - 1 (44 + XO), 45 chromosomes, described by Henry Turner in 1938; cause is non-disjunction of the sex pair in meiosis. Most such pregnancies abort; survivors have short stature, webbed neck, no ovaries (infertility), low hairline, abnormal bone development, many moles, and oedema of hands and feet. Treatments: growth hormone (best started early) and Estrogen Replacement Treatment (ERT) from about age 12–13.

Gene (Point) Mutation Disorders

  • Sickle cell anaemia (Hb SS) — Autosomal recessive point mutation: the 6th amino acid of the haemoglobin beta chain, glutamic acid, is replaced by valine. Abnormal HbS loses oxygen binding capacity; red cells become sickle shaped and deliver less oxygen. Symptoms: painful crises (back, long bones, chest) lasting hours to days; fatigue, fever, paleness, jaundice, organ damage, shortness of breath. Treatment: manage crises with medicines and fluids, blood transfusions (also to prevent stroke), folic acid supplements; bone marrow or stem cell transplant can cure.
  • Phenylketonuria (PKU) — Autosomal recessive point mutation: the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase is defective, so phenylalanine is not converted to tyrosine and toxic phenyl-ketones damage the central nervous system. Symptoms: lighter skin, hair and eyes, delayed mental and social skills, small head, hyperactivity, seizures, skin rashes, tremors. Treatment: a diet extremely low in phenylalanine (avoid milk, eggs), with the special formula Lofenalac usable throughout life.

DNA in Society (STS)

Any two people share 99.9% of their DNA, yet the 3 million differing base pairs (of 3 billion per cell) identify a person uniquely. Forensic scientists scan 13 variable DNA loci to make a DNA profile (fingerprint) from hair, blood, saliva or semen — to identify suspects, exonerate the wrongly accused, identify disaster victims and establish paternity. Harmful mutations are eradicated by natural selection: harmful traits disappear through premature death or reduced reproductive success.

Key Points

  • Mutagens are physical, chemical or biological; mutations may be spontaneous or induced, point or frameshift, structural or numerical.
  • Down's = trisomy 21; Klinefelter's = XXY; Turner's = 45, XO.
  • Sickle cell anaemia and PKU are autosomal recessive point mutations.
  • Most mutations are harmful, but mutation is the primary source of variation for evolution.

mcqs.q: Biological mutagens, as listed in the causes of mutation, include:
options: Viruses, bacteria, and transposons (jumping DNA) that jump to a new place and influence the gene
UV rays, gamma rays and X-rays only
Mustard gas, caffeine and nicotine only
Colchicines and acridine orange only
mcqs.why: Mutagens are grouped as physical (UV, gamma, X-rays), chemical (mustard gas, caffeine, nicotine and others) and biological (viruses, bacteria and transposons), plus errors in meiosis or replication.

mcqs.q: A point mutation is defined as:
options: Insertion or deletion of nucleotides shifting the whole reading frame
A change of one or a few nucleotides, a base replaced by the same type or the opposite type, e.g. sickle cell anaemia and phenylketonuria
Loss or duplication of a whole chromosome segment
Change in the number of whole sets of chromosomes
mcqs.why: Point mutations affect one or a few nucleotides; examples given are sickle cell anaemia, phenylketonuria and alkaptonuria, an enzyme deficiency where urine turns black in air.

mcqs.q: A frameshift mutation results from:
options: A single base replaced by the same type of base
A chromosome segment inverted without any loss
One or more nucleotides inserted or deleted, giving a completely new codon sequence and a non-functional protein, and is thus fatal
Non-disjunction producing an extra chromosome 21
mcqs.why: Insertion or deletion shifts the frame so every following codon changes, producing a non-functional protein, which the notes describe as thus fatal.

mcqs.q: Inversion, as a chromosomal structural change, means:
options: A segment is lost from the chromosome
A segment is repeated in excess
A segment is transferred to a non-homologous chromosome
A segment is inverted and the genetic map is altered
mcqs.why: Structural changes listed are deletion (loss), duplication (repeated), inversion (segment inverted, map altered), translocation (to a non-homologous chromosome) and insertion.

mcqs.q: Aneuploidy from non-disjunction includes monosomy and trisomy, written respectively as:
options: Monosomy 2n minus 1 (Turner's) and trisomy 2n plus 1 (Down's, Klinefelter's)
Monosomy 2n plus 1 and trisomy 2n minus 1
Monosomy 2n minus 2 and trisomy 2n plus 2 only
Whole sets changing as triploidy and tetraploidy
mcqs.why: Aneuploidy changes individual chromosomes: monosomy 2n-1, nullisomy 2n-2 (fatal), trisomy 2n+1 and tetrasomy 2n+2 (fatal); whole-set change is euploidy.

mcqs.q: Down's syndrome (mongolism), described by J. Langdon Down in 1866, is caused by:
options: Monosomy of the sex chromosomes with 45 chromosomes
An extra autosome 21, trisomy with 47 chromosomes, from non-disjunction of chromosome 21 in gamete formation
An XXY sex chromosome combination in males only
A point mutation in the haemoglobin beta chain
mcqs.why: Down's is trisomy 21 (2n+1 = 47 chromosomes) with short stature, poor muscle tone, mental retardation, protruding tongue and flat broad face; the notes give life expectancy about 16 years.

mcqs.q: Klinefelter's syndrome, described by Dr Henry Klinefelter in 1942 and occurring in about 1 in 600 male births, is:
options: Monosomy in females (44 plus XO) with a webbed neck
Trisomy 21 in both sexes with 47 chromosomes
Sex chromosome non-disjunction in males only (XXY), giving a sterile male with some female characters, treated by lifelong Testosterone Replacement Therapy
An autosomal recessive point mutation of haemoglobin
mcqs.why: Klinefelter males are XXY with small testes, no sperm, breasts, high pitched voice, wide hips and tallness; TRT from puberty continues for life but does not restore fertility.

mcqs.q: Turner's syndrome, described by Henry Turner in 1938, is:
options: Trisomy in males (XXY) with 47 chromosomes and tallness
Trisomy 21 with 47 chromosomes and protruding tongue
Euploidy with whole extra sets of chromosomes
Monosomy in females, 2n minus 1 (44 plus XO) with 45 chromosomes, short stature, webbed neck and no ovaries, treated with growth hormone and Estrogen Replacement Treatment from about age 12 to 13
mcqs.why: Turner's results from non-disjunction of the sex pair in meiosis; most pregnancies abort, survivors show webbed neck, infertility, low hairline and oedema of hands and feet.

mcqs.q: Sickle cell anaemia (Hb SS) is an autosomal recessive point mutation in which:
options: The 6th amino acid of the haemoglobin beta chain, glutamic acid, is replaced by valine, so red cells become sickle shaped and deliver less oxygen
The enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase is defective and phenyl-ketones damage the CNS
An extra chromosome 21 changes the haemoglobin structure
Nucleotides are inserted, shifting the frame of the beta chain
mcqs.why: Abnormal HbS loses oxygen binding capacity, causing painful crises, fatigue, jaundice and organ damage; treatment includes fluids, transfusions, folic acid and possible stem cell transplant cure.

mcqs.q: Phenylketonuria (PKU), an autosomal recessive point mutation, occurs because:
options: Glutamic acid is replaced by valine in the beta chain of haemoglobin
The enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase is defective, so phenylalanine is not converted to tyrosine and toxic phenyl-ketones damage the central nervous system
Chromosome 21 fails to separate during gamete formation
A frameshift produces a non-functional haemoglobin protein
mcqs.why: PKU symptoms include lighter skin, hair and eyes, delayed mental skills, small head and seizures; treatment is a diet extremely low in phenylalanine avoiding milk and eggs, with Lofenalac formula.

lessons.title: Evolution: Variation and Selection Pressure

mcqs.q: What is evolution, as defined in this lesson?
options: A sudden change in one individual during its own lifetime
The process by which living organisms change over a long period of time, developing from earlier, simpler forms
The daily adjustment of an organism to its surroundings
The growth of an organism from a young stage to an adult
mcqs.why: The notes define evolution as the process by which living organisms change over a long period of time, explaining how all life today developed from earlier, simpler forms.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, how old is the Earth?
options: About 13.8 billion years
About 3.7 billion years
About 4.5 billion years
About 2.25 billion years
