options: About 4.5 billion years old
About 13.8 billion years old
About 1.9 billion years old
About 3.7 billion years old
mcqs.why: The notes state that the oldest known fossils are about 3.7 billion years old, while the Earth itself is about 4.5 billion years old.

mcqs.q: Who was the first scientist to suggest that organisms could change during their lifetime and pass these changes to their offspring?
options: Jean Baptiste Lamarck
Charles Darwin
Gregor Mendel
Alfred Russell Wallace
mcqs.why: The notes credit Jean Baptiste Lamarck as the first to suggest that organisms could change during their lifetime and pass these changes to their offspring.

mcqs.q: Whose experimental work later proved Lamarck's idea incorrect?
options: Gregor Mendel
August Weismann
Alfred Russell Wallace
Charles Darwin
mcqs.why: The notes state that Lamarck's idea was proved incorrect later by the experimental work of August Weismann.

mcqs.q: Which two scientists independently arrived at the idea of natural selection at about the same time?
options: Charles Darwin and Gregor Mendel
Jean Baptiste Lamarck and Alfred Russell Wallace
Charles Darwin and Alfred Russell Wallace
Gregor Mendel and August Weismann
mcqs.why: The notes say Darwin proposed natural selection and Wallace, around the same time, also thought of natural selection independently; their work together made it the main explanation of evolution.

mcqs.q: What did Gregor Mendel contribute to the understanding of evolution?
options: He proposed the idea of natural selection
He suggested that acquired changes are inherited
He proved Lamarck's theory experimentally wrong
He discovered how traits are inherited through genes, helping explain how variations appear and are passed on
mcqs.why: The notes state that Mendel discovered how traits are inherited through genes, which later helped scientists understand how variations appear and are passed on during evolution.

mcqs.q: Variation between individuals of a species usually comes from which two sources?
options: Random mutations and the mixing of genes during reproduction
Predators and diseases in the environment
Competition for food and changes in climate
Use and disuse of organs during life
mcqs.why: The notes state that variation usually comes from random mutations and from the mixing of genes during reproduction; predators and competition are selection pressures, not sources of variation.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a selection pressure mentioned in the notes?
options: Random mutations in the genes of offspring
Predators, diseases, competition for food and changes in the environment
Mixing of genes during reproduction
Inheritance of traits through genes
mcqs.why: The notes list predators, diseases, competition for food and changes in the environment as selection pressures that challenge survival; mutations and gene mixing produce variation instead.

mcqs.q: In the 24-hour clock model of Earth's history in the notes, when do modern humans (Homo sapiens) appear?
options: At noon, roughly halfway through the clock
At midnight, at the very start of the clock
Only about 2 seconds before midnight at the end of the clock
Shortly after life originated, early in the clock
mcqs.why: In the notes' clock, midnight is Earth's origin 4.5 billion years ago and noon is about 2.25 billion years ago, while modern humans appear only about 2 seconds before midnight at the end.

lessons.notes_html:
Evolution is the process by which living organisms change over a long period of time. It explains how all life today has developed from earlier, simpler forms. According to the Big Bang theory, the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago, and the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. The oldest known fossils are about 3.7 billion years old. Life has been in the process of transformation since its origin.

Scientists Who Built the Idea of Evolution

  • Jean Baptiste Lamarck was the first to suggest that organisms could change during their lifetime and pass these changes to their offspring. His idea was proved incorrect later by the experimental work of August Weismann.
  • Charles Darwin proposed the correct idea of natural selection, in which organisms with traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more successfully.
  • Alfred Russell Wallace, around the same time, also thought of natural selection independently; their work together made natural selection the main explanation of evolution.
  • Gregor Mendel discovered how traits are inherited through genes, which later helped scientists to understand how variations appear and are passed on during evolution.

The history of the Earth can be compressed into a 24-hour clock to make it easier to understand: midnight represents the starting point of evolutionary time (the origin of the Earth, 4.5 billion years ago), noon is roughly halfway through Earth history (about 2.25 billion years ago), life originated at about 3.4–3.8 billion years ago, and modern humans (Homo sapiens) appear only about 2 seconds before midnight at the end of the clock.

13.1 Variations and Selection Pressure

Evolution happens because organisms show variation, meaning they are different from each other. The difference can be in size, colour, speed, strength or many other traits. Variation usually comes from random mutations and from the mixing of genes during reproduction.

At the same time, organisms face selection pressures like predators, diseases, competition for food, and changes in the environment. These pressures challenge their survival. Because of variation, some individuals are better suited to survive and reproduce. They pass their favourable traits to the next generation. Over many generations these small changes add up, leading to evolution: a gradual change in the species. The central idea of biological evolution is that all life on Earth shares a common ancestor, and the force that initiates evolution is variation, arising from mutation.

Key Points

  • Evolution is the change of living organisms over a long time, from earlier simpler forms; Earth is about 4.5 billion years old and the oldest fossils about 3.7 billion years old.
  • Lamarck first suggested change during a lifetime; Darwin (and Wallace independently) gave natural selection; Mendel explained inheritance through genes.
  • Variation comes from random mutations and the mixing of genes during reproduction.
  • Selection pressures — predators, disease, competition and environmental change — favour the best-suited individuals, whose traits pass to the next generation.

lessons.title: Evidence of Evolution from Biogeography

mcqs.q: What is biogeography?
options: The study of similarities between early embryos of vertebrates
The study of shared molecules in different organisms
The study of the geographical distribution of fossils and living organisms (species)
The study of fossils preserved in rock layers
mcqs.why: The notes define biogeography as the study of the geographical distribution of fossils and living organisms; embryology and molecular biology are separate sources of evidence listed in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Closely related species are usually found in close physical proximity, and local fossils resemble modern organisms of the same region. What does this suggest?
options: These species were each created independently in that region
These species reached the region by crossing oceans easily
These species have no evolutionary relationship with each other
These species share a common lineage, and new organisms arise in an area where similar forms already lived
mcqs.why: The notes state that a comparison of fossil types with living organisms in the same area shows new organisms arise where similar forms already lived, suggesting the species share a common lineage.

mcqs.q: The glyptodont is best described as:
options: An extinct giant, heavily armored relative of the living armadillo
A living marsupial found only in Australia
An extinct giant kangaroo of Australia
A finch species of the Galapagos Islands
mcqs.why: The notes describe glyptodonts as extinct giant, heavily armored armadillos, and state that the glyptodont is the extinct relative of the living armadillo.

mcqs.q: Where did armadillos evolve, and under what condition?
options: In Australia, while it was connected to other continents
In South America, millions of years ago, when it was separated from other continents
In North America, after the two Americas connected
In the Galapagos Islands, in complete isolation
mcqs.why: The notes state that armadillos evolved in South America millions of years ago when it was separated from other continents, and barriers like oceans stopped them spreading elsewhere.

mcqs.q: How did some armadillos reach North America, according to the notes?
options: They swam across the ocean from Australia
They were carried there by ocean currents as eggs
They moved there later, when North and South America connected
They evolved separately in North America from glyptodonts
mcqs.why: The notes state that later, when North and South America connected, some armadillos moved to North America from South America.

mcqs.q: Modern kangaroos evolved from which ancestor, according to the notes?
options: A glyptodont-like armored mammal
A common marsupial ancestor in South America
A giant finch of the Galapagos Islands
An extinct giant kangaroo
mcqs.why: The notes state that modern kangaroos appeared only in Australia, where they evolved from an extinct giant kangaroo.

mcqs.q: Why are kangaroos restricted to Australia?
options: Because of their evolutionary history and geographical isolation, since Australia was separated from other continents
Because predators elsewhere killed all kangaroos outside Australia
Because the climate of every other continent is unsuitable for them
Because they cannot survive in the presence of armadillos
mcqs.why: The notes state kangaroos are restricted to Australia because of their evolutionary history and geographical isolation; Australia's separation let them evolve in isolation and thrive without predators.

mcqs.q: How many species of finches did Darwin find in the Galapagos Islands, and what did he conclude about them?
options: 14 species, each of which had arrived separately from a different continent
14 species, which had evolved from a common ancestral group that reached the islands many generations earlier
90 species, which had evolved from a common ancestral group
4 species, which showed no relationship to one another
mcqs.why: The notes state Darwin found 14 species of finches in the Galapagos Islands and concluded they evolved from a common ancestral group that probably reached the island many generations earlier.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of Galapagos finch beaks and foods is correct according to the notes?
options: Long, sharp beaks for cracking seeds; short, strong beaks for eating insects
Long, sharp beaks for drinking nectar; short, strong beaks for catching fish
Long, sharp beaks for eating insects; short, strong beaks for cracking seeds
All species had identical beaks because they ate the same food
mcqs.why: The notes state some finches had long, sharp beaks for eating insects, while others had short, strong beaks for cracking seeds, each species adapting to a different food.

mcqs.q: Darwin noticed rabbits were not recorded in South America even though the climate was very suitable. What did he conclude?
options: Rabbits had lived there but were all eaten by predators
Rabbits evolved into armadillos in South America
The climate of South America was actually unsuitable for rabbits
Rabbits originated somewhere else and could not reach South America because of barriers such as desert, mountain, ocean and harsh climate
mcqs.why: The notes state Darwin concluded rabbits originated somewhere else and could not reach South America because of barriers — desert, mountain, ocean and harsh climate — so suitable but unreachable regions lack a species.

lessons.notes_html:
The evidences to support the theory of evolution are provided by many sources: the fossil record, morphology, biogeography, comparative anatomy, embryology and molecular biology all provide evidence for evolution. This lesson covers the evidence from biogeography.

13.2 What is Biogeography?

The study of the geographical distribution of fossils and living organisms (species) is called biogeography. A comparison of recently formed fossil types with living organisms in the same geographic area shows that new organisms arise in an area where similar forms already lived. Closely related species are usually found in close physical proximity to one another, and the fossils from these regions resemble modern organisms — this suggests that these species share a common lineage.

Armadillos and Glyptodonts

Armadillos (a type of mammal) appeared in North and South America, where glyptodonts (extinct giant, heavily armored armadillos) lived in the past. The glyptodont is the extinct relative of the living armadillo, and armadillos live only in the Americas. They evolved in South America millions of years ago, when it was separated from other continents. Because of continental drift and natural barriers like oceans, armadillos could not easily spread to other parts of the world. Later, when North and South America connected, some armadillos moved to North America.

Kangaroos of Australia

Modern kangaroos appeared only in Australia, where they evolved from an extinct giant kangaroo. Millions of years ago Australia was separated from other continents, so kangaroos evolved in isolation. Due to the unique environment of Australia and the absence of predators, kangaroos thrived. Kangaroos are restricted to Australia because of their evolutionary history and geographical isolation. In the same way, the unique marsupials of Australia suggest they evolved there in isolation from a common ancestor.

Darwin Finches of the Galapagos Islands

Darwin found 14 species of finches in the Galapagos Islands, famous for unique plants and animals found nowhere else in the world. These finches are not found anywhere else on Earth. He concluded that the finches had evolved from a common ancestral group that probably reached the island many generations earlier. In the isolation of the Galapagos Islands, the original finches probably evolved into the 14 species. The beaks of the Darwin finches were different because each species adopted to eat different types of food on the Galapagos Islands: some finches had long, sharp beaks for eating insects, while others had short, strong beaks for cracking seeds.

Barriers Explain Absence Too

Darwin also noticed that rabbits were not recorded in South America, even though the climate was very suitable for them. He concluded that rabbits originated somewhere else and could not reach South America because of some kind of barriers (desert, mountain, ocean and harsh climate). So biogeography works both ways: related forms occur together in one region, and suitable but unreachable regions lack a species.

Key Points

  • Biogeography is the study of the geographical distribution of fossils and living species.
  • Armadillos live only in the Americas, where their extinct relatives, the glyptodonts, also lived — evidence of common descent in one region.
  • Kangaroos evolved in isolated Australia from an extinct giant kangaroo.
  • The 14 Galapagos finch species evolved from a common ancestor, their beaks adapted to different foods.

lessons.title: Evidence from Molecular Biology and Vestigial Structures

mcqs.q: The DNA of all organisms is composed of which four types of nucleotides?
options: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine and Uracil
Adenine, Thymine, Ribose and Phosphate
Guanine, Cytosine, Uracil and Thymine
Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine and Thymine
mcqs.why: The notes state that the DNA in all organisms is composed of 4 types of nucleotides: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine and Thymine, one part of the shared biochemistry of all life.

mcqs.q: Which molecule is described in the notes as the common energy currency in all organisms?
options: ATP
DNA
Cytochrome c
Ribosomal RNA
mcqs.why: The notes state that the ATP molecule is the common energy currency in all organisms; DNA carries the genetic code and cytochrome c is an electron carrier.

mcqs.q: What does a greater similarity in rRNA sequences between two species indicate?
options: The species are more distantly related to each other
The species are more closely related to each other
The species live in the same geographical region
The species have the same body size and structure
mcqs.why: The notes state that by comparing rRNA sequences scientists trace relationships: the greater the similarities in rRNA sequences, the more closely the species are related.

mcqs.q: How do differences in the sequence of cytochrome c relate to species, according to the notes?
options: The differences are identical in every pair of species
The differences depend only on the size of the species
The differences are proportional to the evolutionary distance between species
Cytochrome c is found only in a few closely related species
mcqs.why: The notes state cytochrome c is found in all aerobic organisms and the differences in its sequence are proportional to the evolutionary distance between species.

mcqs.q: Why are shared molecules such as DNA, ATP and cytochrome c strong evidence for evolution?
options: They show each molecule appeared independently in each species
They prove that all species live in the same environment
They show that unrelated species cannot share any molecules
They are best explained by common descent — all organisms inherited the same basic biochemistry from a common ancestor
mcqs.why: The notes argue it would not make sense if each molecule had appeared independently in each species; shared molecules and pathways are strong evidence that organisms descended from a common ancestor.

mcqs.q: What do the small limb bones found inside some whales and dolphins show?
options: Whales and dolphins once had back legs and their ancestors walked on land
Whales and dolphins are slowly evolving new legs for walking
Whales and dolphins are closely related to snakes
The bones are used today for swimming at high speed
mcqs.why: The notes state that inside some whales and dolphins there are small limb bones showing they once had back legs and their ancestors walked on land; these occasionally reappear as tiny rear flippers.

mcqs.q: What do the hip bones found in some snakes indicate?
options: Snakes are evolving four new legs for the future
Snakes once had four legs, like lizards, their close cousins
Snakes use these bones to support their body while crawling
Snakes descended directly from whales and dolphins
mcqs.why: The notes state that some snakes have hip bones, which show they once had four legs like lizards, their close cousins — a reduced remnant of an ancestral structure.

mcqs.q: The human vermiform appendix is a vestige of which structure, and in which animals is that structure functional?
options: The tail, which is functional in monkeys
The third molar, which is functional in carnivores
The caecum, which is functional in herbivores
The ear muscle, which is functional in horses
mcqs.why: The notes list the vermiform appendix as a vestige of the caecum, noting the caecum is functional in herbivores, while in humans the appendix has lost its original function.

mcqs.q: What is the coccyx (tailbone) in humans?
options: A vestige of the caecum
A vestigial third molar
A minimally developed ear muscle
The remnant of a lost tail
mcqs.why: The notes list the coccyx or tailbone among human vestigial structures as the remnant of a lost tail, evidence of what human ancestors were like.

mcqs.q: What were wisdom teeth used for by human ancestors, according to the notes?
options: Helping to grind down plant tissue, as vestigial third molars
Tearing flesh from prey animals
Moving the ears in various directions
Supporting a tail at the base of the spine
mcqs.why: The notes describe wisdom teeth as vestigial third molars that human ancestors used to help in grinding down plant tissue; ear muscles, not teeth, are linked with moving the ears.

lessons.notes_html:
Some of the strongest evidence for evolution comes from molecules shared by all living things, and from vestigial structures — reduced organs that show what an animal's ancestors were like. Inside some whales and dolphins there are small limb bones which show that they once had back legs and that their ancestors walked on land; these occasionally reappear as tiny rear flippers. Some snakes have hip bones, which show they once had four legs like lizards, their close cousins.

13.3 Shared Molecules in All Organisms

  • There are certain key molecules and biochemical mechanisms shared by different organisms. All organisms use DNA and RNA for their genetic codes. The DNA in all organisms is composed of 4 types of nucleotides, i.e. Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine and Thymine.
  • The ATP molecule is the common energy currency in all organisms.
  • The processes of photosynthesis, cellular respiration, transcription and translation are all identical or very similar in various types of organisms.
  • The ribosomal RNA (rRNA) molecules used in protein synthesis are highly conserved across all life forms. By comparing the sequence of rRNA in different organisms, scientists can trace the similarities among different species: the greater the similarities in rRNA sequences, the more closely the species are related.
  • Similarly, cytochrome c, an electron carrier in the electron transport chain, is found in all aerobic organisms (it is the respiratory protein found in all aerobic organisms). The differences in its sequence are proportional to the evolutionary distance between species.

These molecules make sense as important molecules present in most organisms. However, it would not make sense if each of these molecules had appeared independently in each species. These shared biochemical molecules and pathways provide strong evidence for common descent and evolution: all organisms share the same genetic code and basic biochemistry because they descended from a common ancestor.

Vestigial Structures in Man

Human vestigial organs are those organs that have lost all or most of their original functions through evolution. There are about 90 such structures present in our body, some of which are:

  • Vermiform appendix — A vestige of the caecum (functional in herbivores).
  • Coccyx or tailbone — The remnant of a lost tail.
  • Wisdom teeth — Vestigial third molars that human ancestors used to help in grinding down plant tissue.
  • Ear muscles — Minimally developed and non-functional in humans, but some people are able to move their ears in various directions.
  • Tonsils — Listed in the book among the structures removed from the human body.
  • The small finger of the foot has no function in the foot.

Vestigial structures are evidence of divergent evolution and common ancestry: an organ that was useful in an ancestor remains in a reduced, useless form in its descendants. Other evidences of evolution listed in the book are the fossil record (simpler organisms in older rocks, more complex ones in younger rocks, and transitional forms such as Archaeopteryx between reptiles and birds), comparative anatomy (homologous and analogous structures) and embryology (early embryos of vertebrates look very similar).

Key Points

  • All organisms share DNA and RNA with the same 4 nucleotides, ATP as energy currency, and similar photosynthesis, respiration, transcription and translation.
  • rRNA sequences and cytochrome c are highly conserved; greater similarity means closer relationship.
  • Shared molecules are best explained by common descent, not by independent origin in each species.
  • Vestigial structures — appendix, coccyx, wisdom teeth — are reduced remains of organs useful in ancestors; whales keep small limb bones and some snakes keep hip bones.

lessons.title: Convergent and Divergent Evolution

mcqs.q: What is convergent evolution?
options: Species from different evolutionary backgrounds evolve similar traits due to similar environmental pressures or ecological niches
Related species from a common ancestor become more different over time
A species splits into many species in a single generation
Organs lose their function and become vestigial over time
mcqs.why: The notes define convergent evolution as species from different backgrounds evolving similar traits under similar environmental pressures, without sharing a recent common ancestor.

mcqs.q: Analogous structures are structures that:
options: Have the same origin and basic structure but different functions
Have similar functions but different origins and anatomy
Have lost all of their original functions through evolution
Are identical in structure, origin and function
mcqs.why: The notes state analogous organs are anatomically different but function similarly — same function, different origin — and are produced by convergent evolution.

mcqs.q: Why are the wings of birds and insects considered analogous?
options: Both evolved from the same forelimb bones of a common ancestor
Both have the bones humerus, radius and ulna inside them
Both serve the same function, flying, but bird wings evolved from forelimbs while insect wings are not limbs at all
Both are reduced, functionless remains of ancestral organs
mcqs.why: The notes explain the wings of birds and insects both serve flying but have different evolutionary origins: bird wings evolved from forelimbs, while insect wings are not limbs at all.

mcqs.q: The streamlined bodies of sharks and dolphins are given in the notes as an example of:
options: Divergent evolution producing homologous structures
Vestigial structures inherited from a common ancestor
Endosymbiosis between two different organisms
Convergent evolution producing analogous structures
mcqs.why: The notes list the streamlined bodies of sharks and dolphins among the solved-exercise examples of analogous structures — same function, different origin — produced by convergent evolution.

mcqs.q: The eyes of the octopus and humans are cited in the notes as:
options: Analogous structures — same function, different origin
Homologous structures — same origin, different function
Vestigial structures with no remaining function
Identical structures proving a recent common ancestor
mcqs.why: The notes give the eyes of the octopus and humans as an example of analogous structures from the solved exercises: they perform the same function but arose from different origins.

mcqs.q: What is divergent evolution?
options: Unrelated species develop similar traits in similar environments
Two or more related species become more different over time, usually as they adapt to different environments
A structure loses its function and shrinks over generations
One species engulfs another and gains its organelles
mcqs.why: The notes define divergent evolution as related species sharing a common ancestor becoming more different over time, usually because they adapt to different environments.

mcqs.q: Homologous structures are structures that:
options: Have the same function but completely different origins
Are functionless remnants of ancestral organs
Are similar in origin and basic structure but have diverged to perform different roles
Appear only in unrelated species in similar niches
mcqs.why: The notes state homologous structures are similar in origin and basic structure but perform different functions, developing as related species diverge from a common ancestor.

mcqs.q: Which set of bones is shared by the homologous forelimbs of a human, a cat, a bat and a whale?
options: Femur, tibia, fibula and tarsals
Skull, ribs, sternum and vertebrae
Scapula, clavicle and pelvis only
Humerus, radius, ulna, carpals and phalanges
mcqs.why: The notes state these forelimbs have a similar bone structure — humerus, radius, ulna, carpals and phalanges — even though they are used for grasping, walking, flying and swimming.

mcqs.q: In the homologous forelimbs example, which function matches the whale?
options: Swimming, using its flipper
Grasping, using its hand
Flying, using its wing
Walking, using its leg
mcqs.why: The notes pair the functions in order — human grasping, cat walking, bat flying and whale swimming — all built on the same basic forelimb bones, showing divergent evolution.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of pattern and structure is correct?
options: Convergent evolution produces homologous structures; divergent evolution produces analogous structures
Convergent evolution produces analogous structures; divergent evolution produces homologous structures
Both patterns produce only analogous structures
Both patterns produce only vestigial structures
mcqs.why: The notes summarise the contrast directly: divergent evolution gives homologous structures, while convergent evolution gives analogous structures.

lessons.notes_html:
Evolution can bring unrelated animals to look alike, or make related animals grow different. These two opposite patterns are convergent evolution and divergent evolution, and each leaves its own kind of structure as evidence.

13.4 Convergent Evolution and Analogous Structures

Convergent evolution happens when species from different evolutionary backgrounds evolve similar traits due to similar environmental pressures or ecological niches. In convergent evolution, species do not share a recent common ancestor but develop analogous structures. These structures have similar functions but different origins, e.g. the wings of a bird and the wings of a bat are analogous in the book's example of flying structures; more exactly, analogous organs are anatomically different but functioning similarly.

  • The wings of birds and insects both serve the same function, i.e. flying, but they have different evolutionary origins: bird wings evolved from forelimbs, while insect wings are not limbs at all.
  • Other examples from the solved exercises: the streamlined bodies of sharks and dolphins, and the eyes of the octopus and humans — same function, different origin.

Thus, due to similar environmental pressures, organisms independently evolve similar features, resulting in analogous structures. Convergent evolution is therefore directly related to analogous structures.

Divergent Evolution and Homologous Structures

Divergent evolution takes place when two or more related species become more different over time, usually because they adapt to different environments. In divergent evolution, species share a common ancestor and have homologous structures. These structures are similar in origin and basic structure but have diverged to perform different roles, e.g. the forelimbs of a human, a cat, a bat and a whale are homologous: they have a similar bone structure (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals and phalanges) but have evolved to perform different functions — grasping, walking, flying and swimming respectively.

As species evolve from a common ancestor, they modify their structures to adapt to different environments, leading to the development of homologous structures.

Convergent EvolutionDivergent Evolution
Unrelated species, no recent common ancestor.Related species from a common ancestor.
Similar environments or niches produce similar traits.Different environments produce different traits.
Produces analogous structures: different origin and structure, same function.Produces homologous structures: same origin and basic structure, different functions.
Example: wings of birds and insects; bodies of shark and dolphin.Example: forelimbs of human, cat, bat and whale.

Divergent evolution gives homologous structures; convergent evolution gives analogous structures.

Key Points

  • Convergent evolution: unrelated species in similar environments develop similar traits — analogous structures.
  • Divergent evolution: related species from a common ancestor become different in different environments — homologous structures.
  • Homologous organs have the same basic structure and origin but may perform different functions.
  • Analogous organs have the same function but different structure and origin.

lessons.title: Endosymbiotic Theory: Evolution of Eukaryotes

mcqs.q: According to fossil records in the notes, when did eukaryotes evolve from prokaryotes?
options: About 4.5 billion years ago, with the origin of the Earth
Somewhere between 1.9 and 2.1 billion years ago (about 2 billion years ago)
About 3.7 billion years ago, with the oldest fossils
About 13.8 billion years ago, at the Big Bang
mcqs.why: The notes state fossil records indicate eukaryotes evolved from prokaryotes somewhere between 1.9 and 2.1 billion years ago, about 2 billion years ago.

mcqs.q: Which researcher is named in the notes as supporting the endosymbiotic hypothesis for mitochondria and chloroplasts?
options: Charles Darwin
Jean Baptiste Lamarck
Lynn Margulis
Gregor Mendel
mcqs.why: The notes state the research conducted by Lynn Margulis supports the hypothesis that two separate, mutually beneficial invasions of a prokaryote cell produced modern mitochondria and chloroplasts.

mcqs.q: According to the endosymbiotic theory, ancestral mitochondria were:
options: Small photosynthetic cyanobacteria that made food from sunlight
Spirochete bacteria that moved with a spiral motion
Large prokaryotic cells with pseudopodia that engulfed other cells
Small, aerobic, heterotrophic bacteria capable of using oxygen to perform cellular respiration and create useful energy
mcqs.why: The notes describe ancestral mitochondria as small, aerobic, heterotrophic cells capable of using oxygen for cellular respiration; the large pseudopodial cell was the host, not the mitochondrion.

mcqs.q: How did the aerobic bacterium become the mitochondrion inside the host cell?
options: It entered by direct invasion as an internal parasite or as an indigestible food source, and instead of being digested it survived inside the host
It was built piece by piece by the host's own genes
It formed by folding of the host's outer membrane only
It arrived fully formed from outside the cell's environment
mcqs.why: The notes state the bacterium became part of the large prokaryotic cell by invasion or as indigestible food, and instead of being digested it survived inside the host and became the mitochondrion.

mcqs.q: Ancestral chloroplasts are thought to have been:
options: Small aerobic heterotrophic bacteria engulfed in the first invasion
Small photosynthetic cyanobacteria engulfed in a second invasion
Spirochete bacteria that became flagella and cilia
Parts of the host cell's own nucleus
mcqs.why: The notes state a later, second invasion brought ancestral chloroplasts, thought to be small photosynthetic cyanobacteria, so the engulfed cyanobacterium became the chloroplast.

mcqs.q: Flagella and cilia may have been derived through the ingestion of which bacteria?
options: Cyanobacteria
Aerobic heterotrophic bacteria
Spirochete bacteria
Nitrifying bacteria
mcqs.why: The notes state flagella and cilia may have derived through the ingestion of spirochete bacteria, and that flagella and cilia are similar to spirochete bacteria.

mcqs.q: Which size comparison supports the endosymbiotic theory?
options: Mitochondria and chloroplasts are the same size as a whole eukaryotic cell
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are far smaller than any bacterium
Mitochondria and chloroplasts match the size of the host nucleus
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are the same size as an average bacterial cell
mcqs.why: The notes list as evidence that mitochondria and chloroplasts are the same size as an average bacterial cell, making them appear more similar to prokaryotes than to eukaryotes.

mcqs.q: Which contents of mitochondria and chloroplasts resemble those of prokaryotes?
options: Their own small circular DNA and RNA, and 70S ribosomes
A large nucleus with linear chromosomes
80S ribosomes and a cell wall of cellulose
Golgi bodies and large storage vacuoles
mcqs.why: The notes state both organelles are double-membrane structures containing their own small circular DNA and RNA and 70S ribosomes, like bacteria.

mcqs.q: How do mitochondria and chloroplasts reproduce, according to the notes?
options: They are assembled fresh by the nucleus in each cell cycle
They are self-replicating and divide by binary fission, independent of the host's cell cycle
They divide only when the host cell divides, by mitosis
They reproduce by budding from the Golgi apparatus
mcqs.why: The notes state both organelles are self-replicating and divide by binary fission independent of the host's cell cycle, exactly as free-living bacteria divide.

mcqs.q: Why do some primitive eukaryotes (protozoans) with a nuclear membrane but no mitochondria support the theory?
options: They prove mitochondria are not needed by any cell
They show chloroplasts evolved before the nucleus
They match what would be expected for the early stages of eukaryotic evolution, before mitochondria were acquired
They prove endosymbiosis happened in a single step
mcqs.why: The notes state several primitive eukaryotes have a nuclear membrane but no mitochondria, as expected for early stages — before the invasion that produced mitochondria.

lessons.notes_html:
Fossil records indicate that eukaryotes evolved from prokaryotes somewhere between 1.9 and 2.1 billion years ago (about 2 billion years ago). Two hypotheses have been proposed to describe the evolution of eukaryotes: the membrane invagination theory and the endosymbiotic theory. The endosymbiont hypothesis explains the origin of eukaryotes.

13.5 The Endosymbiotic Theory

The endosymbiotic theory states that some of the organelles in today's eukaryotic cells were once prokaryotic ancestors. The research conducted by Lynn Margulis supports the hypothesis that two separate, mutually beneficial invasions of a prokaryote cell produced the modern-day mitochondria and chloroplasts as eukaryotic organelles.

  • First invasion — mitochondria — Ancestral mitochondria were small, aerobic, heterotrophic cells (bacteria) capable of using oxygen to perform cellular respiration and thereby create useful energy. They became part of a large prokaryotic pseudopodial cell (bacteria) either by direct invasion as an internal parasite or as an indigestible food source. Instead of being digested, the aerobic bacterium survived inside the host and became the mitochondrion.
  • Second invasion — chloroplasts — A later, second invasion brought ancestral chloroplasts, which are thought to be small photosynthetic cyanobacteria. The engulfed cyanobacterium became the chloroplast, so the host cell could make its own food.
  • Flagella and cilia may have derived through the ingestion of spirochete bacteria.

Evidence for Endosymbiosis

  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts are the same size as an average bacterial cell.
  • Both are double membrane organelles containing their own small circular DNA and RNA, and 70S ribosomes.
  • Both organelles are self-replicating and divide by binary fission, independent of the host's cell cycle.
  • They therefore appear to be more similar to prokaryotes than to eukaryotes.
  • Several primitive eukaryotes (protozoans) have a nuclear membrane but no mitochondria, as expected for early stages.
  • Flagella and cilia are similar to spirochete bacteria.

Endosymbiosis: a host prokaryote engulfed an aerobic bacterium (→ mitochondrion) and a cyanobacterium (→ chloroplast).

Key Points

  • Eukaryotes evolved from prokaryotes about 1.9–2.1 billion years ago.
  • Margulis proposed that mitochondria came from engulfed aerobic bacteria and chloroplasts from engulfed photosynthetic cyanobacteria.
  • Both organelles have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, a double membrane, and divide by binary fission like bacteria.
  • The endosymbiotic theory explains the origin of eukaryotes.

lessons.title: Lamarckism: Inheritance of Acquired Characters and Its Drawbacks

mcqs.q: In which book, and in which year, did Lamarck present his ideas?
options: Philosophie Zoologique, in 1744
Origin of Species, in 1809
Philosophie Zoologique (Zoological Philosophy), in 1809
Philosophie Zoologique, in 1880
mcqs.why: The notes state Lamarck wrote the book Philosophie Zoologique (Zoological Philosophy) in 1809; 1744 is the year of his birth, not of the book.

mcqs.q: What does Lamarck's idea of use and disuse of organs state?
options: Organs change only through random mutations in genes
The best-adapted organs are chosen by natural selection
Organs are formed new whenever the environment requires them
An organ used more and more becomes bigger and stronger, while one that is not used becomes weak and eventually disappears
mcqs.why: The notes give use and disuse as the first of Lamarck's two ideas: used organs grow bigger and stronger, unused organs weaken and eventually disappear.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the inheritance of acquired characters?
options: Any feature improved through use during an organism's life is passed to its offspring
Traits are inherited only through genes, never through use
Offspring inherit only the traits present at birth in parents
Acquired features disappear completely in the next generation
mcqs.why: The notes state Lamarck's second idea: a feature of an organism improved through use is passed to its offspring, so changes acquired during life are inherited by the next generation.

mcqs.q: According to Lamarck, how did the giraffe get its long neck?
options: Giraffes with naturally longer necks survived and reproduced more, passing on their genes

Horse-like ancestors with small necks stretched their necks and forelimbs to eat leaves from tall plants where ground vegetation was rare, and this acquired elongation was transmitted over generations
A sudden mutation gave one giraffe a long neck in a single generation
Giraffes grew long necks because predators attacked shorter-necked ones
mcqs.why: The notes give Lamarck's giraffe example: ancestors like horses stretched neck and forelimbs for leaves on tall plants, these parts elongated, and the acquired trait was transmitted to successive generations.

mcqs.q: How did Lamarck explain the loss of limbs in snakes?
options: Snakes never had limbs at any stage of their ancestry
Limb loss was caused by a single mutation in one snake
Snakes evolved from lizard-like ancestors with two pairs of limbs; through disuse the limbs became weaker and shorter and eventually disappeared, and this loss was inherited
Natural selection removed limbs because limbed snakes were eaten
mcqs.why: The notes state snakes are believed to have evolved from lizard-like ancestors with two pairs of limbs, and due to disuse the limbs weakened, shortened and disappeared, the loss being inherited.

mcqs.q: According to Lamarck's theory, why did birds such as the ostrich become flightless?
options: Their wings were removed by predators over many generations
They never possessed wings in their ancestry
Cold climates froze and damaged their wings permanently
Their ancestors could fly, but with plenty of food and good protection they did not use their wings, so the wings became vestigial
mcqs.why: The notes state the ancestors of birds such as the ostrich were able to fly, but with abundant food and protection they did not use their wings, and the wings became vestigial through disuse.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is listed in the notes as a drawback of Lamarckism?
options: There is no experimental proof of the theory
The theory was proved by too many experiments
The theory explains the genetic basis of heredity in detail
The theory was immediately accepted by all biologists
mcqs.why: The notes list as the first drawback that there is no experimental proof of Lamarck's theory, along with the lack of a genetic basis and the fact that acquired characters are not necessarily transmitted.

mcqs.q: Why does Lamarckism have no genetic basis, according to the notes?
options: Genes were unknown, so the theory could not be written down
Bodily characteristics produced by the environment cannot be inherited by the next generation
Acquired characters are stored in the blood, not in genes
New organs are always formed in organisms by requirement
mcqs.why: The notes state there is no genetic basis because bodily characteristics that come due to the environment cannot be inherited to the next generation; they also note new organs are not formed by requirement.

mcqs.q: What did August Weismann's experiment with mice show?
options: After a few generations, mice began to be born without tails
The offspring of tailless mice had noticeably shorter tails
He removed the tails of 68 mice repeatedly for many generations, yet no mice were born without a tail or even with a shorter tail
Mice regrew stronger tails because of repeated use
mcqs.why: The notes state Weismann, in the 1880s, removed the tails of 68 mice for many generations and reported that no mice were born without a tail or even with a shorter tail, disproving inheritance of acquired characters.

mcqs.q: How does modern biology explain the giraffe's long neck and the snake's lost limbs?
options: By inheritance of acquired characters
By stretching and disuse passed to offspring
By organs forming whenever they are required
By natural selection, not by use and disuse
mcqs.why: The notes state plainly that modern biology explains the giraffe's long neck and the snake's lost limbs by natural selection, not by use and disuse.

lessons.notes_html:
Jean Baptiste de Lamarck (August 1, 1744 – December 28, 1829) was a French naturalist and an early proponent of the idea that evolution (descent with modification) occurred and proceeded in accordance with natural laws. Lamarck, however, is remembered today mainly in connection with his now rejected theory of heredity, the inheritance of acquired traits. He was regarded as a premier authority on plants and invertebrate zoology, was well known as a toponymist (an expert in the study of place names), and wrote the book Philosophie Zoologique (Zoological Philosophy) in 1809.

13.6 Lamarck's Theory of Evolution (Lamarckism)

The theory about evolution presented by Lamarck is called Lamarckism. It involved two ideas:

  • (i) Use and disuse of organs — An organ which is used more and more by an organism becomes bigger and stronger, and one that is not used becomes weak and eventually disappears.
  • (ii) Inheritance of acquired characters — Any feature of an organism that is improved through use is passed to its offspring. So changes acquired during the lifetime of an organism are inherited by the next generation.

Examples Given to Support Lamarck's Theory

  • Evolution of the giraffe — According to Lamarck, the ancestors of the giraffe looked like horses, with a small neck and forelimbs. They lived in areas where there was rare ground vegetation, so they had to stretch their neck and forelimbs to eat leaves from tall plants. Consequently, these parts got elongated. This acquired trait was transmitted in the successive generations, producing the long-necked giraffe of today.
  • Extinction of limbs in snakes — Snakes are believed to have evolved from lizard-like ancestors that had two pairs of limbs. Due to disuse of the limbs, the limbs got weaker and shorter and eventually disappeared, and this loss was inherited.
  • Flightless birds — It is believed that the ancestors of birds such as the ostrich were able to fly. Due to some environmental changes, they had a lot of food and were well protected. They did not use their wings, and as a result the wings became vestigial.

13.7 Drawbacks of Lamarckism

Lamarck's theory of acquired characters could not gain popularity and acceptance due to the following drawbacks:

  • (i) There is no experimental proof of his theory.
  • (ii) New organs are not formed in organisms by requirement.
  • (iii) It is not necessary that an acquired character transmits into a new generation.
  • (iv) There is no genetic basis of this theory, because bodily characteristics which came due to the environment cannot be inherited to the next generation.

Moreover, the German biologist August Weismann, in the 1880s, disproved Lamarck's theory of inheritance by giving experimental proof. He removed the tails of 68 mice, repeatedly for many generations, and reported that no mice were born without a tail or even with a shorter tail. This rejects the theory of inheritance of acquired characters: a change acquired in the body during life is not passed to the offspring. Modern biology explains the giraffe's long neck and the snake's lost limbs by natural selection, not by use and disuse.

Key Points

  • Lamarck (Philosophie Zoologique, 1809) gave two ideas: use and disuse of organs, and inheritance of acquired characters.
  • His examples: giraffes stretched their necks longer, snakes lost limbs by disuse, and flightless birds lost used wings.
  • Drawbacks: no experimental proof, no genetic basis, and acquired characters are not necessarily inherited.
  • Weismann cut off the tails of 68 mice for many generations; all offspring were born with tails, disproving Lamarckism.

lessons.title: Darwin's Theory of Natural Selection and Radiometric Dating

mcqs.q: What is 'descent with modification', one of the two main points of Darwin's theory?
options: Passing on traits acquired by use during a parent's lifetime
Producing more offspring than can possibly survive
Competition between members of the same species for food
Passing on traits from parent organisms to their offspring, with changes — all species descended from only a few life forms modified over time
mcqs.why: The notes define descent with modification as passing traits from parents to offspring with changes, and say Darwin held that all species descended from only a few life forms modified over time.

mcqs.q: In Darwin's elephant example of overproduction, a single breeding pair giving six offspring in its 90-year lifespan would produce what population in 750 years?
options: A population of 19 million elephants
A population of 19 thousand elephants
A population of 750 elephants
A population of 2.5 million elephants
mcqs.why: The notes state that if each breeding pair of elephants produces six offspring during its 90-year lifespan, in 750 years a single pair will give rise to a population of 19 million — yet elephants have not overrun the planet.

mcqs.q: Which pair of overproduction figures matches the notes?
options: A salmon produces more than 200 eggs in one season; a grasshopper lays 2.5 million eggs at a time
A salmon produces more than 2.5 million eggs in one season; a grasshopper lays more than 200 eggs at a time
A salmon produces 19 million eggs in one season; a grasshopper lays six eggs at a time
A salmon and a grasshopper each produce about 750 eggs
mcqs.why: The notes give both figures under overproduction: a salmon fish produces more than 2.5 million eggs in one season, and a grasshopper lays more than 200 eggs at a time, though only a few offspring reach reproductive age.

mcqs.q: Competition among organisms of the SAME species is called:
options: Interspecific struggle
Environmental struggle
Intraspecific struggle
Survival of the fittest
mcqs.why: The notes divide the struggle for existence into intraspecific struggle — competition among organisms of the same species — interspecific struggle between different species, and environmental struggle against conditions.

mcqs.q: Which type of struggle is the struggle against various environmental conditions?
options: Intraspecific struggle
Interspecific struggle
Descent with modification
Environmental struggle
mcqs.why: The notes list the third form of the struggle for existence as environmental struggle — the struggle against various environmental conditions — alongside intraspecific and interspecific competition.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, variation needed for evolution by natural selection can result from:
options: Permanent changes, or mutation, in an organism's genes — and the variations must be heritable
Stretching of organs during an individual's lifetime
Changes produced by the environment in the body only
The amount of food an individual eats while growing
mcqs.why: The notes state variation necessary for natural selection can result from permanent changes, or mutation, in an organism's genes, and variations in skin, colour and body structure must be heritable.

mcqs.q: In Darwin's flood example of survival of the fittest, which organisms have the better chance to survive?
options: Those that are largest and heaviest
Those that can swim or respire in water
Those that produced the most offspring before the flood
Those that can run fastest on dry land
mcqs.why: The notes give the flood example under survival of the fittest: if there is a flood, only organisms that can swim or respire in water have a better chance to survive, while others die.

mcqs.q: What does natural selection do to alleles within a population, according to the notes?
options: It increases all alleles equally in the population
It removes favourable alleles and keeps unfavourable ones
It increases favourable alleles and decreases unfavourable alleles
It stops all change in allele frequencies over generations
mcqs.why: The notes state the process of natural selection causes an increase in favourable alleles and a decrease in unfavourable alleles within the population, producing better adapted populations and new species.

mcqs.q: What is the half-life of carbon-14, and what does half-life mean?
options: 11,200 years — the time for all of the isotope to decay completely
5600 years — the time for the whole fossil to form in rock
750 years — the time for a population to double in size
5600 years — the time for one half of the initial amount of the parent radioactive isotope to decay to the daughter isotope
mcqs.why: The notes define half-life as the time for one half of the parent radioactive isotope to decay to the daughter isotope, and give the half-life of carbon-14 as 5600 years.

mcqs.q: A fossil has a carbon-14 to carbon-12 ratio that is one-fourth of the atmosphere's ratio. About how old is it?
options: About 11,200 years old
About 5,600 years old
About 1,400 years old
About 22,400 years old
mcqs.why: Working: one-fourth = (1/2) x (1/2), so two half-lives have passed; 2 x 5600 years = 11,200 years. The notes give exactly this result for a fossil with one-fourth the atmosphere's ratio.

lessons.notes_html:
Darwin's theory of evolution (given in detail in the book's Additional Information) states that various types of plants, animals and other living things on Earth have their origin in other pre-existing types, and that the distinguishable differences are due to modifications in successive generations.

The Two Main Points of Darwin's Theory

  • Descent with modification — Passing on the traits from parent organisms to their offspring, with changes. According to Charles Darwin, all species descended from only a few life forms that had been modified over time. This descent with modification, as he called it, forms the backbone of his theory of evolution.
  • Natural selection — The process in nature by which organisms better adapted to their environment tend to survive and reproduce more than those less adapted to their environment.

The Four Observations About Natural Selection

  • (a) Overproduction — Each species has the capacity to produce more offspring than can possibly obtain food for survival. If all offspring of any species remained alive and reproduced, they would soon overcrowd the Earth and could destroy all other species. For example: if each breeding pair of elephants produces six offspring during its 90-year lifespan, in 750 years a single pair of elephants will give rise to a population of 19 million — yet elephants have not overrun the planet. A salmon fish produces more than 2.5 million eggs in one season. A grasshopper lays more than 200 eggs at a time; however, only a few of these offspring reach reproductive age, because all eggs do not find suitable conditions.
  • (b) Struggle for existence — Individuals increase enormously in number, but the space and food available remain almost constant, so there is always active competition. This three-fold struggle to ensure living, to obtain the maximum amount of food and a better place, results in natural selection. The struggle for existence may be: (1) Intraspecific — competition among the organisms of the same species; (2) Interspecific — competition among the organisms of different species living together; (3) Environmental struggle — struggle against various environmental conditions. Human populations grow faster than the resources they depend on; when populations become too large, famine and disease break out, and in the end this keeps populations in check by killing off the weakest members.
  • (c) Variations — The individuals in a population exhibit variation in their traits. Variation is an inherited trait which makes an individual unique from other members of the species. Some of these traits improve the chances of an individual's survival and reproductive success, whereas other traits do not. Variation necessary for evolution by natural selection can result from permanent changes, or mutation, in an organism's genes; the variations in skin, colour and body structure of humans must be heritable.
  • (d) Survival of the fittest — As a result of competition among the organisms, the stronger win and survive (variant), while the weaker, less variant are rooted out. For example, if there is a flood, only those organisms that can swim or respire in water have a better chance to survive and others will die. Darwin called it natural selection; it is also called survival of the fittest. The process of natural selection thus causes an increase in favourable alleles and a decrease in unfavourable alleles within the population. Over succeeding generations, individual members become better adapted to local conditions, thus leading to the evolution of new species.

Note: "use and disuse of organs" is Lamarck's idea, not one of Darwin's observations. Darwin's four observations are overproduction, struggle for existence, variation and survival of the fittest.

Natural selection: overproduction leads to struggle; favourable variations survive and reproduce.

Radiometric Dating of Fossils (Science, Technology and Society)

Geologists and palaeontologists use several techniques to determine the actual ages of rocks and the fossils they contain. The most common method is radiometric dating (radioactive dating), based on the fact that living organisms contain certain radioactive isotopes in certain ratios. For example, living organisms have the same constant ratio of carbon-14, a radioactive isotope, to carbon-12, a stable isotope, as does the Earth's atmosphere. However, when an organism dies, its ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 starts to drop, because carbon-14 decays to other chemical elements and the organism no longer obtains any carbon-14 from the atmosphere.

Each radioactive isotope has a fixed rate of decay known as its half-life: the amount of time it takes for one half of the initial amount of the parent radioactive isotope to decay to the daughter isotope. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5600 years. Knowing both the half-life of a radioactive isotope and the ratio of radioactive to stable isotope in a fossil enables us to tell how old the fossil is: a fossil with a carbon-14 to carbon-12 ratio half that of the atmosphere is about 5600 years old, and a fossil with one-fourth the atmosphere's ratio is about 11,200 years old.

Key Points

  • Darwin's two main points are descent with modification and natural selection.
  • Four observations: overproduction, struggle for existence (intraspecific, interspecific, environmental), heritable variation, and survival of the fittest.
  • Natural selection increases favourable alleles and decreases unfavourable ones, producing better adapted populations and new species.
  • Radiometric dating uses half-life: carbon-14 has a half-life of 5600 years, so a fossil with half the atmospheric ratio is about 5600 years old.

lessons.title: Species, Population, Community, Ecosystem and Modes of Nutrition
lessons.notes_html:
Ecology (environmental biology) is the branch of biology which deals with the relationship between organisms and their environment. The term was introduced by Ernst Haeckel in 1866, from two Greek words: Oikos — house or living place, and Logos — study or discussion. Every organism lives under a specific set of conditions called its environment.

14.1 Species, Population, Community and Ecosystem

  • Species — A group of similar organisms which can interbreed naturally and produce fertile offsprings, e.g., cow, man, rose, mango.
  • Population — A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time, e.g., all the grasses in a lawn make up the grass population.
  • Community — A group of different populations living and interacting together within the same area, e.g., in a pond there are populations of plants, insects, frogs and fish. Members interact with their own species and with other species, e.g., predation, symbiosis, grazing.
  • Ecosystem — A community along with its environment. It has two components: abiotic (non-living) components, e.g., water, air, light, and biotic (living) components, e.g., plants, animals, micro-organisms.

14.2 Various Modes of Nutrition

Nutrition is the process by which living organisms take in and utilize food substances. On this basis organisms are of two types:

  • Autotrophs — Green plants with chlorophyll in their leaves. They prepare their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis from simple inorganic substances (CO₂, H₂O). They are also called producers, and all other organisms directly or indirectly depend upon them.
  • Heterotrophs — Organisms which cannot prepare their own food and depend upon autotrophs. All animals and fungi are heterotrophs. They are of three main types:
  • Parasites — Get food from living organisms called hosts, living on or inside the host; they may be beneficial, harmful or harmless, and may be plants or animals, e.g., Plasmodium spreads malaria in human beings; Cuscuta is a parasitic plant which absorbs water and nutrients from other plants.
  • Saprobes — Get food from dead bodies or decaying matter, e.g., fungi and bacteria.
  • Holozoic — Food is taken into the body and digested inside, e.g., human, cat, lion.

14.3 Plants as Producers

Green plants prepare food by photosynthesis in the presence of sunlight, using water and CO₂. The light energy of the sun is converted into chemical energy in the form of carbohydrates (especially glucose), so life on earth depends upon photosynthesis. Plants are called producers because they provide the basic food for living things and form the basis of the food chain. Their chemical energy passes through the trophic levels — plants are eaten by herbivores, herbivores by carnivores, and from both the energy is supplied to decomposers (bacteria and fungi).

Key Points

  • Ecology (Haeckel, 1866) studies organisms and their environment: Oikos (house) + Logos (study).
  • Species → population → community → ecosystem (community + environment, with abiotic and biotic components).
  • Autotrophs (producers) make food by photosynthesis; heterotrophs are parasites, saprobes or holozoic.
  • Plants convert light energy into chemical energy (glucose) and form the basis of every food chain.

mcqs.q: Who introduced the term 'ecology', and in which year?
options: Ernst Haeckel, in 1866
Charles Darwin, in 1809
Ernst Haeckel, in 1966
Gregor Mendel, in 1866
mcqs.why: The notes state the term ecology was introduced by Ernst Haeckel in 1866, from the Greek words Oikos (house or living place) and Logos (study or discussion).

mcqs.q: In a pond, the populations of plants, insects, frogs and fish living and interacting together form:

A population
A single species

mcqs.q: An ecosystem consists of:

mcqs.q: Why are green plants called producers?
options: They produce offspring faster than any other organisms
They produce oxygen only, and no food substances

mcqs.q: Which pairing of parasite and example is correct according to the notes?
options: Plasmodium, which feeds on dead bodies, and Cuscuta, which digests food inside its body
Cuscuta, which prepares its own food, and Plasmodium, which lives only on dead matter
Fungi, which spread malaria, and bacteria, which are parasitic plants
Plasmodium, which spreads malaria in human beings, and Cuscuta, a parasitic plant absorbing water and nutrients from other plants
mcqs.why: The notes list parasites as heterotrophs getting food from living hosts, giving Plasmodium spreading malaria in humans and Cuscuta as a parasitic plant absorbing water and nutrients from other plants.

mcqs.q: Saprobes obtain their food from:

Living hosts, on or inside the host's body
Food taken into the body and digested inside
Sunlight, water and carbon dioxide by photosynthesis

mcqs.q: Holozoic nutrition, as in human, cat and lion, means:
options: Food is absorbed from a living host's body
Food is taken into the body and digested inside
Food is obtained from dead and decaying matter
Food is manufactured inside leaves using sunlight
mcqs.why: The notes define the holozoic type of heterotrophs as those in which food is taken into the body and digested inside, giving human, cat and lion as examples.

lessons.title: Trophic Levels and Loss of Energy between Trophic Levels
lessons.notes_html:
In an ecosystem, each stage of the food chain is called a trophic level. The organisms are arranged in different feeding levels which indicate the positions of organisms in a food chain, and also the source of energy and nutrients of different organisms.

14.4 The Five Trophic Levels

LevelGroupExamples
T1Autotrophs (producers) — produce organic food through photosynthesisPlants, algae
T2Herbivores or primary consumers — feed directly on autotrophsGoat, deer
T3Carnivores or secondary consumers — feed on herbivoresWolf, snakes
T4Secondary carnivores or tertiary consumers — feed on other carnivoresLion, big fish like tuna
T5Apex predators or quaternary consumers — top predators, not normally preyed uponSharks, eagles

Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) do not occupy a specific trophic level; they are considered a part of all trophic levels, because they can feed at any trophic level in an ecosystem.

The five trophic levels, from producers (T1) at the base to apex predators (T5) at the top.

14.5 Loss of Energy between Trophic Levels

Energy decreases as it moves from one trophic level to another: not all the energy produced in one level is transferred to the next. On average, about 10% of the net energy production at one trophic level is passed to the next — this is called the 10% rule. The remaining 90% is lost. The book's energy-flow figure shows this: of 1,000,000 J of sunlight, primary producers fix 10,000 J (1%), primary consumers receive 1,000 J, secondary consumers 100 J and tertiary consumers only 10 J.

Reasons for the loss:

  • A large amount of energy is used in life processes like digestion, growth, movement, reproduction and production of wastes.
  • Organisms do not eat every part of another organism, e.g., bones and fur are not eaten by carnivores.
  • A large amount of energy is lost as heat during respiration.
  • Some parts of food are not digested, e.g., cellulose in plants is not easily digested by herbivores.
  • When organisms die, decomposers decompose their bodies and the energy is lost as heat; the nutrients are released into the soil and taken in by producers, but the energy is not available for the next trophic level.

Key Points

  • Trophic levels: T1 producers, T2 herbivores, T3 carnivores, T4 tertiary consumers, T5 apex predators.
  • Decomposers have no fixed trophic level — they feed at every level.
  • 10% rule: only about 10% of energy passes to the next level; about 90% is lost, mainly as heat, in undigested food and in life processes.

mcqs.q: What is a trophic level?
options: The total mass of living organisms in an ecosystem
Each stage of the food chain, indicating the position of organisms in the chain and their source of energy and nutrients
The rate at which plants fix solar energy
A group of populations living in the same area
mcqs.why: The notes define each stage of the food chain as a trophic level, showing the positions of organisms in a food chain and the source of energy and nutrients of different organisms.

mcqs.q: Which organisms occupy trophic level T1, and what is their role?
options: Herbivores such as goat and deer, which feed on autotrophs
Carnivores such as wolf and snakes, which feed on herbivores
Autotrophs (producers) such as plants and algae, which produce organic food through photosynthesis
Apex predators such as sharks and eagles
mcqs.why: The notes place autotrophs (producers) — plants and algae producing organic food through photosynthesis — at T1, the base of the five trophic levels.

mcqs.q: Goat and deer are placed at T2 because they are:
options: Carnivores or secondary consumers that feed on herbivores
Tertiary consumers that feed on other carnivores
Decomposers that feed at every trophic level
Herbivores or primary consumers that feed directly on autotrophs
mcqs.why: The notes place herbivores or primary consumers such as goat and deer at T2, feeding directly on the autotrophs of T1.

mcqs.q: Wolf and snakes are given as examples of which trophic level and group?
options: T3 — carnivores or secondary consumers that feed on herbivores
T2 — herbivores or primary consumers
T4 — secondary carnivores or tertiary consumers
T5 — apex predators or quaternary consumers
mcqs.why: The notes list wolf and snakes at T3 as carnivores or secondary consumers feeding on herbivores; lion and tuna are the T4 examples, and sharks and eagles the T5 examples.

mcqs.q: Lion and big fish like tuna occupy T4 because they:
options: Feed directly on producers like plants and algae
Are secondary carnivores or tertiary consumers that feed on other carnivores
Are top predators that nothing normally preys upon
Decompose dead bodies at every trophic level
mcqs.why: The notes place lion and big fish like tuna at T4 as secondary carnivores or tertiary consumers feeding on other carnivores; 'not normally preyed upon' describes the T5 apex predators.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes the T5 apex predators such as sharks and eagles?
options: They feed directly on autotrophs for their energy
They decompose the bodies of organisms at all levels
They are quaternary consumers — top predators not normally preyed upon
They are the first consumers in every food chain
mcqs.why: The notes define T5 as apex predators or quaternary consumers — top predators such as sharks and eagles that are not normally preyed upon.

mcqs.q: Why do decomposers (bacteria and fungi) not occupy a specific trophic level?
options: They produce their own food by photosynthesis like producers
They are eaten by apex predators at the top level only
They obtain energy directly from sunlight alone
They are considered part of all trophic levels because they can feed at any trophic level in an ecosystem
mcqs.why: The notes state decomposers do not occupy a specific trophic level; they are considered part of all trophic levels because they can feed at any trophic level in an ecosystem.

mcqs.q: In the book's energy-flow figure, 1,000,000 J of sunlight reaches the ecosystem. How much energy do the primary producers fix?
options: 10,000 J, which is 1% of the sunlight
100,000 J, which is 10% of the sunlight
1,000 J, which is 0.1% of the sunlight
10 J, which is 1% of the sunlight
mcqs.why: Working: 1% of 1,000,000 J = 1,000,000 x 0.01 = 10,000 J. The notes' figure shows primary producers fixing 10,000 J (1%) of the 1,000,000 J of sunlight.

mcqs.q: Using the book's figure — producers fix 10,000 J — how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
options: Only 10 J
mcqs.why: Working with the 10% rule: producers 10,000 J, primary consumers 10% of 10,000 = 1,000 J, secondary consumers 10% of 1,000 = 100 J, tertiary consumers 10% of 100 = 10 J, exactly as the notes' figure shows.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a reason given in the notes for energy loss between trophic levels?
options: Energy is recycled back to the producers at each level
Consumers eat every part of an organism, including bones and fur
A large amount of energy is lost as heat during respiration, and some food parts such as cellulose are not easily digested
Decomposers return all the energy of dead bodies to the next level
mcqs.why: The notes list heat lost in respiration, undigested parts like cellulose, uneaten parts like bones and fur, and energy used in life processes; energy from dead bodies is lost as heat, not returned to the next level.

lessons.title: Greenhouse Effect, Acid Rain, Global Warming and Ocean Acidification
lessons.notes_html:
Human activities have badly affected the natural environment through industrialization, urbanization, deforestation, mining and burning of fossil fuels. This lesson covers four linked problems: the greenhouse effect, acid rain, global warming and ocean acidification.

14.6 Greenhouse Effect

The greenhouse effect is a natural process in which gases in the earth's atmosphere trap heat and warm the planet. Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the ground and plants; this energy is released as heat, but the heat cannot escape back into space easily because gases like CO₂, methane (CH₄), sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and nitrous oxide trap it. These are called greenhouse gases: they let sunlight in but stop some heat from going out.

The main cause is carbon dioxide. Its concentration has increased due to urbanization, deforestation, industrialization and burning of fuels in factories, furnaces and vehicles. About half of this CO₂ is absorbed by plants and oceans; the rest forms a thick layer in the lower atmosphere which allows sunlight to pass and heat the earth but does not allow the heat to radiate out. This layer acts like the glass of a greenhouse, so the atmospheric temperature increases.

Harmful Effects of Greenhouse Gases

Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, NO₂, O₃, SO₂, etc.) keep the earth warm — without them the temperature would be too low for life to survive. But at too high levels they harm the environment and life:

  • They cause air pollution, leading to breathing problems and other health issues in people and animals.
  • They damage the ozone (O₃) layer, so more ultraviolet (UV) rays reach the earth; UV rays are harmful for ecosystems, micro-organisms, plants and animals.
  • Too much CO₂ leads to ocean acidification, harming the marine ecosystem and marine life.
  • They are the main cause of global warming: loss of biodiversity, sea level rise from melting glaciers and ice caps, climate change, human health effects (heat stroke, dehydration) and disturbed quality and quantity of crop yield.

14.7 Acid Rain

Precipitation with acidic components that falls on the ground from the atmosphere is called acid rain. It may occur as wet deposition (rain, snow, hail or fog) or as dry deposition (dry gases or dust). It occurs when pollutants like sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and nitrogen oxides (NO₂), which come mainly from burning fuel in vehicles, factories and power plants, mix with water vapours in the atmosphere.

Water is neutral, with a pH of 7, and normal rain water is slightly acidic due to its reaction with CO₂. When SO₂ and NO₂ dissolve in water vapours, sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) and nitric acid (HNO₃) are formed; the acidity increases (pH becomes low) and the acids return to the ground along with rain water. Acid rain often falls hundreds or thousands of kilometres away from its source.

Effects: it kills decomposers and micro-organisms; destroys crops; increases acidity in water, affecting aquatic life, and increases soil acidity; causes stone cancer by its corrosive effect on stones; affects the colours of houses and automobiles; makes plants poisoned and weak; and forests suffer when it weakens trees and washes away nutrients from the soil.

14.8 Global Warming

The long-term rise in the earth's average temperature is called global warming. It is primarily caused by the increase of greenhouse gases (especially CO₂) due to human activities: burning fossil fuels (coal, petrol, natural gas) produces CO₂, greenhouse gases are also produced by industrial processes, and deforestation increases the amount of CO₂. Some greenhouse gases are also produced by natural processes, i.e., decomposition of dead bodies and volcanic eruptions.

Effects: ecosystems are disturbed, so wildlife and biodiversity are affected; with the increase in heat waves, the risks of heatstroke and dehydration have increased; agriculture patterns are changing, affecting food production; floods, wildfires and storms have damaged buildings and roads, affecting the economy; the increased temperature has contributed to climate change and extreme weather like hurricanes and droughts; glaciers and ice caps are melting, so sea level is rising — dangerous for coastal areas, with increased danger of flooding from rivers; and increased temperature damages and destroys crops and forests and causes danger to life.

14.9 Ocean Acidification

Ocean acidification is the phenomenon in which ocean water becomes acidic due to the absorption of CO₂ from the atmosphere. The CO₂ dissolves in sea water and forms carbonic acid: H₂O + CO₂ → H₂CO₃, so the pH of the ocean decreases.

It especially affects coral reefs — massive structures in the sea built by the exoskeleton of corals, which is made of CaCO₃ (calcium carbonate). Ocean acidification reduces the availability of carbonate ions, which are necessary for the production of the CaCO₃ skeleton, so growth rates become slow and the structure of corals becomes weak; weakened corals cannot bear storms and wave action, so their bodies are damaged.

Effects of coral reefs on the aquatic ecosystem: the health of a marine ecosystem depends upon the growth of coral reefs. They provide a suitable habitat for a vast variety of marine organisms (micro-organisms, invertebrates, fish) — thousands of species can be found on one reef, so they are called the Rain Forests of the Sea. They provide a place for breeding and are the shelter house for new young ones; they are essential for nutrient cycling and an important component of the marine food web, so any decline reduces food for many marine animals and disturbs the ecosystem. Their growth is disturbed by changes in temperature, ocean acidification and pollution. Healthy coral reefs act as a natural barrier that protects coastlines from storm and erosion.

Key Points

  • Greenhouse gases (mainly CO₂) trap heat like greenhouse glass; in excess they cause global warming.
  • Acid rain forms when SO₂ and nitrogen oxides dissolve in water vapour to form sulphuric acid and nitric acid; it harms crops, aquatic life, soil, forests and stone (stone cancer).
  • Global warming: melting glaciers, rising sea level, extreme weather, disturbed agriculture and health.
  • Ocean acidification (CO₂ + H₂O → carbonic acid) weakens coral skeletons; coral reefs shelter thousands of species and protect coastlines.

The long-term rise in the earth's average temperature
A natural process in which gases in the earth's atmosphere trap heat and warm the planet — they let sunlight in but stop some heat from going out
The absorption of CO2 by ocean water making it acidic

mcqs.q: Which gas is named in the notes as the main cause of the greenhouse effect, and why has it increased?
