Carbon dioxide, increased by urbanization, deforestation, industrialization and burning of fuels in factories, furnaces and vehicles

mcqs.q: What happens to the carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere, according to the notes?
options: About half is absorbed by plants and oceans; the rest forms a thick layer in the lower atmosphere that lets sunlight pass but does not allow heat to radiate out
All of it is absorbed by plants within a few days
All of it escapes into space as heat radiation
About half escapes to space and the rest dissolves in rain

mcqs.q: Which harmful effect of excess greenhouse gases is correctly stated?
options: They strengthen the ozone layer and block all ultraviolet rays
They damage the ozone (O3) layer, so more ultraviolet rays reach the earth, harming ecosystems, micro-organisms, plants and animals
They cool the earth so much that life cannot survive

mcqs.q: Acid rain forms when which pollutants dissolve in water vapour, and which acids result?
options: Carbon dioxide dissolves to form sulphuric acid and nitric acid

mcqs.q: The corrosive effect of acid rain on stones, damaging buildings and monuments, is called:
options: Ocean acidification
The greenhouse effect
Desertification
Stone cancer
mcqs.why: The notes list among the effects of acid rain that it causes stone cancer by its corrosive effect on stones, alongside killing decomposers, destroying crops and increasing soil and water acidity.

mcqs.q: Global warming is best defined as:
options: The long-term rise in the earth's average temperature, primarily caused by increased greenhouse gases (especially CO2) from human activities
A short spell of hot weather in one region for a few days
The natural trapping of heat that keeps the earth warm enough for life

mcqs.why: The notes define global warming as the long-term rise in the earth's average temperature, primarily caused by the increase of greenhouse gases, especially CO2, from burning fossil fuels, industrial processes and deforestation.

mcqs.q: Which effect of global warming is correctly stated in the notes?
options: Sea level is falling as more water freezes into ice caps
Glaciers and ice caps are melting, so sea level is rising, increasing the danger of flooding for coastal areas and from rivers
Heat waves have decreased, reducing heatstroke and dehydration
Agriculture patterns have become completely stable everywhere

mcqs.q: Ocean acidification happens because:
options: SO2 dissolves in sea water and forms sulphuric acid, raising the pH
Oceans release CO2 into the air, so their pH increases
CO2 dissolves in sea water and forms carbonic acid — H2O + CO2 -> H2CO3 — so the pH of the ocean decreases

mcqs.why: The notes state ocean acidification occurs as CO2 is absorbed from the atmosphere and dissolves in sea water forming carbonic acid, H2O + CO2 -> H2CO3, so the pH of the ocean decreases.

mcqs.q: Why are coral reefs called the 'Rain Forests of the Sea', and how does acidification harm them?
options: They grow on land like forests, and acidification makes their skeletons grow faster
Only a few species live on reefs, and acidification strengthens their CaCO3 skeletons
They produce rain over the sea, and acidification increases carbonate ions
Thousands of species can be found on one reef, and acidification reduces carbonate ions needed to build their CaCO3 skeletons, so growth slows and the structure weakens
mcqs.why: The notes state thousands of species can be found on one reef, hence 'Rain Forests of the Sea', and acidification reduces carbonate ions necessary for the CaCO3 skeleton, slowing growth and weakening corals.

lessons.title: Biogeochemical Cycles: Water Cycle and Nitrogen Cycle
lessons.notes_html:
A biogeochemical cycle is the flow of chemical elements and compounds between living organisms and their physical environment. Chemicals absorbed or ingested by organisms are passed through the food chain and returned to the soil, air and water as respiration, excretion and decomposition. As an element moves through the cycle, it often forms compounds with other elements, by metabolic processes in living tissues or by natural reactions in the atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water) or lithosphere (the outer rigid, strong layer of the earth).

14.10 Primary Reservoirs of Nutrients

Chemicals held for long periods in one place are in a reservoir, e.g., coal deposits storing carbon for a long time. Chemicals held for only a short period are in exchange pools, e.g., plants and animals. Plants absorb minerals and nutrients from the soil and store them in their bodies, along with carbohydrates produced in photosynthesis; these pass to herbivores. Animals also store nutrients (minerals, vitamins, proteins, fats) in their tissues; carnivores obtain them from other animals and omnivores from both plants and animals. Generally reservoirs are abiotic factors, and carbon is held for a relatively short time in plants and animals in comparison to coal deposits. The period for which a chemical is held in one place is called its residence time.

14.11 Water Cycle

There is as much water today as there was thousands of years ago, because of the water cycle. The ocean is the major source, containing about 97% of the total water. The cycle is driven by solar energy, which evaporates water, and by gravity, which draws water back to earth as precipitation, i.e., rain, snow, dew or hail.

Water in the environment: some water evaporates from the soil, lakes and streams, and a portion runs off the land back to the oceans. Some rain water sinks or percolates into the ground and saturates the earth to a certain level; the top of the saturation zone is called the water table. Water in basins appears at the level of the water table as lakes and ponds, and water in channels is called streams or rivers. Sometimes ground water is located in underground rivers called aquifers.

Water in living bodies: the bodies of living things contain roughly 70% water. Water is absorbed by the roots of plants, and much of it is evaporated back to the atmosphere from their leaves. A small amount is combined with carbon dioxide during photosynthesis to produce high-energy molecules, which are broken down during cellular respiration, releasing water back to the environment. Heterotrophs get water from their food or by drinking, and some is released back by vaporization.

14.12 Water Table and Aquifers

The water table is the upper surface of the saturation zone; it describes the boundary between water-saturated ground and unsaturated ground. Below the water table, rocks and soil are full of water. An aquifer is an underground layer where the material contains water; aquifers are the sources of wells, springs, etc.

14.13 Nitrogen Cycle

Nitrogen is the necessary element of organic molecules such as amino acids, nucleic acids and proteins. The nitrogen cycle is the movement of nitrogen between the earth and the atmosphere, converting nitrogen gas into organic substances and returning them to nitrogen in the atmosphere. It is a continuous cycle maintained by decomposers and other bacteria, explained in four types of reactions: decomposition, nitrogen fixation, assimilation and denitrification.

1. Decomposition — the breakdown of complex organic substances into simple components; decomposition of organic nitrogen compounds is the first source of soil nitrates. It occurs in two steps:

  • Ammonification — Nitrogenous wastes of animals and nitrogenous compounds of dead organisms are decomposed by saprophytic soil bacteria and fungi into simple substances like water, carbon dioxide, amino acids and energy. The amino acids are converted into ammonia or ammonium ions; this production of ammonia by ammonifying bacteria (e.g., Clostridium, Streptomyces) is ammonification.
  • Nitrification — Much of the ammonia and ammonium ions are converted into nitrates by nitrifying bacteria: Nitrosomonas converts ammonia to nitrites, and Nitrobacter converts nitrites to nitrates. It takes place only in well-aerated soils, because the bacteria are aerobic in nature.

2. Nitrogen fixation — any process of combining atmospheric nitrogen with other elements, either by chemical means or by bacterial action. Nitrogen gas (N₂) has two atoms linked by a very strong triple bond, making it chemically unreactive, and a large amount of energy is required to break the bond. It can be fixed in three ways:

  • Atmospheric fixation (about 5–8%) — Fixation occurring spontaneously by lightning. The high temperature of lightning breaks the bonds of N₂; free nitrogen atoms combine with oxygen to form oxides of nitrogen (NOx), which dissolve in rain to form nitric acid. This falls with rain water and reacts with mineral elements to form nitrates, which are used by plants. Lightning energy also causes nitrogen and water to form ammonia.
  • Industrial fixation — The synthesis of nitrogen-containing fertilizers.
  • Biological fixation (about 60%) — Fixation by living organisms. Maximum fixation is done by nitrogen-fixing bacteria, e.g., Rhizobia, living in the root nodules of legume plants (pea, beans); their enzymes break the strong bonds in N₂. The conversion requires 16 molecules of ATP and a complex set of enzymes: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Some bacteria are free-living in soil, e.g., Azotobacter (aerobic) and Clostridium (anaerobic), and fixed nitrogen is made available to plants by the death and lysis of these bacteria. Blue green algae (Nostoc, Anabena) also fix nitrogen.

3. Assimilation — the formation of organic nitrogen compounds like amino acids from inorganic nitrogen compounds present in the environment. Plants obtain nitrogen as ammonia and nitrates from the soil, whereas animals take their nitrogen from eating plants or other animals.

4. Denitrification — nitrates are converted into molecular nitrogen (N₂) by denitrifying bacteria, e.g., Pseudomonas, in an oxygen-free (anaerobic) environment. The bacteria use nitrates as an energy source, and the gas is released back into the atmosphere in the steps: NO₃ (nitrate) → NO₂ (nitrite) → NO (nitric oxide) → N₂O (nitrous oxide) → N₂ (nitrogen gas).

The main steps of the nitrogen cycle; denitrification returns nitrogen to the air, completing the cycle.

Key Points

  • Reservoirs hold chemicals for a long time (coal deposits); exchange pools hold them briefly (plants and animals); residence time is the time a chemical stays in one place.
  • The water cycle is driven by solar energy and gravity; the ocean holds about 97% of all water and living bodies roughly 70%; aquifers below the water table supply wells and springs.
  • Nitrogen cycle: decomposition (ammonification, then nitrification by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter), fixation (atmospheric 5–8%, industrial, biological about 60%), assimilation, and denitrification by Pseudomonas.
  • Biological fixation by Rhizobia in legume root nodules needs enzymes and 16 ATP: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.

mcqs.q: A biogeochemical cycle is:
options: The one-way flow of energy from the sun through a food chain
The replacement of one community by another over time
The movement of water between the ocean and the atmosphere only
The flow of chemical elements and compounds between living organisms and their physical environment, with chemicals returned to soil, air and water by respiration, excretion and decomposition
mcqs.why: The notes define a biogeochemical cycle as the flow of chemical elements and compounds between living organisms and their physical environment, returned as respiration, excretion and decomposition.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a reservoir and an exchange pool?
options: A reservoir holds chemicals for long periods (e.g. coal deposits storing carbon), while exchange pools hold them only briefly (e.g. plants and animals); the time held is the residence time
A reservoir holds chemicals briefly in living bodies, while exchange pools hold them for long periods in rocks
Both hold chemicals for exactly the same length of time
Reservoirs are always living factors and exchange pools are always non-living
mcqs.why: The notes state chemicals held for long periods are in a reservoir such as coal deposits, chemicals held briefly are in exchange pools such as plants and animals, and the holding period is called residence time.

mcqs.q: In the water cycle, the ocean contains about what percentage of total water, and what drives the cycle?
options: About 70% of the total water; the cycle is driven by wind and ocean currents
About 97% of the total water; the cycle is driven by solar energy, which evaporates water, and by gravity, which draws water back as precipitation
About 50% of the total water; the cycle is driven by gravity alone
About 97% of the total water; the cycle is driven by volcanic heat from the earth
mcqs.why: The notes state the ocean is the major source containing about 97% of total water, and the cycle is driven by solar energy evaporating water and gravity drawing it back as precipitation — rain, snow, dew or hail.

mcqs.q: The water table and an aquifer are correctly described as:
options: The water table is an underground river; an aquifer is the surface of a lake
The water table is the level of the ocean; an aquifer is water stored in plant leaves
The water table is the upper surface of the saturation zone; an aquifer is an underground layer whose material contains water and is a source of wells and springs
Both terms describe water vapour present in the atmosphere
mcqs.why: The notes define the water table as the upper surface (top) of the saturation zone, below which rocks and soil are full of water, and an aquifer as an underground layer containing water, the source of wells and springs.

mcqs.q: In the nitrogen cycle, assimilation means:
options: The conversion of nitrates back into molecular nitrogen gas by bacteria
The breakdown of dead organisms' nitrogen compounds into ammonia
The combining of atmospheric nitrogen with other elements by lightning

The formation of organic nitrogen compounds like amino acids from inorganic nitrogen compounds in the environment — plants take up ammonia and nitrates, animals get nitrogen by eating plants or other animals
mcqs.why: The notes define assimilation as forming organic nitrogen compounds like amino acids from inorganic compounds; plants obtain nitrogen as ammonia and nitrates from soil, animals from eating plants or other animals.

mcqs.q: Ammonification is the process in which:
options: Saprophytic soil bacteria and fungi decompose nitrogenous wastes and dead organisms, and the amino acids are converted into ammonia or ammonium ions by ammonifying bacteria such as Clostridium and Streptomyces
Nitrosomonas converts ammonia into nitrites in well-aerated soil
Pseudomonas converts nitrates into nitrogen gas without oxygen
Rhizobia in root nodules combine nitrogen gas with hydrogen
mcqs.why: The notes place ammonification inside decomposition: wastes and dead organisms are broken down by saprophytic bacteria and fungi, and amino acids are converted to ammonia or ammonium ions by ammonifying bacteria e.g. Clostridium, Streptomyces.

mcqs.q: In nitrification, which bacteria perform each step?
options: Nitrobacter converts ammonia to nitrites, and Nitrosomonas converts nitrites to nitrates
Nitrosomonas converts ammonia to nitrites, and Nitrobacter converts nitrites to nitrates — in well-aerated soils, because the bacteria are aerobic
Pseudomonas converts ammonia directly to nitrogen gas
Rhizobia convert nitrites to nitrates inside root nodules
mcqs.why: The notes state nitrification converts ammonia and ammonium ions into nitrates: Nitrosomonas converts ammonia to nitrites and Nitrobacter converts nitrites to nitrates, only in well-aerated soils as the bacteria are aerobic.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of nitrogen fixation type and share is correct?
options: Atmospheric fixation is about 60%; biological fixation is about 5-8%
Industrial fixation is about 60%; atmospheric fixation is about 40%
Atmospheric fixation by lightning is about 5-8%; biological fixation by living organisms is about 60%
Biological fixation is about 5-8%; industrial fixation is about 60%
mcqs.why: The notes give atmospheric fixation (by lightning) as about 5-8% and biological fixation as about 60%, with maximum fixation done by nitrogen-fixing bacteria; industrial fixation is the synthesis of nitrogen-containing fertilizers.

mcqs.q: Biological fixation by Rhizobia in the root nodules of legumes such as pea and beans involves:
options: No energy input, because the N2 bond is weak and breaks easily
Conversion of nitrates into nitrites using 16 molecules of ATP
Release of nitrogen gas back into the atmosphere: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3
Enzymes that break the strong triple bond of N2, requiring 16 molecules of ATP: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3
mcqs.why: The notes state Rhizobia live in legume root nodules, their enzymes break the strong triple bond in N2, and the conversion requires 16 molecules of ATP and a complex set of enzymes: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3.

mcqs.q: Denitrification is carried out by which bacteria, under what conditions, and with what result?
options: Pseudomonas, in an oxygen-free (anaerobic) environment, converts nitrates back into molecular nitrogen (N2) released into the atmosphere
Nitrobacter, in well-aerated soil, converts nitrites into nitrates for plants
Rhizobia, inside root nodules, converts nitrogen gas into ammonia
Azotobacter, in oxygen-rich soil, converts ammonia into nitrites
mcqs.why: The notes state denitrification converts nitrates into molecular nitrogen by denitrifying bacteria e.g. Pseudomonas in an anaerobic environment, following NO3 -> NO2 -> NO -> N2O -> N2, returning nitrogen to the air.

lessons.title: Productivity, Food Chains, Food Webs and Ecological Pyramids
lessons.notes_html:
This lesson links three ideas: how much food energy an ecosystem produces (productivity), how energy moves through organisms (food chains, food webs and energy flow), and how ecologists draw that movement as pyramids.

14.14 Productivity

The rate at which plants convert solar energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis is called productivity. The ultimate source of energy for ecosystems is the sun, and only 1% of solar energy is incorporated into the ecosystem. The total amount of solar energy fixed by the producers during photosynthesis in a given area over a specific time is called gross primary productivity (GPP). The amount of energy that remains available for plant growth, after subtracting the fraction that plants use for respiration, is net primary productivity (NPP), or biomass:

NPP = GPP - Respiration

In grasslands, NPP varies widely with rainfall, temperature and soil fertility, and it is vital for supporting herbivores and maintaining ecosystem balance. Productivity depends on temperature and moisture: it rises with temperature up to about 30°C, after which it declines, and it is positively correlated with moisture. On land it is highest in warm, wet tropical zones (tropical forest biomes) and lowest in desert shrub ecosystems, which are extremely hot and dry. In aquatic ecosystems, light and nutrients are the controlling factors: in oceans, light penetrates only up to 500 m, and marine productivity is high near coastlines. Algal beds and coral reefs have the highest net primary production, while the open ocean has the lowest rates, due to a lack of nutrients in the illuminated surface layers.

14.15 Food Chain, Food Web and Energy Flow

Food chain: the transfer of food energy from the producers (green plants) through a series of organisms, with repeated stages of eating and being eaten. Each organism feeds on and derives energy from the preceding one, and is itself consumed by the next, e.g., producers → herbivores → carnivores → top carnivores. At each step, a larger part of the fixed energy is lost. A food chain shows the flow of nutrients and energy, helps us understand the ecosystem and the impact of human activities, and explains the interconnected relationship among organisms.

Food web: linear food chains interconnected to form a complicated network. It shows the feeding relationships among different species in an ecosystem. In a complex ecosystem there are many alternate sources of food for the herbivores, and herbivores may be preyed upon by several different predators; producers may be eaten by primary, secondary or tertiary consumers, and a primary consumer may be eaten by secondary or tertiary consumers. Food webs help maintain the balance in an ecosystem, facilitate the transfer of nutrients and their cycling, and are necessary to understand the function, conservation and management of an ecosystem.

Energy flow: nutrients move in a circular path (biogeochemical cycles, e.g., the nitrogen cycle), but energy cannot be recycled — it flows in one direction only. The main source is the sun: green plants convert solar energy into chemical energy (glucose), used by plants and consumers. Some ingested food is not digested; this egested portion is used by micro-organisms. At each level, a portion of food is egested and a large part of energy is lost during respiration as heat. From the last consumer, energy is lost into space as heat and is not available again. So less energy is available for top carnivores, and large food chains lose greater amounts of energy than short food chains.

14.16 Ecological Pyramids

The diagram that shows the relative amount of energy or matter or numbers of organisms within each trophic level in a food chain or food web is called an ecological pyramid — a graphical representation of ecological data. There are three types:

  • Pyramid of energy — Shows the relative amount of energy available at different trophic levels. Energy is lost as heat during respiration at every level, through undigested matter egested by consumers, and through excretory products, e.g., urea. Total energy decreases progressively along the food chain, so this pyramid is always broad at the base and narrow towards the apex. Normally about 90% of energy is lost at each transfer. This progressive loss explains why food chains are generally short, and why more energy is available to a human feeding directly on crop plants than eating cattle that feed on plants.
  • Pyramid of biomass — Shows the total mass of living organisms in each trophic level, with producers at the base and quaternary consumers at the top. Biomass decreases gradually from base to top: maximum in producers, because they support all other levels, then herbivores, carnivores and tertiary consumers, with quaternary consumers having the least. The book's figure shows producers 1000 Kg, herbivores 100 Kg, primary carnivores 10 Kg and top carnivore 1 Kg. It helps us understand the flow of energy and the efficiency of an ecosystem.
  • Pyramid of numbers — Shows the relative number of organisms at different trophic levels. In the book's example (grass → rabbits → snakes → hawks), 10 hawks each need one snake per day, so in one month they need 300 snakes; the 300 snakes need 4,500 rabbits in one month; and a rabbit may require 20 or more grass plants per day, so about 2,700,000 grass plants are needed in one month. The pyramid is broad at the base and narrow towards the top.

Key Points

  • Productivity: only 1% of solar energy enters the ecosystem; NPP = GPP - Respiration.
  • Nutrients cycle, but energy flows in one direction only and is lost as heat, so longer chains lose more energy.
  • A food web is many interconnected food chains; it maintains balance and nutrient cycling.
  • Pyramids show energy (always upright, about 90% lost per level), biomass or numbers at each trophic level.

mcqs.q: Productivity is defined in the notes as:
options: The rate at which plants convert solar energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis — and only 1% of solar energy is incorporated into the ecosystem
The total mass of organisms present at each trophic level
The number of organisms counted in a food chain
The rate at which decomposers break down dead bodies
mcqs.why: The notes define productivity as the rate at which plants convert solar energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis, and state only 1% of solar energy is incorporated into the ecosystem.

mcqs.q: Net primary productivity (NPP) is calculated as:
options: NPP = GPP + Respiration
NPP = GPP - Respiration — the energy left for plant growth after subtracting what plants use in respiration
NPP = GPP x Respiration
NPP = Respiration - GPP
mcqs.why: The notes define GPP as the total solar energy fixed by producers, and NPP (or biomass) as what remains for plant growth after subtracting the fraction used for respiration: NPP = GPP - Respiration.

mcqs.q: How do temperature and moisture affect productivity, according to the notes?
options: Productivity keeps rising without limit as temperature increases
Productivity falls as moisture increases in an ecosystem
Productivity rises with temperature up to about 30°C, after which it declines, and it is positively correlated with moisture
Productivity is highest at 30°C only in desert ecosystems
mcqs.why: The notes state productivity depends on temperature and moisture: it rises with temperature up to about 30°C, after which it declines, and it is positively correlated with moisture.

mcqs.q: Which statements about aquatic productivity match the notes?
options: Light penetrates to the deepest ocean floor, so the open ocean has the highest production
Algal beds and coral reefs have the lowest net primary production
Nutrients are most abundant in the illuminated surface layers of the open ocean
Light penetrates only up to 500 m in oceans, marine productivity is high near coastlines, and algal beds and coral reefs have the highest net primary production while the open ocean has the lowest
mcqs.why: The notes state that in oceans light penetrates only up to 500 m, productivity is high near coastlines, algal beds and coral reefs have the highest NPP, and the open ocean the lowest due to lack of nutrients in surface layers.

mcqs.q: A food chain shows:
options: The transfer of food energy from producers through a series of organisms, with repeated stages of eating and being eaten, each organism feeding on the preceding one and being consumed by the next
A complicated network of many interconnected feeding relationships
The total number of species living in an ecosystem
The circular movement of nutrients between soil and organisms only
mcqs.why: The notes define a food chain as the transfer of food energy from producers through a series of organisms with repeated eating and being eaten — producers, then herbivores, carnivores and top carnivores; the network description fits a food web.

mcqs.q: A food web differs from a food chain because it:
options: Shows only one single line of eating and being eaten
Is formed by linear food chains interconnected into a complicated network, giving herbivores many alternate food sources and several possible predators
Contains producers but no consumers at all
Moves energy in a circle back to the producers
mcqs.why: The notes define a food web as linear food chains interconnected to form a complicated network, with alternate food sources for herbivores and several predators, helping maintain balance and nutrient cycling.

mcqs.q: Which contrast between energy flow and nutrient movement is correct?
options: Energy moves in a circle, but nutrients flow in one direction only
Both energy and nutrients are recycled completely in an ecosystem
Nutrients move in a circular path through biogeochemical cycles, but energy cannot be recycled — it flows in one direction only and is finally lost into space as heat
Energy returns to the sun after passing through top carnivores
mcqs.why: The notes state nutrients move in a circular path (e.g. the nitrogen cycle) but energy flows in one direction only, is lost as heat during respiration, and from the last consumer is lost into space, unavailable again.

mcqs.q: Why is the pyramid of energy always broad at the base and narrow towards the apex?
options: Energy increases at each level as consumers grow larger
Producers contain the least energy of any trophic level
Energy is recycled, so every level holds the same amount
Total energy decreases progressively along the food chain — normally about 90% is lost at each transfer as heat, undigested matter and excretory products
mcqs.why: The notes state energy is lost as heat in respiration, through egested undigested matter and excretory products like urea, with about 90% lost at each transfer, so the energy pyramid is always upright and food chains stay short.

mcqs.q: In the book's pyramid of biomass figure, the masses at successive levels are:
options: Producers 1000 Kg, herbivores 100 Kg, primary carnivores 10 Kg and top carnivore 1 Kg
Producers 1 Kg, herbivores 10 Kg, primary carnivores 100 Kg and top carnivore 1000 Kg
Producers 1000 Kg, herbivores 500 Kg, primary carnivores 250 Kg and top carnivore 125 Kg
Every level has exactly 100 Kg of biomass
mcqs.why: Working: each level is one-tenth of the one below — 1000 x 0.1 = 100, 100 x 0.1 = 10, 10 x 0.1 = 1 Kg. The notes' figure shows producers 1000 Kg, herbivores 100 Kg, primary carnivores 10 Kg and top carnivore 1 Kg.

mcqs.q: In the book's pyramid of numbers (grass -> rabbits -> snakes -> hawks), 10 hawks each need one snake per day. How many grass plants are needed in one month?
options: About 270,000 grass plants
About 2,700,000 grass plants
About 90,000 grass plants
About 4,500 grass plants
mcqs.why: Working from the notes: 10 hawks x 30 days = 300 snakes needed in a month; the 300 snakes need 4,500 rabbits in a month; each rabbit needs 20 or more grass plants per day, so 4,500 x 20 x 30 = 2,700,000 grass plants in one month.

lessons.title: Ecological Succession, Xerarch Succession and Characteristics of a Population
lessons.notes_html:
Communities do not stay the same forever. This lesson explains how one community replaces another over time (ecological succession), the step-by-step succession on bare rock (xerarch succession), and the characteristics used to describe a population.

14.17 Ecological Succession

Ecological succession is a process of ecological change in an ecosystem where one community is replaced by another community over time. A new community begins in a new habitat, or in an area disturbed by fire, hurricanes, earthquake, volcanic action or retreating glaciers. Earlier species are replaced by later species because the later species are better able to grow and reproduce under the new environmental conditions. Individual successions are called seres and the developmental phases are called seral stages. The trends in this process include species structure, organic structure, energy flow and environmental conditions. There are two stages: pioneer stage and seral stage.

  • Pioneer stage — The first stage. Migrants of plants and animals from the surrounding areas enter a bare area; these migrants are called pioneers. They gain equilibrium with the climatic conditions, adapt to the new environment and increase their number; they also die due to competition, so their number decreases.
  • Seral stage — Due to the death and decay of pioneers, the organic matter, moisture and nitrogen contents of the soil increase. This enriched soil becomes suitable for new invaders, called seral communities; each community develops one seral stage. The invaders compete with other species and modify the environment by their activities; the changed environment becomes unsuitable for their own growth, so new groups of plants and animals occupy the area.
  • Climax community — After several seral communities, a relatively stable community is set up, e.g., trees in a forest. It is generally believed that once developed it does not change at all, but this is not exactly true: a climax community can be changed by biotic factors, abiotic factors, diseases, aging, floods, storm, lightning, etc.

14.18 Types of Succession

On the basis of origin:

  • Primary succession — A new area of land is populated by organisms for the first time: the start of vegetation on a bare or newly exposed area, such as land exposed by soil erosion or melting of glaciers. Only a few species can grow in such areas; the first entrants are pioneer species or primary invaders. Primary succession modifies the habitat, creating conditions suitable for the growth of other species.
  • Secondary succession — The regrowth of an ecosystem after a disturbance, in areas previously occupied by organisms but disturbed by factors such as fire, grazing, etc.

On the basis of location: Hydrarch — succession which begins in ponds, lakes, marshes or elsewhere in water; its stages are called hydrosere. Xerarch — succession initiated on bare rocks, sand dunes, rocky slopes, etc., where there is extreme deficiency of water; its stages are called xerosere.

14.19 Xerarch Succession

The stages of xerosere, in order, are:

  • Crustose lichen stage — The pioneers are always lichens, e.g., Rindodina, Lecidea, Licarnora, which flourish during short moist periods but withstand long periods of drought. They cause accumulation of some organic matter and dust, providing a base for higher lichens.
  • Foliose lichen stage — Crustose lichens are gradually replaced by foliose lichens such as Parmelia, Umbilicaria, Dermatocarpon. These absorb more and lose less water; more organic matter accumulates, providing a base for mosses.
  • Moss stage — Xerophytic mosses like Polytrichum and Tortula occupy the soil formed by the lichens. They absorb much more water and nutrients owing to their longer rhizoids, and can withstand desiccation. A thick layer of humus forms, capable of supporting herbs and grasses.
  • Herbaceous stage — Annual herbs invade for a few generations, with poor growth. Their dead parts decay and form humus, enriching the soil, and biennial and perennial herbs appear (e.g., lavender, oregano). These plants reduce evaporation and increase temperature, increasing soil moisture. Gradually a soil layer a few inches thick, rich in organic contents, is produced, which can support shrubs.
  • Shrub stage — The soil becomes suitable for xerophytic shrubs, which start from seeds or invade from adjacent areas by rhizomes. The shrubs overshadow the herbs, which cannot compete, so the area is occupied by shrubs, e.g., creosote bush, sage brush.
  • Climax stage or tree stage — Soil conditions become favourable for trees. First xerophytic trees develop (e.g., Acacia, mesquite), widely spaced; they increase in number and spread as the soil deepens. Mesophytic herbs (e.g., rose, lilacs) develop in the humid air and richer soil, and at last mesophytic trees (e.g., oak, maple) develop. When conditions become fully favourable, a forest is formed.

The six stages of xerarch succession on bare rock, from crustose lichens to the climax forest.

14.20 Characteristics of a Population

A population is a group of individuals of a single species living in a specific area at a specific time. Its members rely on the same resources, are influenced by similar environmental factors and have a high likelihood of interacting and breeding with one another. Its characteristics are:

  • Growth — Increase in the number of individuals. If a few individuals enter an unoccupied area with enough food and not too severe diseases, reproduction occurs and the number increases. At first there is a lag phase as individuals settle into the new environment; then the population shows exponential growth, doubling at regular intervals — it grows geometrically.
  • Density — The number of individuals per unit area or volume, e.g., apple trees per square kilometre in Ziarat, or E. coli bacteria per millilitre in a test tube.
  • Distribution — The way a population is spatially distributed across an area, driven largely by food supply or other resources. Three patterns: clumped (individuals aggregate in patches), uniform (evenly spaced) and random (unpredictable spacing).
  • Carrying capacity — The maximum population size that a particular environment can support. Ecosystems cannot exceed it for long; otherwise species will deplete sources of food, water, etc.
  • Viable size — The minimum number of individuals a species needs to survive and continue over time. A smaller population may be at risk and may not survive long. Viable size ensures enough genetic variety, so the population can recover from environmental changes or diseases.

Key Points

  • Succession replaces one community by another: pioneer stage → seral stages → relatively stable climax community.
  • Primary succession starts on bare, newly exposed land; secondary succession is regrowth after disturbance (fire, grazing).
  • Xerarch (xerosere) stages: crustose lichens → foliose lichens → mosses → herbs → shrubs → trees; hydrarch begins in water (hydrosere).
  • Population characteristics: growth (lag phase, then exponential), density, distribution (clumped, uniform, random), carrying capacity and viable size.

mcqs.q: Ecological succession is:
options: The flow of energy from producers to top carnivores
A process of ecological change in an ecosystem where one community is replaced by another community over time
The geographical distribution of species over continents
The maximum population size an environment can support
mcqs.why: The notes define ecological succession as a process of ecological change where one community is replaced by another over time; individual successions are called seres and their phases seral stages.

mcqs.q: In the pioneer stage of succession:
options: A stable forest of trees becomes permanently established
Seral communities enrich the soil with nitrogen and humus
Migrants of plants and animals from surrounding areas, called pioneers, enter a bare area, gain equilibrium with the climate, adapt and increase in number, though some die due to competition
The area is occupied by shrubs overshadowing the herbs
mcqs.why: The notes describe the pioneer stage as the first stage, in which migrants called pioneers enter a bare area, adapt to the new environment and increase in number, while some die due to competition.

mcqs.q: What happens in a seral stage of succession?
options: The first migrants enter a completely bare area for the first time
A fully stable community forms that can never change again
Succession begins in ponds and lakes as a hydrosere

Death and decay of pioneers increase the soil's organic matter, moisture and nitrogen, making it suitable for new invaders (seral communities), which modify the environment until it becomes unsuitable for their own growth and new groups take over
mcqs.why: The notes state that in seral stages the enriched soil from dead pioneers supports seral communities, whose activities modify the environment until it becomes unsuitable for themselves and new groups occupy the area.

mcqs.q: A climax community, such as trees in a forest, is best described as:
options: A relatively stable community set up after several seral communities — but it can still be changed by biotic and abiotic factors, diseases, aging, floods, storm and lightning
A community that, once developed, can never change at all under any circumstances
The very first community to enter a bare area
A community found only in ponds and marshes
mcqs.why: The notes state a climax community is relatively stable, and correct the belief that it never changes: it can be changed by biotic factors, abiotic factors, diseases, aging, floods, storm and lightning.

mcqs.q: Primary succession is:
options: The regrowth of an ecosystem after a disturbance such as fire or grazing
The start of vegetation on a bare or newly exposed area populated for the first time, such as land exposed by soil erosion or melting of glaciers
Succession that begins in ponds, lakes and marshes
Succession that takes place on sand dunes with plenty of water
mcqs.why: The notes define primary succession as a new area populated for the first time — vegetation starting on bare or newly exposed land such as after soil erosion or melting glaciers; regrowth after fire or grazing is secondary succession.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of succession type and starting place is correct?
options: Hydrarch begins on bare rocks and its stages are a xerosere; xerarch begins in ponds and its stages are a hydrosere
Both hydrarch and xerarch begin in water bodies

Hydrarch begins in water — ponds, lakes, marshes — and its stages are a hydrosere; xerarch begins on bare rocks, sand dunes and rocky slopes with extreme deficiency of water, and its stages are a xerosere
Xerarch begins in water because it needs abundant moisture
mcqs.why: The notes classify succession by location: hydrarch begins in water (hydrosere), while xerarch is initiated on bare rocks, sand dunes and rocky slopes where there is extreme deficiency of water (xerosere).

mcqs.q: Which is the correct order of the stages of xerarch succession (xerosere)?
options: Moss stage -> crustose lichens -> foliose lichens -> shrub stage -> herbaceous stage -> trees
Herbaceous stage -> shrub stage -> moss stage -> foliose lichens -> crustose lichens -> trees
Crustose lichens -> moss stage -> shrub stage -> foliose lichens -> herbaceous stage -> trees
Crustose lichens -> foliose lichens -> moss stage -> herbaceous stage -> shrub stage -> climax (tree) stage
mcqs.why: The notes list the xerosere stages in order: crustose lichen stage, foliose lichen stage, moss stage, herbaceous stage, shrub stage, and finally the climax or tree stage forming a forest.

mcqs.q: During a population's growth in a new area, the notes describe the pattern as:
options: First a lag phase as individuals settle into the new environment, then exponential growth — doubling at regular intervals, growing geometrically
Immediate exponential growth with no settling period at all
Steady decline because food is always insufficient
Growth that stops permanently at the lag phase
mcqs.why: The notes state that after a few individuals enter an unoccupied area with enough food, there is first a lag phase as they settle, then the population shows exponential growth, doubling at regular intervals — growing geometrically.

mcqs.q: Which set lists the three distribution patterns of a population given in the notes?
options: Pioneer, seral and climax distributions
Clumped (individuals aggregate in patches), uniform (evenly spaced) and random (unpredictable spacing)
Primary, secondary and tertiary distributions
Hydrarch, xerarch and mesarch distributions
mcqs.why: The notes state distribution — the way a population is spatially spread, driven largely by food supply — has three patterns: clumped, uniform and random.

mcqs.q: Carrying capacity and viable size are correctly distinguished as:
options: Carrying capacity is the minimum number needed to survive; viable size is the maximum the environment can support
Both terms mean the number of individuals per unit area
Carrying capacity is the maximum population size a particular environment can support; viable size is the minimum number of individuals a species needs to survive and continue over time
Carrying capacity applies only to plants and viable size only to animals
mcqs.why: The notes define carrying capacity as the maximum population an environment can support, and viable size as the minimum number needed to survive, which ensures enough genetic variety to recover from environmental changes or diseases.

lessons.title: Human Impacts, Important Ecosystems of Pakistan and Conservation
lessons.notes_html:
Human beings once lived simple lives requiring few environmental resources, but as human population increased, resources began falling short and human activities brought undesirable changes in the environment. This lesson covers human impacts, the four important ecosystems of Pakistan, and how environmental resources are monitored and conserved.

14.21 Human Impacts on an Ecosystem

Human activity has been affecting the environment for thousands of years. Population growth leads to the loss of natural habitat. Deforestation causes loss of species of fauna and flora, and loss of oxygen production and carbon dioxide elimination. Ozone layer depletion, water pollution, global warming, desertification and increased erosion of land are directly caused by human activities such as the use of nuclear fuel, industrialization, urbanization, transportation, etc.

14.22 Important Ecosystems of Pakistan

Pakistan has a diverse range of ecosystems due to its wide-ranging geography, topography and climate, from high mountains to coastal areas. Each has its own specific characteristics, temperature, plants and animals:

EcosystemLocation and climateVegetationAnimal life
1. Coniferous alpine and boreal forestsNorthern mountainous areas of Hindukush, Himalayas and Karakoram, at 1000–4000 m: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Chitral, Swat, Dir, Malakand, Mansehra, Abbottabad), Azad Kashmir, and also Balochistan. Average temperature may be as low as 10°C; long winters below freezing point; precipitation moderate to high, rain in summer, snow in winter.Cone-bearing, needle-leaved evergreen trees: blue pine, chir pine, fir, spruce, deodar; chilghoza pine and juniper most common in Balochistan. Little vegetation on the forest floor: shrubs like willow and dogwoods, herbaceous plants like buttercup.Snow leopard, red fox, brown bear; golden eagle, griffon vultures; squirrel and crossbills. Decomposers are bacteria, but decomposition is slow due to snow and low temperature, so nutrients are not properly available in the soil and productivity is low.
2. Temperate deciduous forestsNorthern regions: Himalayan and sub-Himalayan foothills at 1500–3000 m — Neelam Valley (Azad Kashmir), Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (Shangla, Swat, Kaghan, Shogran valley). Temperature 4°C–30°C, average yearly about 10°C; moderate rainfall, rain in summer, snow and hailstorms in winter.Mixed forests, rich in biodiversity: some trees evergreen, some shed broad leaves in autumn — pine, deodar, oak, ash, walnut, maple; also shrubs, ferns, herbaceous plants, mosses, lichens.Snail, millipedes, butterflies; lizards, snakes; owl, hawks, pheasants; brown bear, snow leopard, deer, monkeys. Bacteria and fungi decompose dead plants and animals quickly (favourable humidity and moderate temperature), so the soil is very fertile — a major cause of the rich biodiversity.
3. Grassland ecosystemOpen flat areas dominated by grasses and herbaceous plants with few trees. Temperate: northern mountain ranges (lower Chitral, Gilgit, Kashmir, Waziristan), summer 25°C–35°C, winter below 0°C, rainfall 150–500 mm. Tropical and sub-tropical: Potohar plateau, Salt Range (Punjab) and Balochistan, summer often above 40°C, winter 10°C–20°C, rainfall 200–400 mm. Arid and semi-arid: large parts of Sindh, southern Punjab, western Balochistan, summer above 45°C, winter below 0°C, rainfall less than 200–250 mm.Grasses from tall species (150–250 cm) to short species (not exceeding 15 cm): velvet grass, spear grass, buffel grass, marvel grass, silky bushma grass. Woody plants generally absent due to low rainfall.Herbivore mammals (wild goat, gazelles, antelopes, deer), burrowing mammals (rabbits, lizards), predators (wolves, jackals, foxes), birds (parrots, hawks, taloor). Bacteria and fungi decompose dead bodies, so the soil is rich in humus. Productivity: moderate to high in tropical grasslands, less in temperate, least in arid grasslands.
4. Desert ecosystemVery dry, barren land with very low or very high temperature and less, widely spaced vegetation. Warm deserts: Thal in western Punjab (Mianwali, Bhakkar); Cholistan in southern Punjab (Fort Abbas, Bahawalnagar, Yazman, Bahawalpur, Khanpur, Rahim Yar Khan); Thar in Sindh; Kharan in Balochistan. Cold desert: Katpana in Gilgit-Baltistan. Warm: summer exceeds 40°C, sometimes 50°C, winter may fall below 10°C, rainfall 100–250 mm, unreliable and dependent on the monsoon. Cold: summer 24–27°C, winter from -17°C to -25°C, rainfall less than 250 mm, snowfall common in winter. Strong winds cause damage to plants.Plants adapted to get and conserve water: Acacia, prickly pear, palms, cacti, many grasses, Euphorbia.Wild cats, jackals, desert foxes; lizards, uromastix, snakes; falcons, hoopoes, weavers, teloor, desert finch, swifts; camel, caracal, blackbuck, goitered gazelle; ants, beetles, scorpion.

Adaptations of Organisms for Desert Life

  • Plants — Some have deep roots to absorb water from deeper layers of the soil; some have shallow roots and absorb water quickly before it evaporates. Opuntia stores water in leaves covered by cuticle or cutin; cacti and Euphorbia store water in fleshy stems. Stomata of many desert plants are sunk into pits to reduce water loss, and leaves of some plants are modified into spines.
  • Animals — Many do not drink water and depend on water in their succulent food, like cactus plants; some store water in their bodies. Desert animals lack sweat glands, reducing water loss. Many are nocturnal (active at night, e.g., reptiles), escaping the heat of the day. Many live in burrows, where humidity is higher and temperature lower than outside (e.g., rodents, reptiles). Some excrete concentrated urine to reduce water loss.

14.23 Methods Used to Monitor and Conserve Environmental Resources

To maintain biodiversity, ecosystems and overall global ecological health, it is extremely important to monitor and conserve environmental resources (habitat, restoration, conservation). The book's methods:

  • Launch tree plantation campaigns twice a year, involving students and common people, who should care for their planted trees until they are well set in the soil.
  • Stop illegal cutting of forest, which is fatal for the forest ecosystem.
  • Use camera traps and drones to monitor forest condition.
  • Raise awareness in local communities about degradation of the environment and the importance of wildlife and forests.
  • Replant native vegetation and trees in areas that have become barren, e.g., deforested areas in Pakistan like Bunair in KPK.
  • Discourage overgrazing, because it makes the land barren.
  • Use soil erosion control techniques, as soil erosion disturbs plants and animals in an ecosystem.
  • Make long-term plans to restore degraded grasslands, deforested areas, wetlands, etc.
  • Check overfishing, especially in the breeding season.
  • Create and effectively manage protected areas like National Parks, wildlife sanctuaries and marine protected areas.
  • Enforce environmental protection laws and biodiversity action plans.
  • Strengthen laws to protect endangered species, aiming at improvement of habitats, not only at the killing of game animals.
  • Reduce pollution and wastes, especially plastics and chemicals.

Key Points

  • Human impacts: habitat loss, deforestation, ozone depletion, water pollution, global warming, desertification and erosion.
  • Pakistan's four major ecosystems: coniferous alpine and boreal forests, temperate deciduous forests, grassland and desert.
  • Desert plants conserve water (deep or shallow roots, fleshy stems, sunken stomata, spiny leaves); desert animals are often nocturnal, live in burrows, lack sweat glands and excrete concentrated urine.
  • Conservation: tree plantation twice a year, stop illegal cutting, camera traps and drones, protected areas, control of overgrazing and overfishing, and enforced environmental laws.

mcqs.q: Which human impact is correctly matched with its consequence in the notes?
options: Deforestation increases oxygen production and carbon dioxide elimination
Population growth creates new natural habitat for species
Deforestation causes loss of species of fauna and flora, and loss of oxygen production and carbon dioxide elimination
Industrialization has removed desertification and land erosion
mcqs.why: The notes state population growth leads to loss of natural habitat, and deforestation causes loss of fauna and flora species plus loss of oxygen production and CO2 elimination; ozone depletion, water pollution, global warming, desertification and erosion are also human-caused.

mcqs.q: Pakistan's coniferous alpine and boreal forests are found:
options: In the warm deserts of Thal, Cholistan and Thar below 250 m
In the Potohar plateau and Salt Range, dominated by grasses
Only along the coastline, in mangrove swamps
In northern mountainous areas of the Hindukush, Himalayas and Karakoram at 1000-4000 m, with cone-bearing needle-leaved evergreens such as blue pine, chir pine, fir, spruce and deodar
mcqs.why: The notes place coniferous alpine and boreal forests in the northern mountains (Hindukush, Himalayas, Karakoram) at 1000-4000 m, with needle-leaved evergreens like blue pine, chir pine, fir, spruce and deodar; chilghoza pine and juniper are most common in Balochistan.

mcqs.q: Why is productivity low in the coniferous alpine forests, according to the notes?
options: Decomposers are bacteria, but decomposition is slow due to snow and low temperature, so nutrients are not properly available in the soil
Decomposition is very fast, which removes all nutrients quickly
There are no decomposers of any kind in these forests
Rainfall is less than 200 mm, so no plants can grow
mcqs.why: The notes state that in coniferous forests decomposition is slow due to snow and low temperature, so nutrients are not properly available in the soil and productivity is low — the opposite of the fertile temperate deciduous forests.

mcqs.q: Why is the soil of temperate deciduous forests very fertile, supporting rich biodiversity?
options: Snow and low temperature slow decomposition all year round
Bacteria and fungi decompose dead plants and animals quickly because of favourable humidity and moderate temperature
Grasses dominate and woody plants are absent
Rainfall is under 200 mm, concentrating nutrients in the soil
mcqs.why: The notes state that in temperate deciduous forests (1500-3000 m, 4°C-30°C) bacteria and fungi decompose dead matter quickly under favourable humidity and moderate temperature, making the soil very fertile — a major cause of the rich biodiversity.

mcqs.q: Which grassland rainfall pairing matches the notes?
options: Temperate: less than 200 mm; tropical: 150-500 mm; arid: 400-500 mm
All three types receive 100-250 mm of rainfall
Temperate grasslands: 150-500 mm; tropical and sub-tropical: 200-400 mm; arid and semi-arid: less than 200-250 mm
Arid grasslands receive the highest rainfall, 500 mm or more
mcqs.why: The notes give temperate grassland rainfall as 150-500 mm, tropical and sub-tropical as 200-400 mm, and arid and semi-arid as less than 200-250 mm, with productivity moderate to high in tropical, less in temperate and least in arid grasslands.

mcqs.q: Which desert pairing is correct according to the notes?
options: The cold desert is Thar in Sindh; warm deserts include Katpana
Warm deserts receive 500 mm of reliable monsoon rain yearly
Kharan is a cold desert with winter temperatures of -25°C
Warm deserts include Thal, Cholistan, Thar and Kharan; the cold desert is Katpana in Gilgit-Baltistan, with winter temperatures from -17°C to -25°C
mcqs.why: The notes list warm deserts Thal (western Punjab), Cholistan (southern Punjab), Thar (Sindh) and Kharan (Balochistan), and the cold desert Katpana in Gilgit-Baltistan, where winter falls from -17°C to -25°C.

mcqs.q: Which plant adaptation to desert life is correctly stated?
options: Cacti and Euphorbia store water in fleshy stems, stomata of many desert plants are sunk into pits to reduce water loss, and leaves of some plants are modified into spines
Desert plants keep large thin leaves to lose water quickly
Opuntia stores water only in its roots, never in its leaves
Desert plants have stomata raised on stalks to increase evaporation
mcqs.why: The notes list desert plant adaptations: deep or shallow quick-absorbing roots, Opuntia storing water in cuticle-covered leaves, cacti and Euphorbia storing water in fleshy stems, sunken stomata and leaves modified into spines.

mcqs.q: Which set of animal adaptations to desert life matches the notes?
options: Most are active at midday, sweat freely and excrete very dilute urine
Many are nocturnal, live in burrows where humidity is higher and temperature lower, lack sweat glands, and some excrete concentrated urine to reduce water loss
All desert animals must drink water several times daily
They avoid burrows because burrows are hotter than the surface
mcqs.why: The notes state desert animals may depend on water in succulent food or store water, lack sweat glands, are often nocturnal, live in burrows with higher humidity and lower temperature, and some excrete concentrated urine.

mcqs.q: Which conservation method from the notes involves local people and students directly?
options: Planting trees once every ten years with no follow-up care
Using camera traps and drones to count planted trees only
Launching tree plantation campaigns twice a year, involving students and common people, who should care for their planted trees until they are well set in the soil
Allowing illegal cutting so that new trees can be planted
mcqs.why: The notes list as the first monitoring and conservation method launching tree plantation campaigns twice a year involving students and common people, who care for their trees until well set in the soil; camera traps and drones are a separate monitoring method.

mcqs.q: Which measure protects wildlife populations and breeding, according to the notes?
options: Encouraging overgrazing so grasslands stay short and open
Weakening laws so endangered species can be hunted freely
Removing protected areas so land can be used without rules
Checking overfishing, especially in the breeding season, and creating and effectively managing protected areas like National Parks, wildlife sanctuaries and marine protected areas
mcqs.why: The notes list checking overfishing especially in the breeding season, discouraging overgrazing, and creating and managing protected areas — National Parks, wildlife sanctuaries and marine protected areas — with enforced environmental laws.
